He said: and so I saw it in the codex of ʿAbdullāh: "فجزاؤه" with the hāʾ. And whoever puts (مثل) in the accusative means: then it is upon him to recompense the like of what he killed of livestock.
﴿فإن فاءوا﴾ — it is said: fāʾū yafīʾūna fayʾan and fuyūʾan. Al-fayʾ is that he returns to his wife and has intercourse.

farraa:228-228.t: His saying: ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is "بردتهن".

farraa:1-2.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿الۤمۤ ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ﴾. The spelled-out letters (al-hijāʾ) are pausal throughout the Qur'an. This is not a jazm (jussive) that can properly be called jazm; it is only speech made quiescent by the intention of pausing on each of its letters. So treat all the spelled-out letters this way, whether few or many. The readers read "آلمَ اللهُ" in "Āl ʿImrān", giving the mīm a fatḥa, only because the mīm was quiescent through the intention of pausing on it; and when a letter is intended to be paused on, what follows it is intended as a fresh start, so the reading was "ا ل مَ اللهُ": the Arabs dropped the hamza of the alif of "الله", and its fatḥa passed to the mīm because the mīm was quiescent. Had the mīm been quiescent in a way that truly required quiescence, it would have been given a kasra, as in "قِيل ادخلِ الجنة". One of the grammarians — Abū Jaʿfar al-Ruʾāsī, who was a righteous man — read it ﴿الۤمۤ أَلله﴾, cutting off the alif [Translator's note: i.e. pronouncing the hamza], whereas the [Translator's note: accepted] reading drops the hamza. Al-Farrāʾ said: It has reached me that ʿĀṣim read it with the hamza cut off.

When the spelled-out letters come at the beginning of a surah and consist of a single letter, as in His words "ص", "ن" and "ق", there are two ways in Arabic. If you intend them as spelled-out letters, you leave them quiescent and write them as a single letter. If you make them a name for the surah, or treat them as an oath, you write them as they are spelled out — "نون", "صاد" and "قاف" — and give kasra to the dāl of صاد and the fāʾ of قاف, and fatḥa to the final nūn of "نون", saying: "نونَ والقلم", "صادِ والقرآن" and "قافِ", because it has become like a particle (adāt), just as they said رجلانِ, giving kasra to the nūn of رجلانِ because an alif precedes it, and fatḥa to the nūn in "المسلمونَ" and "المسلمينَ" because a yāʾ and a wāw precede it.

Do the same with "ياسينَْ والقرآن": you may give the nūn of "ياسين" a fatḥa or leave it quiescent.

Likewise "حم" and "طس". But this is not permissible in anything longer than these letters, such as "طا سين ميم", because they do not resemble nouns, while "طس" resembles قابيل (Qābīl). Nor is this permissible in anything of the Qur'an such as "الم", "المر" and the like.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿ذَلِكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ﴾. (ذَلِكَ) is appropriate here in two respects, and "هذا" would be appropriate in one respect. One of the two respects of "ذلك" is the meaning: These letters, O Aḥmad, are that Book which I promised you I would reveal to you. The other is that "ذلك" has a meaning in which "هذا" would also be appropriate, because "هذا" and "ذلك" are both appropriate in any speech where something is mentioned and you then follow it with one of them to report about it. Do you not see that you say: "So-and-so has arrived", and the listener says: "That has reached us" or "That news has reached us"? "هذا" is appropriate there because the thing is close to his answer, so it is like something present to which you point; and "ذلك" is appropriate because it has ended, and what has ended is like something absent. But if it were something standing there and visible, "هذا" would not be permissible in place of "ذلك", nor "ذلك" in place of "هذا". Allah, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ﴾ up to His words ﴿وَكُلُّ مِنَ الأَخْيَارِ﴾, then He said: ﴿هَذَا ذِكْرٌ﴾.

And He, Majestic and Mighty is He, said in another place: ﴿وَعِنْدَهُمْ قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ أَتْرَابٌ﴾, then He said: ﴿هَذَا مَا تُوعَدُونَ لِيوْمِ الْحِسَابِ﴾. And He, Majestic is His mention, said: ﴿وَجَاءَتْ سَكْرَةُ الْمَوْتِ بِالْحَقِّ﴾, then He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ مَا كُنْتَ مِنْهُ تَحِيد﴾. Had "هذا" been said in such speech in place of "ذلك", or "ذلك" in place of "هذا", it would have been correct.

In the reading of ʿAbdallāh ibn Masʿūd it is "هَذَا فَذُوقُوهُ", and in our reading "ذَلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ".

As for where "هذا" is not permissible in place of "ذلك", nor "ذلك" in place of "هذا": if you saw two men, one of whom you did not know, you would say to the one you know: مَن هذا الذى معك؟ (who is this with you?); and here مَن ذلك؟ (who is that?) is not permissible, because you see him with your own eyes.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿هُدىً لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾, it is nominative in two ways and accusative in two ways. If you intend «الكتاب» to be a naʿt (adjective) of "ذلك", then «الهدى» is in the position of the nominative because it is the khabar (predicate) of "ذلك", as though you had said: ذلك هُدًى لا شكّ فيه (that is guidance in which there is no doubt). And if you make ﴿لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ its khabar, you also put ﴿هُدىً﴾ in the nominative, making it follow the position of "لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ", as Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿وَهَذَا كِتَابٌ أَنْزَلْنَاهُ مُبَارَكٌ﴾, as though He said: This is a Book, and this is blessed, and this is of such-and-such a description. There is a third way of the nominative: if you wish, you put it in the nominative as a fresh start (istiʾnāf), since what precedes it is complete, just as the readers read "الم. تِلْكَ آيَاتُ الْكِتَابِ الْحَكيم. هُدًى وَرَحْمَةٌ لِلْمُحْسِنينَ" in the nominative and the accusative; and like His words in the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbdallāh: ﴿أَأَلِدُ وأَنَا عَجُوزٌ وَهَذَا بَعْلِى شَيْخٌ﴾, which in our reading is "شَيْخاً".

As for the accusative, one of its two ways is that you make «الكتاب» the khabar of "ذلك" and put "هُدًى" in the accusative by qaṭʿ (detachment) [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's Kufan term, corresponding to ḥāl (circumstantial)], because "هُدًى" is an indefinite joined to a definite whose khabar is already complete, so you put it in the accusative, since an indefinite cannot serve as a descriptor of a definite. And if you wish, you put "هُدىً" in the accusative by qaṭʿ from the hāʾ in "فيه", as though you had said: لا شك فيه هاديا (there is no doubt in it, as guidance).

Know that when "هذا" is followed by a noun bearing alif and lām, it runs on three meanings. The first: you see the noun after "هذا" just as you see "هذا" [Translator's note: i.e. it is present before you], and then its predicate (fiʿl) [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ uses «فعل» here for the predicate/complement] is nominative, as in your saying: هذا الحمار فارهٌ (this donkey is sprightly): you made «الحمار» an adjective of «هذا» since both are present, and the accusative is not permissible here. The second: what follows "هذا" is a single item standing for its whole genus, and then the predicate is accusative, as in your saying: ماكان من السباع غير مخوف فهذا الأسد مخوفا (whatever beasts of prey are not feared, this — the lion — is feared): do you not see that you are reporting fearsomeness of all lions? The third meaning: what follows "هذا" is a single thing that has no peer, and then too the predicate is accusative. You put the predicate in the accusative only because "هذا" is not an adjective qualifying «الأسد»; it is introduced only as taqrīb [Translator's note: a Kufan term for this use of the demonstrative, which functions like kāna], and the statement would be better without "هذا": do you not see that if you said: ما لا يضرّ من السباع فالأسد ضارّ (whatever beasts of prey do no harm, the lion does harm), it would be clearer? As for the meaning of taqrīb: "this is the first thing I tell you about"; they could not avoid putting «هذا» in the nominative by means of "الأسد" [Translator's note: in the Kufan view of mutual government (al-murāfaʿa), subject and predicate raise each other], while its khabar is still awaited; and when «الأسد» was occupied with the mutual government with "هذا", its predicate, which it used to govern in the nominative, was put in the accusative because it was left free. The like is "والله غفور رحيم": if you introduce "كان" into it, [Translator's note: the subject] becomes nominative through it, and the khabar that completes the speech is still awaited, so you put it in the accusative because it is left free. As for their putting in the accusative the predicate of a single thing that has no peer, as when you say: هذه الشمس ضياءً للعباد (this — the sun — is a light for the servants) and هذا القمر نوراً (this — the moon — is a radiance): the moon is a single thing that has no peer, so it too has no need of your saying "هذا"; do you not see that when you say: طلع القمر (the moon has risen), the mind does not go to some absent thing so that you need to say "هذا" to show that it is present? So it was put in the nominative by «هذا» and was not an adjective, and you put its khabar in the accusative because of the need for it.

farraa:7-7.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ وَعَلَىٰ أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾. The meaning of the sealing ends at His words ﴿وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ﴾. "الغشاوة" was put in the nominative by "على"; had you put it in the accusative by implying "وجعل" (and He placed), it would have been correct. Al-Mufaḍḍal claimed that ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd used to read it in the accusative, after the pattern of His words in al-Jāthiya: ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتَ مَنِ اتَّخذَ إِلهَهُ هَوَاهُ وأَضَلَّهُ اللَّهُ عَلَى عِلْمٍ وَخَتَمَ عَلَى سَمْعِهِ وقلْبِهِ وجَعَلَ عَلَى بَصَرِهِ غِشَاوةً﴾; and the meaning of the two is one — and Allah knows best. Implication (iḍmār) is good only in speech whose parts belong together and whose beginning points to its end, as in your saying: قد أصاب فلان المال، فبنى الدورَ والعبيدَ والإماءَ واللباسَ الحسن (so-and-so came into wealth, and built houses, and slaves, and slave-girls, and fine clothing): you see that building does not apply to slaves and slave-girls, nor to riding animals, nor to clothes; but they are all among the marks of affluence, so the implication was good since it was understood. Similar to it in Sūrat al-Wāqiʿa: ﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدَانٌ مُخَلَّدُنَ. بِأَكْوَابٍ وَأَبَارِيقَ وَكَأْسٍ مِنْ مَعِينٍ﴾, then He said: ﴿وَفَاكِهَةٍ مِمَّا يَتَخَيَّرونَ. ولَحْمِ طَيْرٍ مِمّا يَشْتَهُونَ. وحُورٍ عِينٍ﴾: some readers read الحور العين in the genitive and some in the nominative.

Those who read it in the nominative said: The ḥūr ʿīn are not carried around; so they read it in the nominative with the meaning: "and with them are ḥūr ʿīn", or "and along with that, ḥūr ʿīn". Then it was said [Translator's note: in reply]: Fruit and meat are not carried around either; only wine is carried around — and Allah knows best — yet the end of the speech was made to follow its beginning. This is frequent in the speech of the Arabs and their poetry. Someone of the Banū Asad recited to me, describing his mare:
عَلَفْتُهَا تِبْناً وماءً بارداً * حتى شَتَتْ هَمَّالةً عَيْنَاهَا
(I fed her straw and cool water, until she wintered with her eyes streaming.) [Translator's note: water is not "fed"; the verb for "giving to drink" is implied — the point of the citation.]
And the Book is more eloquent Arabic and stronger as proof than poetry. As for where the implied element is not good because the parts rarely belong together, it is your saying: قد أعتقت مبارَكا أمس وآخرَ اليوم ياهذا (I freed Mubārak yesterday, and another one today, you there), when you mean: "and I bought another one today"; because these are different and it is not known that you meant "I bought". Nor may you say: ضربت فلانا وفلانا (I struck so-and-so and so-and-so), meaning by the second "and I killed so-and-so", because there is no indication here.

In these two ways there is that by which you can recognise whatever comes before you, if Allah wills.

farraa:16-16.t: His words: ﴿فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِّجَارَتُهُمْ﴾. Someone might say: How can trade profit, when it is only the man, the trader, who profits? That is part of the speech of the Arabs: ربح بَيْعُك وخسر بيعُك (your sale has profited, your sale has lost); saying so is good because profit and loss occur only in trade, so its meaning is known. Similar to it in the speech of the Arabs: هذا ليل نائم (this is a sleeping night). And similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿فَإذَا عَزَمَ اْلأَمْرُ﴾, though resolve belongs only to men. Such implication is permissible only in the like of this. If someone said: قد خسر عبدك (your slave has lost), it would not be permissible, (if you) mean to make the slave a piece of merchandise on which profit or loss is made; because the slave may himself be a trader who profits or loses, so the meaning when he himself profits cannot be told apart from the meaning when he is the thing traded in. But if someone said: قد ربحتْ دراهمُك ودنانيرُك، وخسر بَزُّك ورقيقك (your dirhams and dinars have profited, and your cloth and your slaves have lost), it would be permissible, because each part points to the other.

farraa:17-17.t:
His words: ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي ٱسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾. The parable was struck — and Allah knows best — for the action, not for the persons of the men; it is only a parable of hypocrisy. So He said: "their likeness is as the likeness of the one who kindled a fire", and did not say: "those who kindled". It is as Allah said: ﴿تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهْم كالَّذِى يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْْتِ﴾, and His words: ﴿مَاخَلْقُكُمْ وَلاَ بَعْثُكُمْ إِلاَّ كَنَفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ﴾, whose meaning — and Allah knows best — is: except like the raising of a single soul. Had the comparison been to the men themselves, it would have been plural, as He said: ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ خُشُبٌ مُسَنَّدَةٌ﴾, meaning their statures and bodies; and He said: ﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍ﴾: it was plural when He meant to compare the persons of the men. So run the speech on this basis. If you come across, in poetry, a comparison of a plural of men made singular, allow it; and if you come across, in poetry, a comparison of a single person made plural, the action is likewise intended, so allow it — as when you say: ما فِعْلك إلا كفعل الحَمِير (your doing is nothing but like the doing of donkeys) and ما أفعالكم إلا كفعل الذِّئب (your doings are nothing but like the doing of the wolf). Build on this; then you drop «فعل» and say: ما فعلك إلأا كالحَمِير وكالذِّئب (your doing is nothing but like donkeys, like the wolf).

Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said ﴿ذَهَبَ ٱللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْْ﴾ only because the meaning turned to the hypocrites, so He used the plural for that reason. Had it been singular, it would have been correct, like His words: ﴿إنّ شَجَرَةَ الزَّقُّومِ. طَعامُ الأَثِيمِ. كالْمُهْلِ تغْلِى فى الْبُطُونِ﴾ and "يَغْلِى": whoever uses the feminine refers to the tree, and whoever uses the masculine refers to «المهل» (the molten metal). Similar to it are His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أَمَنَةً نُعَاساً تَغْشَى طَائِفَةً منْكُمْ﴾ — [Translator's note: with tāʾ] referring to «الأمنة» (security), and "ويَغْشَى" [Translator's note: with yāʾ] referring to «النعاس» (slumber).

farraa:18-18.t:
His words: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لاَ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾. They are nominative although the nouns they refer to at the beginning of the speech are accusative, because the speech was complete and a verse ended with it; then ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ was begun afresh in another verse, which made the fresh start (istiʾnāf) stronger. Had the speech been complete without being the end of a verse, the fresh start would also have been permissible. Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿جَزَاءً مِنْ رَبِّكَ عَطَاءً حِسَاباً. رَبُّ السَّمَوات وَالأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا الرَّحْمَنُِ﴾: "الرحمن" is read nominative and genitive in its i'rab, and what precedes it is not the end of a verse. As for fresh starts at the heads of verses, they are many; among them the word of Allah: ﴿إنَّ اللهَ اشْتَرَى مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ﴾ up to His words ﴿وَذَلِكَ هُوَ الْفَوْزُ الْعَظِيمُ﴾; then He, Majestic is His countenance, said: ﴿التَّائِبُونَ الْعَابِدُونَ الْحامِدُونَ﴾, in the nominative in our reading, while in the version (ḥarf) of Ibn Masʿūd it is "التائِبِين العابِدِين الحامِدِين". And He said: ﴿أَتَدْعُونَ بَعْلاً وَتَذَرُونَ أَحْسَنَ الْخَالِقِينَ.اللهُ رَبُّكُمْ﴾, which is read in the nominative and the accusative, as I have explained to you. In the reading of ʿAbdallāh: "صُمّاً بُكْماً عُمْياً", in the accusative.

Its accusative can be explained in two ways: if you wish, with the meaning "He left them deaf, dumb and blind"; and if you wish, you let «الترك» (leaving) fall on them [Translator's note: only] "in darkness", and then begin "صُمّاً" afresh as a censure of them.

The Arabs put words in the accusative for censure and for praise, because with such nouns there is something like the meaning of their sayings: وَيْلاً له (woe to him), وثَوَاباً له (reward to him), and بُعْداً (away!), سَقْياً (watering!), رَعْياً (care!).

farraa:19-19.t:
His words: ﴿أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾ refer back to His words: ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾. ﴿أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ﴾ means: or like the likeness of a downpour. The mention of ﴿الَّذِى اسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾ made it unnecessary, so the nouns that ought to have accompanied «الصيّب» were dropped, and the meaning points to them, because the parable was struck for hypocrisy. So He said: ﴿فِيهِ ظُلُمَاتٌ وَرَعْدٌ وَبَرْقٌٌ﴾: He likened the darkness to their unbelief, the lightning — when it lights up for them and they walk in it — to their faith, and the thunder to the threats that come in the Qur'an. Another view has been given about it: it was said that the thunder was mentioned only as a parable for their fear of fighting when they are called to it. Do you not see that He said in another place: ﴿يَحْسَبونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, i.e. they think they will always be defeated?

Then He said: ﴿يَجْعَلُونَ أَصَابِعَهُمْ فِيۤ آذَانِهِم مِّنَ ٱلصَّوَاعِقِ حَذَرَ ٱلْمَوْتِ﴾. He put "حَذَرَ" in the accusative without the verb falling on it [Translator's note: as its object]: He does not mean "they make them [Translator's note: their fingers] a caution"; it is only like your saying: أعطيتك خَوْفاً وفَرَقاً (I gave to you out of fear and dread): you do not give him fear; you give to him because of fear. So it is put in the accusative as tafsīr [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term here for what is later called mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose)], not by the verb, as in His words, Majestic and Mighty is He: ﴿يَدْعُونَنَا رَغَباً وَرَهَباً﴾, and His words: ﴿ادْعُوا رَبَّكُمْ تَضَرُّعاً وَخُفْيَةً﴾. Both definite and indefinite nouns serve as tafsīr in this position, and its accusative is not due to the dropping of "مِن". This is something from which the beginner can draw guidance for learning.

farraa:124-124.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذِ ٱبْتَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِمَاتٍ﴾ — it is said: He commanded him with ten practices of the Sunna, five in the head and five in the body. Those in the head are: parting the hair, trimming the moustache, rinsing the nose, rinsing the mouth and the tooth-stick (siwāk).
Those in the body are: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, clipping the nails, and plucking the rufghayn, meaning the armpits. Al-Farrāʾ said: * and the singular is called rufgh * — and cleansing after relieving oneself (istinjāʾ).
﴿فَأَتَمَّهُنَّ﴾: he acted upon them. So Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿إِنِّي جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَاماً﴾: your guidance will be followed and your practice taken as a model. So he said: "My Lord, ﴿وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِي﴾", by way of request.
His saying: ﴿لاَ يَنَالُ عَهْدِي ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾ — He says: the Muslims will not have a polytheist leader. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمُونَ". This is explained by the fact that whatever reaches you, you have reached it, as you say: "I attained your good" and "your good reached me".

farraa:125-125.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ جَعَلْنَا ٱلْبَيْتَ مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ﴾ — they return (yathūbūn) to it — from al-mathāba and al-mathāb; He meant: from every place. Al-mathāba in the speech of the Arabs is like the singular [form without tāʾ], like al-maqām and al-maqāma.
His saying: ﴿وَأَمْناً﴾ — it is said that whoever commits a crime or incurs a ḥadd (prescribed punishment) and then takes refuge in the Sanctuary, his ḥadd is not carried out on him until he leaves the Sanctuary; and it is ordered that he not be mixed with or traded with, and that he be pressed (until he leaves) so that the ḥadd may be carried out on him; that is his security. Whoever of the people of the Sanctuary commits a crime or incurs a ḥadd, it is carried out on him in the Sanctuary.
His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّخِذُواْ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ مُصَلًّى﴾ — the Readers have read it in the sense of the jussive [i.e. as an imperative] [and the exegesis is with those who read the jussive]. Whoever reads "واتَّخَذوا" with fatḥa on the khāʾ makes it a statement; He says: We made it a place of return for them, and they took it as a place of prayer. All is correct, if Allah wills.
His saying: ﴿أَن طَهِّرَا بَيْتِيَ﴾ — He means: from the idols, that they not be hung in it.
His saying: ﴿لِلطَّائِفِينَ وَٱلْعَاكِفِينَ﴾ means its people, ﴿والرُّكَّعِ السُّجُودِ﴾ means the people of Islam.

farraa:126-126.t: His saying: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ is from the speech of Allah, blessed and exalted; ﴿فَأُمَتِّعُهُ﴾ is a statement. In the reading of Ubayy: "وَمنْ كَفَرَ فَنُمَتِّعُه قَلِيلاً ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُ إلى عذابِ النارِ" (this is one view). Ibn ʿAbbās used to make it connected to the request of Ibrāhīm, Allah bless him, in the sense: "My Lord, and whoever disbelieves, give him enjoyment (fa-amtiʿhu) a little, then compel him (iḍṭarrahu)" (accusative [i.e. with fatḥa], connected). He means "then iḍṭarir-hu"; when you drop the unfolding of the doubled letter you give it fatḥa; and in this approach the kasra on the rāʾ is permissible in the dialect of those who say "muddihi". Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read: "فَإِمْتِعُه قلِيلا ثم إضطَرُّة" with kasra on the alif, as you say "أَنا إعلَم ذلك" (I know that).

farraa:127-127.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ﴾ — it is said they are the foundations of the House. Its singular is qāʿida; and of women who have ceased menstruating, [one says] qāʿid, without the hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa]. A man's wife is called his qaʿīda.
His saying: ﴿رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ﴾ — He means: the two of them say, "Our Lord". In the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is "ويقولانِ ربنا".

farraa:128-128.t: His saying: ﴿وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "وأَرِهِم مناسِكهم", referring to the offspring. In "وأرِنا" he joined them to himself, so they became like those speaking for themselves. What shows you this is His saying ﴿وابعث فيهم رسولا﴾: He returned to the offspring specifically.

farraa:130-130.t: His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ — the Arabs make "سفِه" act upon (نَفْسه) although it is definite. Likewise His saying ﴿بِطرت معِيشتها﴾; it is a definite noun functioning like an indefinite, because it is an explanatory element (mufassir, i.e. tamyīz), and the explanatory element in most speech is indefinite, as in your saying "ḍiqtu bihi dharʿan" (I was at a loss with it, lit. narrow in reach), and His saying ﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَنْ شَىءٍ مِّنْهُ نَفْساً﴾. The verb belongs to "dharʿ", because you say "ḍāqa dharʿī bihi"; when you made the narrowness attributed to yourself and said "ḍiqtu", "dharʿ" came as an explanation, because the narrowness is in it — as you say "He is the most spacious of you in house (dāran)": "house" came in to show that the spaciousness is in it, not in the man. Likewise their saying "wajiʿta baṭnaka" (your belly ached), and "wathiqta raʾyaka" — or "wafiqta" [Abū ʿAbdullāh said: I most likely think it is "wathiqta" with thāʾ] — the verb really belongs to the thing; when the verb was attributed to the man, the accusative became sound in what refers back to him, by way of explanation (tafsīr). For that reason it may not be put first: one does not say "raʾyahu safiha Zaydun", just as "dāran anta awsaʿuhum" is not permissible; because even though it is definite it has the sense of an indefinite, and receives the accusative in the position of the accusative of the indefinite and does not go beyond it.

farraa:132-133.t:
His saying: ﴿وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ﴾ — in the codices of the people of Medina: "وأَوصى"; both are correct and common in speech.
His saying: ﴿وَيَعْقُوبُ﴾ — i.e. and Yaʿqūb also enjoined this. In one of the two readings, the reading of ʿAbdullāh or the reading of Ubayy: "أَنْ يَا بنَىَّ إن الله اصطفى لكم الدين" — he makes "وصّى" act upon "أن", meaning: he enjoined them "that…". There is no "أن" in our reading, and all is correct. Whoever drops it says: enjoining (waṣiyya) is a saying, and any speech that goes back to saying permits the entry of "أَنْ" and permits dropping "أنْ", as Allah, mighty and majestic, said in al-Nisāʾ: ﴿يوصِيكم اللّهُ فى أولادِكم لِلذكرِ مثل حظِّ الأنثيين﴾, because enjoining is like saying. Al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
إنى سأُبدى لك فيما أُبدى * لى شَجَنان شَجن بنجد * وشجَن لى ببلاد السِنْد
(I shall disclose to you, in what I disclose: I have two longings — a longing in Najd, and a longing of mine in the land of Sind.)
— because disclosing is, in meaning, with his tongue. Similar is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿وَعَدَ اللّهُ الَّذينَ آمنُوا وعَمِلوا الصالِحاتِ مِنْهم مغفِرةً﴾, because a promise is a saying. Upon this is built whatever comes of its kind.
The saying of the grammarians, "he only meant 'أن' and it was dropped", is nothing; because if that were so, it would be permissible to drop it both with what has the sense of saying and with other than it.
When the place contains something whose meaning is the meaning of saying, and then "أن" appears in it overtly, it has fatḥa on the alif. And when that word does not go back to the meaning of saying, "أن" falls out of the speech.
As for what comes with the meaning of saying and "أن" appears in it with fatḥa: the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿إنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحاً إلى قَوْمِه أَنْ أَنذِر قومك﴾ — "أن" came with fatḥa because a message is a saying.
Likewise His saying ﴿فانْطَلَقُوا وهم يَتَخَافَتُونَ. أَنْ لاَ يَدْخُلنا﴾ — and whispering is a saying. Likewise everything in the Qur'an, and it is much; of it is the saying of Allah ﴿وآخِرُ دَعْوَاهُمْ أَنِ الحمدُ لِلّه﴾.
Similar is: ﴿فَأَذَّنَ مُؤَذِّنٌ بَيْنَهُمْ أَنْ لَعْنَةُ اللّهِ [عَلَى الظَّالِمين]﴾ — calling out is a saying, and a claim (daʿwā) is originally a saying.
As for what has no sense of saying and so "أن" did not enter it: the saying of Allah ﴿ولو تَرَى إِذ المجرِمون ناكِسُوا رُءُوسِهِم عِندَ رَبّهِم رَبَّنَا أَبْصِرنَا﴾. Since in "أبصرنا" there is no word indicating saying, you imply "saying" and drop "أن", because what follows saying is a quotation (ḥikāya) with which "أن" does not occur. Of it is the saying of Allah ﴿والملائِكةُ باسِطوا أَيدِيهم أَخرِجوا أَنفسكم﴾, meaning: saying, "Bring out…". And of it is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبراهِيمُ القَواعِدَ مِن البيتِ وإِسمعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنّا﴾, meaning: the two of them say "رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ منَّا"; and this is much. So measure by this whatever comes to you.
[And His saying: … قَالُواْ نَعْبُدُ إِلَـٰهَكَ وَإِلَـٰهَ آبَائِكَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ إِلَـٰهاً وَاحِداً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ 133].
The Readers read "نعبد إِلهك وإِله آبائِك", and some of them read "وإِله أَبِيك" in the singular. It is as if the one who said "أبيك" (thought that an uncle is not permissible among the fathers), so he said "وإِله أبِيك إِبراهِيم" and then, after the father, enumerated the uncle. The Arabs treat paternal uncles like fathers, and the mother's kin like maternal uncles; that is frequent in their speech.

farraa:135-135.t: His saying: ﴿قُلْ بَلْ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفاً﴾ — Allah commanded Muḥammad ﷺ. If you put it in the accusative by "نكون" it is correct; and if you put it in the accusative by an implied verb it is correct, as if you said: "rather, we follow «مِلّة إِبراهِيم»". Allah only commanded the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, saying: "قل بل مِلّة إِبراهِيم".

farraa:136-136.t: His saying: ﴿لاَ نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِّنْهُمْ﴾ — He says: we do not believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and the Christians did.

farraa:138-138.t: His saying: ﴿صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ is accusative, referred back to "the religion" (al-milla). It was only said "صبغة اللهِ" (the dye of Allah) because some of the Christians, when a child was born, would put him in a water of theirs, making that a purification for him like circumcision. So it is too in one of the two readings. Say: "صِبغة اللّهِ", and it is circumcision; Ibrāhīm ﷺ was circumcised, so He said "صِبغة اللّهِ", commanding Muḥammad ﷺ with it. So "dye" was applied to circumcision because they dyed the boys in water. Had you put "الصبغة" and "الملّة" in the nominative it would have been correct, as the Arabs say "jadduka lā kadduka" and "jaddaka lā kaddaka" (your fortune, not your toil). Whoever uses the nominative means: it is the religion of Ibrāhīm, it is the dye of Allah, it is your fortune. Whoever uses the accusative implies a verb such as I told you.

farraa:143-143.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنَاكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطاً﴾ means just (ʿadl). ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ﴾ — it is said that every prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection and say "I conveyed", and his nation will say "No", thus belying the prophets. (Then the nation of Muḥammad ﷺ will be brought, and they will confirm the prophets and their Prophet.) Then the Prophet ﷺ will come and confirm his nation. That is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكُمْ شَهِيداً﴾. And of it is the saying of Allah: ﴿فكيف إذا جِئنا مِن كل أمَّةٍ بِشهيدٍ [وجئنا بك على هؤلاء شهيدا]﴾.
His saying: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَانَكُمْ﴾ — He attributed the faith to the living among the believers, while the meaning concerns those Muslims who died before the qibla was changed. They said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What of the prayer of our brothers who died upon the first qibla?" So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَانَكُمْ﴾, meaning their faith, because they are included with them in the religion. It is like your saying to a people, "We killed you and routed you", meaning "we killed some of you": you confront them with the killing while they are alive.

farraa:144-144.t: His saying: ﴿فَوَلُّواْ وُجُوِهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾ — He means: towards it and facing it. Similar in speech: "Turn your face shaṭrahu (towards it), tilqāʾahu and tujāhahu."

farraa:145-145.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلْكِتَابَ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ مَّا تَبِعُواْ قِبْلَتَكَ﴾ — (لئن) was answered with what "لو" is answered with. "لو" is past in meaning and "لئن" is future, but the verb appeared in both in the form faʿala, so they were answered with one answer and each was likened to the other. The answer of (لئن) in speech is with the future, as in your saying: "la-in qumta la-aqūmanna" (if you stand, I will surely stand), "la-in aḥsanta la-tukramanna" (if you do good, you will surely be honoured), and "la-in asaʾta lā yuḥsan ilayka" (if you do wrong, no good will be done to you). And you answer "لو" with the past, saying "law qumta la-qumtu" (had you stood, I would have stood); you do not say "law qumta la-aqūmanna". This is what is practised. When "لو" is answered with the answer of "لئن", [the reason is] what I told you about the form of both their verbs being past. Do you not see that you say "law qumta" and "la-in qumta", and you hardly see (yafʿalu coming) after them, though it is permissible? For that reason He said ﴿ولئن أرسلنا رِيحا فرأَوْه مُصْفَرّاً لَظَلُّوا﴾, answering (لئن) with the answer of (لو); and He answered (لو) with the answer of (لئن), saying ﴿ولو أنهم آمنوا واتقَوْا لمثوبة مِن عِندِ الله خير﴾ — the verse.

farraa:146-147.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّ فَرِيقاً مِّنْهُمْ لَيَكْتُمُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾ — the meaning is that they do not believe that the qibla to which Muḥammad ﷺ was turned is the qibla of Ibrāhīm, Allah bless him and all the prophets. Then He began afresh with (الحقُّ), saying: O Muḥammad, it is ﴿ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾ — it is the qibla of Ibrāhīm — ﴿فَلاَ تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْمُمْتَرِينَ﴾: so do not doubt that at all. Al-mumtarī is the doubter.

farraa:229-230.t:
His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ أَن يَخَافَآ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is "إلا أَنْ تخافوا" ("unless you fear"), and Ḥamza read it in line with this meaning: "ألا أَنْ يُخافا" ("unless the two are feared for") [Translator's note: so written; read إلا أن يُخافا], and that does not please me. Some of the people of Medina read it as Ḥamza read it. In the reading of Ubayy it is "إِلا أَنْ يَظنَّا أَلاَّ يُقيِمَا حُدُودَ الله" ("unless they think that they will not keep the limits of Allah"); fear and thinking are close to each other in the speech of the Arabs.
Of that: a man says: "Your slave has gone out without your permission," and you say: "I thought so (ẓanantu dhāka)," and "I feared so (khiftu dhāka)," and the meaning is one. The poet said:
أتانى كلامَ عن نُصَيب بقوله * وما خفتُ يا سلاَّم أنك عائبى
(Words reached me from Nuṣayb in what he said — and I did not think, O Sallām, that you would find fault with me.)
And the other said:
إذا مت فادفنّى إلى جَنْب كَرْمة * تُرَوِّى عظامى بعد موتى عروقها
[ولا تدفنَنِّى فى الفلاة فإننى * أخاف إذا ما متُّ أن لا أذوقُها]
(When I die, bury me beside a vine whose roots will water my bones after my death; [and do not bury me in the desert, for I fear that once I die I shall not taste it.])
Fear in this place is like thinking. He put "أذوقُها" in the nominative just as they put in the nominative ﴿وحَسِبُوا ألا تكون فِتنة﴾. And it is narrated from him ﷺ: "I was commanded to use the tooth-stick until I feared that I would surely lose my teeth (la-adradanna)," just as you say: "He thought he would surely go (la-yadhhabanna)."
As for what Ḥamza said: if he intended to follow the reading of ʿAbdullāh, he did not get it right — and Allah knows best — because the fear falls only on (أن) alone, since he [ʿAbdullāh] said: "unless you fear that … not," while Ḥamza made the fear fall on the man and the woman and on an; do you not see that their [dual] noun in the fearing is nominative as the deputy agent of a verb whose agent is not named? Had he meant: "unless they are feared for in this (ʿalā hādhā)," or "feared for by this," or "because of this," so that it is not based on following ʿAbdullāh's reading, it [would have been] permissible, as you say to a man: "You are feared because you are wicked," and "for that you are…," and "on account of your being…."
His saying: ﴿فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَلاَّ يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا﴾ — it is asked: how did He say "there is no sin upon the two of them," when the sin — according to what people take it to be — is only upon the husband, because he took back what he gave? There are two ways regarding that. One: that the husband is meant and not the woman, even though both have been mentioned. In Sūrat al-Raḥmān: ﴿يَخْرُجُ مِنْهُمَا اللُّؤْلُؤُ وَالْمَرْجَانُ﴾, whereas pearls and coral come out only from the salt water, not from the fresh. And of it: "نَسِيَا حُوتَهُما" ("the two forgot their fish"), whereas the one who forgot was Moses' companion alone. Similar to it in speech is that you say: "I have two mounts that I ride and draw water with," whereas one of them is ridden and water is drawn with the other; and it is possible that both are ridden and both used to draw water. This is from the breadth of Arabic, whose breadth is cited as proof. Similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿وَمِنْ رَحْمَتِهِ جعل لكم الليل والنهار لِتسكنوا فِيهِ ولتبتغوا مِن فضله﴾. It is sound in speech to say: "Allah has made for us night and day in which we earn our living and in which we sleep," and if you wish you assign the sleeping to the night and the earning of a living to the day.
The other way is that both share in there being no sin upon them, since she gives that in which sin has been negated from the husband; she was made to share in it because when she gives that in which the sin is removed, she herself needs the same. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فمن تعجَّلَ فى يومين فلا إِثم عليهِ ومن تأخَّر فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾, whereas the place for removing sin is in the one who hastens; so He granted to the one who delays — and he is the one who did not fall short — the like of what He granted to the one who falls short. Similar to it in speech is your saying: "If you give charity in secret, it is good, [and if you give charity openly, it is good]."
In His saying ﴿ومن تأخّر فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾ there is another way: that He means: let not the one who hastens say to the one who delays, "You fall short," nor the one who delays say the like to the one who hastens; so His saying ﴿فلا إِثم عليهِ﴾ means: let neither of them accuse the other of sin.
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَآ أَن يَتَرَاجَعَآ﴾ — He means: there is no sin upon them in returning to each other. (أَن) is in the position of the accusative when the preposition (al-ṣifa) is removed, as if you said: there is no sin upon them that he take her back. He said: al-Kisāʾī used to say: its position is genitive. Al-Farrāʾ said: I do not recognize that.
His saying: ﴿إِن ظَنَّآ أَن يُقِيمَا﴾ — (أن) is in the position of the accusative because the thinking falls on it.

farraa:231-231.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَاراً لِّتَعْتَدُواْ﴾ — when a man among them divorced his wife, he had the greater right to take her back so long as she had not washed from the second menstruation. When he wanted to harm her, he would leave her until she menstruated the third menstruation and then take her back, and he would do that in the second divorce as well. So his prolonging her return is the harming of her.

farraa:232-232.t:
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾ — He says: do not constrain them from returning to their husbands with a new dower when one of them has been separated from her husband. This was the sister of Maʿqil: she wanted to marry her first husband after her waiting period had ended, and Maʿqil said to her: "My face is forbidden to your face if you go back to him." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ أَن يَنكِحْنَ أَزْوَاجَهُنَّ﴾.
His saying ﴿ذٰلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾ — He did not say: dhālikum, and both are correct. It is permissible to address a people with "dhālika" only because it is a word that has become so frequent in speech that the kāf is imagined to be (part of the word) and not an address. Whoever says "dhālika" makes the kāf with fatḥa even when addressing a woman, two women or women. Whoever says "dhālikum" drops that imagining, and so he says when addressing one [woman]: "What did that man (dhāliki al-rajul) do?" and "those two men (dhālikumā)," and "those men (ulāʾikum)." [And] what occurs is measured on this. In the rest of the nouns, when you address, it is not permissible to say it except by bringing out the addressee in the dual, the plural and the feminine, as when you say to a woman: "Your boy (ghulāmuki) did that"; it is not permissible to give the kāf a fatḥa, nor to make it singular, in ghulām, because the kāf here is not imagined to be part of ghulām.
And it is permissible to say: "Your boy (ghulāmuki) did dhāki" and "dhāka," according to what I explained to you: taking the kāf to be part of the noun.

farraa:233-233.t:
His saying: ﴿ٱلرَّضَاعَةَ﴾ — the Readers read it with fatḥa on the rāʾ. Al-Kisāʾī claimed that some of the Arabs say: al-riḍāʿa with kasra. If so, it is like al-wikāla and al-wakāla, al-dilāla and al-dalāla, and "mahartu al-shayʾa mihāratan and mahāratan"; and al-raḍāʿ and al-riḍāʿ are similarly so, except that fatḥa on the rāʾ is more common. Similar to it: al-ḥiṣād and al-ḥaṣād.
His saying ﴿لاَ تُضَآرَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا﴾ — He means: lā tuḍārar, and it is in the position of the jussive (jazm). Kasra in it is permissible: "lā tuḍārri wālidatun." It is not permissible to give the rāʾ ḍamma with the intention of the jussive, but we would read it with ḍamma as a statement (khabar). As for His saying ﴿وإِن تَصْبِرُوا وتَتَّقُوا لا يضرُّكم كَيْدُهُمْم شَيْئا﴾, it may be ḍamma with the intention of the jussive, because the first rāʾ originally has ḍamma, so it is permissible for the second to have ḍamma following it. (لا تضارُّ) with ḍamma is not permissible, because if the rāʾ is tufāʿal it has fatḥa, and if it is tufāʿil it has kasra; so ḍamma does not come to it unless it is in the sense of the nominative. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb read: "ولا يضارَرْ كاتِب ولا شهيد".
The meaning of ﴿لاَ تُضَآرَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا﴾: He says: let her child not be taken from her while she is healthy and has milk, and handed over to someone else. ﴿ وَلاَ مَوْلُودٌ لَّهُ بِوَلَدِهِ﴾ means the husband. He says: when she has nursed her infant and it has grown attached to her and knows her, let her not harm the husband regarding handing his child over to him.

farraa:234-235.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجاً يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾ — it is asked: how did the predicate (khabar) come to be about the women, with no predicate for the husbands, when the predicate ought to have been about (الذين)? That is permissible: when nouns are mentioned and then nouns attached to them are mentioned that carry the meaning of the predicate, you leave the first and the predicate is about what is attached to it. This is of that kind, because the meaning — and Allah knows best — is only: whoever's husband dies, she waits. So the first was left without a predicate and the second was aimed at, because the predicate and the meaning are in it. He said: and someone recited to me:
بنى أسَد إنّ ابن قيس وقتلَه * بغير دم دارُ المذَلَّة حُلَّت
(O Banū Asad, Ibn Qays — and his being killed for no blood — is the abode of humiliation that has been entered.)
So he dropped (ابن قيس) and gave a predicate about his killing, that it is humiliation. Similar to it:
لعلِّىَ إن مالت بِىَ الرِّيح مَيْلة * على ابن أبى ذِبَّان أن يتندَّما
(Perhaps, if the wind swings me once against Ibn Abī Dhibbān, he may come to regret.)
He said "laʿallī" and then said "an yatanaddamā," because the meaning is: perhaps Ibn Abī Dhibbān will regret if the wind swings me. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿والذِين يتوفَّوْن مِنكم ويذرون أَزواجا وصِيَّةً لأزواجِهِم﴾, except that the hāʾ in His saying ﴿وصِيَّة لأزواجِهِم﴾ refers back to (الذين), so the i'rab in it is clearer, because the returning reference can be a predicate, as when you say: "ʿAbdullāh, I hit him."
He said: ﴿وَعَشْراً﴾ and did not say "ʿasharatan." That is because when the Arabs leave a number of nights and days unspecified, they give the nights precedence over it, so much so that they say: "We have fasted ten (ʿashran) of the month of Ramaḍān," because of how often they give nights precedence over days. When they state the specification alongside the number, the feminines take it without the hāʾ and the masculines with the hāʾ, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿سَخَّرها عليهِم سبع ليالٍ وثمانية أَيامٍ حُسُوما﴾ — He put the hāʾ on [the number of] the days when they were stated, and it was not put on [the number of] the nights when they were stated.
If you make the number not connected to the days as the governing genitive is connected to what follows it, you again give the nights precedence over the days. If they are mixed, being nights and days, you give the feminine precedence, saying: "Seven (sabʿ) have passed for him," and then after it you say: "days in which there was severe cold." As for the mixed case, it is the poet's saying:
أقامت ثلاثا بين يوم وليلة * وكان النكير أن تضِيف وتَجْارا
(She stayed three [nights and days], between day and night, and her only protest was to shy away and cry out.)
He said thalāthan and among them are days. And you say: "I have three (thalātha) between a slave boy and a slave girl," and thalāth is not permissible here, because [only] nights, with regard to days, take precedence over days. Similar to that in speech is that you say: "I have ten (ʿashr) camels," even if you mean male camels, and "ten of sheep and cattle." And every collective whose singular has the hāʾ and whose plural drops the hāʾ — such as al-baqar, whose singular is baqara — you say: "I have ten (ʿashr) of the cattle," even if you intend males. When they are mixed and the specifying item of one of the two kinds comes before its companion, you run the number on it, saying: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) she-camels and he-camels," making it feminine because you began with the she-camel and gave it precedence.
If you begin with the he-camel you say: "I have fifteen (khamsata ʿashara) he-camels and she-camels." If you say "between she-camel and he-camel," so that it is not a specification, you give the feminine precedence and do not mind whether you began with the he-camel or the she-camel; you say: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) between he-camel and she-camel." It is not permissible to say: "I have fifteen (khamsa ʿashrata) slave women and slave men," nor "between slave woman and slave man," except with the masculine, because the males of anything other than what I mentioned to you are not covered by the females, and because the male of them is marked with a mark other than the female's mark; whereas with sheep and cattle, shāt and baqara apply to the male and the female, so it is permissible to make the masculine feminine because of this hāʾ which has attached to both the masculine and the feminine.
His saying ﴿مِنْ خِطْبَةِ ٱلنِّسَآءِِ﴾ — al-khiṭba is a maṣdar (verbal noun) like al-khiṭb, and it is like your saying: "He has a fine way of sitting (al-qiʿda wa-l-jilsa)," meaning sitting (al-quʿūd wa-l-julūs). Al-khuṭba is like a letter that has a beginning and an end. He said: I heard one of the Arabs [say]: "O Allah, lift from us this ḍughṭa (distress)," as if he took it to have a beginning and an end; had he meant one time he would have said: al-ḍaghṭa, and had he meant the manner of the act he would have said al-ḍighṭa, as one says al-mishya. And I heard another say: "[So-and-so] overpowered me over a quṭʿa of my land," meaning a plot set apart like a piece, not divided; if you mean that it is a piece of something [cut from it], you say: qiṭʿa.
His saying: ﴿ أَوْ أَكْنَنتُمْ﴾ — the Arabs have two dialects for aknantu al-shayʾa when you have concealed it: kanantuhu and aknantuhu. He said: and they recited to me the poet's saying:
ثلاثٌ من ثلاثِ قُدَامياتٍ * من اللاتى تَكُنّ من الصَقِيع
(Three [feathers] from three foremost ones, of those that shelter from the frost.)
and some of them [narrate it] tukinnu, from aknantu. As for His saying: "لؤلؤ مكنون" and "بَيْض مكنون", it is as though it is a way of speaking of a thing that is guarded, and each of the two is close to the other.
His saying: ﴿وَلَـٰكِن لاَّ تُوَاعِدُوهُنَّ سِرّاً ﴾ — He says: let none of you describe himself to her during her waiting period as desiring marriage and doing much of it. Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Ḥibbān narrated to me from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: al-sirr in this place is marriage [Translator's note: i.e. intercourse]. And he recited on his authority the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays:
ألا زعمت بَسْباسة اليوم أننى * كبِرتُ وأَلاَّ يشهدَ السِرَّ أَمثالى
(Bisbāsa claimed today that I have grown old, and that the likes of me do not attend to al-sirr.)
Al-Farrāʾ said: and he holds that it is among the things Allah alluded to by metonymy, [as] He said: "أو جاء احد منكم من الغائط".

farraa:236-236.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ عَلَى ٱلْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُ وَعَلَى ٱلْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُ﴾ in the nominative. Had it been put in the accusative it would be correct, on the repetition of the verb in intention, i.e. let the well-off give according to his means, and the one in straitened circumstances according to his means. It is like the saying of the Arabs: "I took their alms: for every forty sheep, a sheep (shātun)"; had you put the last shāt in the accusative it would be correct.
His saying ﴿مَتَاعاً بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is accusative, coming out of al-qadar [Translator's note: i.e. as a ḥāl from it], because it is indefinite and al-qadar is definite.
And if you wish, it comes out of His saying "وَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ" — matāʿan and mutʿatan [i.e. as its maṣdar].
As for ﴿حَقّاً﴾, it is accusative from the intention of the statement, not as an adjective of al-matāʿ. It is like your saying in speech: "ʿAbdullāh is in the house, truly (ḥaqqan)." Al-ḥaqq is put in the accusative only from the intention of the informant's speech, as if he said: "I inform you of a true report," and "of that, truly"; and it is ugly to make it follow definites or indefinites, because truth and falsehood are not in the nouns themselves; they come only with statements. Of that: you say: "You owe me the money, truly (ḥaqqan)," and it is ugly to say: "You owe me the true money (al-māl al-ḥaqq)," or "You owe me true money (māl ḥaqq)," unless you take it to mean that it is a right of mine against you, so that you treat it as [describing] the money and not in the manner of the statement.
Everything in the Quran in which there is an indefinite or definite form of al-ḥaqq, or what is in the meaning of al-ḥaqq, the proper way of speech in it is the accusative, such as His saying "وَعْدَ الحقِ" and "وعد الصدق", and like His saying ﴿إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُم جَمِيعا وَعْدَ اللّهِ حقاً﴾; this is according to the first explanation.
As for His saying ﴿هنالِك الوَلاية لِلّه الحقِّ﴾, the accusative in al-ḥaqq is permissible, meaning ḥaqqan, i.e. I inform you that that is true. If you wish, you put al-ḥaqq in the genitive, making it an attribute of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And if you wish, you put it in the nominative, making it an attribute of al-walāya. Likewise His saying ﴿ورُدُّوا إلى اللّهِ مَوْلاَهُم الحقّ﴾: you make it an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Had you put it in the accusative it would be correct, and had it been put in the nominative on the intention of a fresh start (istiʾnāf) it would be correct, as He said: ﴿الْحَقُّ مِن ربَّك فَلاَ تَكُونَنَّ مِن المُمْتَرِين﴾. And you would say, when you hear a man relating something: [ḥaqqan, i.e.] you have spoken truly, and al-ḥaqqu, i.e. that is the truth. As for His saying in Ṣād ﴿قَالَ فالْحقُّ والحقَّ أقول﴾, al-Farrāʾ [Translator's note: so in the text; the sense requires "the Readers" (al-qurrāʾ)] have read the first in the nominative and in the accusative. It is narrated from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās that they read the first in the nominative and said its explanation is: the truth is from Me, and I speak the truth; so they put the second in the accusative by "aqūlu". Many of them put both in the accusative, taking the first in the sense of: by the truth "لأملأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ", and putting the second in the accusative because the saying falls on it. His saying ﴿ذلِكَ عِيسَى بنُ مَرْيَمَ قَوْلَ الحقّ﴾ — Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read it in the nominative, and they took al-Ḥaqq to be Allah, Blessed and Exalted, because in the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is "ذَلِكَ عِيسَى بْنُ مَرْيَمَ قالَ اللّهِ", like your saying: "the Word of Allah"; so they make (qāl) equivalent to qawl, as they said al-ʿāb and al-ʿayb.
Some read it in the accusative, meaning: that is Jesus son of Mary — a true saying.

farraa:237-237.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِن طَلَّقْتُمُوهُنَّ مِن قَبْلِ أَن تَمَسُّوهُنَّ﴾ — tumāssūhunna and tamassūhunna are one, and it is intercourse: al-mumāssa and al-mass.
He said ﴿إَلاَّ أَن يَعْفُونَ﴾ with the nūn only because it is the verb of the women, and the verb of women has the nūn in every case. One says: hunna yaḍribna, lam yaḍribna, lan yaḍribna, because if you dropped the nūn from them for the accusative or the jussive, their femininity would not be evident. The Arabs said "lan yaʿfū" for a group [of men] and "lan yaʿfuwā" for two men only because they added for the dual an alif and a nūn to the verb; so when they drop the nūn of the dual for the jussive or the accusative, the alif indicates the dual. Likewise the wāw of yafʿalūna indicates the plural when the nūn is dropped in the jussive or the accusative.
﴿أَوْ يَعْفُوَاْ ٱلَّذِي بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ ٱلنِّكَاحِ﴾ — and he is the husband.

farraa:238-238.t: His saying: ﴿حَافِظُواْ عَلَى ٱلصَّلَوَاتِ وٱلصَّلاَةِ ٱلْوُسْطَىٰ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "وعلى الصلاة الوسطى" ("and over the middle prayer"); for that reason the Readers preferred the genitive. Had it been put in the accusative, as urging it with an implied verb, it would have been a good way. It is like your saying in speech: "Hold to your kin — and the mother!", singling her out for kindness.

farraa:240-240.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجاً وَصِيَّةً﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is: "كتب عليهم الوصية لأزواجِهم" ("the bequest to their wives is prescribed for them"), and in the reading of Ubayy: "يتوفون منكم ويذرون أزواجا فمتاع لأزواجهم" ("…then a provision for their wives"). This is evidence for the nominative of al-waṣiyya. Some put it in the accusative, among them Ḥamza, on an implied verb as though it were a command, i.e. let them bequeath a bequest to their wives.
It cannot be accusative by having "wa-yadharūna" act on it.
﴿غَيْرَ إِخْرَاجٍ﴾ — He says: without your turning them out. Similar to it in speech: "I came to you out of desire for you." Similar to it: ﴿وأَدْخِل يَدَكَ فى جَيْبِك تَخْرُجْ بيْضَاء مِن غيرِ سُوءٍٍ﴾; had you dropped "min" you would say: ghayra sūʾin. Al-sūʾ here is leprosy (al-baraṣ). Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Sharīk narrated to us from Yazīd ibn Ziyād from Miqsam from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: without leprosy. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is as though He said: it will come out white, not leprous.

farraa:245-245.t: His saying: ﴿مَّن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يُقْرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضاً حَسَناً فَيُضَاعِفَهُ لَهُ﴾ — it is read in the nominative and the accusative. Whoever uses the nominative makes the fāʾ conjoined onto the ṣila (relative clause) of (الذى); whoever uses the accusative takes it out of the ṣila and makes it an answer to (من), because it is an interrogative. The one in al-Ḥadīd is like it.

farraa:20-20.t:
His words: ﴿يَكَادُ ٱلْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ﴾. The readers read "يَخَطِّفُ أَبْصاَرَهُمْ", with fatḥa on the yāʾ and the khāʾ and with doubling. Some give fatḥa to the yāʾ, kasra to the khāʾ and double the ṭāʾ, saying: "يَخِطِّفُ". Some give kasra to the yāʾ and the khāʾ and double, saying: "يِخِطِّفُ". And some of the readers of the people of Medina make the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ quiescent, combining two quiescent letters, saying: "يَخْطِّف". As for the one who says "يَخَطِّفُ", he transferred the vowel of the assimilated tāʾ to the khāʾ, since the khāʾ was quiescent. As for the one who gives kasra to the khāʾ, he was seeking the kasra of the alif in اختطف and الاختطاف. Some grammarians have said about it: The khāʾ was given kasra only because it was quiescent and the tāʾ after it was made quiescent, so two quiescent letters met and you gave the first a kasra, as one says: اضربِ الرجل, giving kasra to the bāʾ because it meets the lām.

What they said is worth nothing, because if it were as they said, the Arabs would have said in يَمُدّ: يَمِدّ, since the mīm (was) quiescent and the first of the two dāls was made quiescent; and they would have said in يَعَضّ: يَعِضّ. As for the one who gives kasra to both the yāʾ and the khāʾ, he too was seeking the kasra of the alif, because it had kasra at the beginning of the word. As for the one who combines the two quiescent letters, he is like one who builds on clear separate pronunciation (tibyān), except that it is a hidden assimilation. In His words ﴿أَم مَّنْ لاَ يَهِدِّى إلاَّ أَنْ يُهْدَى﴾ and in His words ﴿تَأخُذُهُمْ وَهُمْ يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾ the same explanation applies — except that Ḥamza al-Zayyāt read "تَأخُذُهُمْ وَهُمْ يَخْصِمُونَ" with a quiescent khāʾ, and that is a different meaning.

His words: ﴿كُلَّمَا أَضَآءَ لَهُمْ مَّشَوْاْ فِيهِ﴾: there are two dialects in it; one says أضاءَ القمرُ and ضاءَ القمرُ (the moon shone). Whoever says ضاء القمرُ says: يضوء ضَُوءا. And الضّوء has two dialects: ḍamma on the ḍād and fatḥa.

﴿وَإِذَآ أَظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْْ﴾: there are two dialects in it: أظلم الليل and ظَلِم (the night grew dark).

His words: ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَذَهَبَْ﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: had Allah willed, He would have taken away (لأذهب) their hearing. It is the way of the Arabs to say أذهبت بصره (I took away his sight), with the alif, when they drop the bāʾ; and when they make the bāʾ overt, they drop the alif from "أذهبت". Some readers read: "يَكَادُ سَنَا بَرْقِهِ يُذْهبُ بِالأَبْصَارِ", with ḍamma on the yāʾ and with the bāʾ in the phrase. And some read: "وَشَجَرَةً تَخْرُجُ مِنْ طُورِ سَينَاءَ تُنْبِتُ بالدُّهْنِ". So you see — and Allah knows best — that those who used ḍamma, with the meaning of the alif, likened the presence and absence of the bāʾ in these two words to their saying: خذْ بالخطام and خُذِ الخطامَ (take hold of the halter), and تعلَّقتُ بزيدٍ and تعلَّقتُ زيدا (I clung to Zayd). This is frequent in speech and poetry, but I do not favour it [Translator's note: i.e. combining the alif and the bāʾ] because it is rare. Of this kind are His words: ﴿آتِنَا غَدَاءَنَا﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: bring us (ايتنا) our morning meal; when the bāʾ was dropped they added an alif to faʿaltu [Translator's note: i.e. made it a fourth-form verb]. Of this kind too are His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿قَالَ آتُونِى أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْراً﴾, the meaning — according to what has come down — being: bring me molten copper that I may pour over it. And of this kind are His words: ﴿فَأَجَاءَهَا الْمَخَاضُ إِلَى جِذْعِ النَّخْلَةِ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: the pains of childbirth brought her (فجاء بها) to the trunk of the palm tree.

farraa:23-23.t: His words: ﴿فَأْتُواْ بِسُورَةٍ مِّن مِّثْلِهِِ﴾: the hāʾ is a pronoun (kināya) referring to the Qur'an: so bring a surah like the Qur'an. ﴿وَٱدْعُواْ شُهَدَآءَكُمْ﴾: He means your gods. He says: call on them for help. It is like your saying to a man: If you meet the enemy when you are alone, call (فادع) the Muslims — meaning: seek the help and support of the Muslims.

farraa:24-24.t:
His words: ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ تَفْعَلُواْ وَلَن تَفْعَلُواْ فَٱتَّقُواْ ٱلنَّارَ ٱلَّتِي وَقُودُهَا ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱلْحِجَارَةُ﴾: people are its fuel and stones are its fuel. They claimed that it [Translator's note: the stone] is like sulphur that is heated, and that it is the hottest of stones when heated. Then He said: ﴿أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ﴾, meaning the Fire.

His words: ﴿وَأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشَابِهاً﴾: it seemed alike to them, according to what has been mentioned, in its colour; but when they tasted it they knew that it was other than what had come before it. [Translator's note: this phrase belongs to verse 25; it stands in this entry in the source.]

farraa:26-26.t:
His words: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لاَ يَسْتَحْى أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلاً مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا﴾. If someone says: Where is the speech to which this is the answer? We do not see it in Sūrat al-Baqara. It has been mentioned to us that when Allah said: ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللهِ أَوْلِيَاءَ كَمَثَلِ الْعَنْكَبُوتِ اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتاً﴾, the Jews, the enemies of Allah, said: "What kind of parable is this?" And they said the like of that when He revealed: ﴿يَأَيُّهَا النَّاسُ ضُرِبَ مَثَلٌ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ منْ دُون اللَّهِ لَنْ يَخْلُقُوا ذُبَاباً﴾ — up to His words — ﴿ضَعُفَ الطَّالِبُ وَالْمَطْلُوبُ﴾, because of the mention of the fly and the spider. So Allah revealed: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لاَ يَسْتَحْى أَن يَضْرِبَ مَثَلاً مَّا بَعُوضَةً فَمَا فَوْقَهَا﴾. By what is "فَوْقَهَا" (above it) He means what is bigger than it, namely the spider and the fly. Had you used "فما فوقها" in similar speech meaning smaller than it, that would be permissible, but I do not consider it good, because the gnat is, as it were, the extreme of smallness, so I prefer to take "مَا فوقها" as bigger than it. Do you not see that you say: يُعطَى من الزكاة الخمسُون فما دونها (fifty and below is given from the zakāt) and الدرهمُ فما فوقه (a dirham and above)? The expression would be awkward if you said "above it" in both, or "below it" in both. As for where it is good in speech: someone says: إن فلانا لشريف (so-and-so is noble), and the listener says: وفوق ذاك (and above that), meaning praise; or he says: إنه لبخيل (he is miserly), and the other says: وفوق ذاك, meaning by both a greater degree. But if you know the man and say: دونَ ذلك (below that), it is as if you lower him from the extreme of nobility or the extreme of miserliness. Do you not see that when you say: إنه لبخيلٌ وفوق ذاك, you mean above miserliness, and "above that" [Translator's note: in the other case means] above nobility? And when you say: دون ذاك, you are someone who knows him and has brought him down a little from his rank. So never say وفوق ذاك except in praise or censure.

Al-Qurrāʾ [Translator's note: so in the text — "the readers"; probably a slip for al-Farrāʾ] said: As for their putting "بعوضة" in the accusative, it can be in three ways. The first: you let «الضرب» (striking [Translator's note: a parable]) fall on «البعوضة» and make "ما" a ṣila (redundant particle), as in His words: ﴿عَمّا قَلِيلٍ لَيُصْبِحُنَّ نَادِمِينَ﴾ [meaning عن قليل]; the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: Allah is not ashamed to strike a gnat and what is above it as a parable.

The second way: you make "ما" a noun and «البعوضة» its ṣila (complement), and you give it the inflection of "ما". That is permissible with "مَنْ" and "ما" because they are definite in one case and indefinite in another, as Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:
فَكَفَى بِنا فَضْلاً علَى مَنْ غَيْرِنا * حُبُّ النَّبِىءِ مُحَمّدٍ إِيّانا
(It suffices us as a distinction over anyone other than us, that the Prophet Muḥammad loves us.)
[Al-Farrāʾ said: It is also narrated: * ...على مَنْ غَيرُنا *.] The nominative in "بعوضة" here is permissible, because the ṣila is nominative while its noun [Translator's note: i.e. «ما»] is accusative or genitive. As for the third way — and it is the one I like best — you take the meaning to be: Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of whatever lies between a gnat and what is above it. When the Arabs drop "بَيْنَ" from speech at whose end "إِلَى" would be appropriate, they put in the accusative the two words that would have been genitive, one governed by "بَيْنَ" and the other by "إلى". So they say: مُطرْنا ما زُبالَةَ فالثّعْلبيةَ (we had rain from Zubāla to al-Thaʿlabiyya), له عشرون ما ناقةً فجملاً (he has twenty, from she-camel to he-camel), and هى أحسن الناس ما قَرْناً فقدَماً (she is the most beautiful of people from head to foot), meaning: between her head and her foot. You may also make القرن and القدم definite and say: هى حسنةٌ ما قرنَها فقدمَها.

When "إلى" is not appropriate at the end of the speech, dropping "بَيْن" is not permissible. An example is your saying: دارى ما بَيْنَ الكوفة والمدينة (my house is between Kufa and Medina): you may not say: دارى ما الكوفةَ فالمدينةَ, because "إلى" is appropriate only if everything between Medina and Kufa is your house, just as the rain covered everything from Zubāla to al-Thaʿlabiyya. Nor is the fāʾ appropriate in place of the wāw where "إلى" is not appropriate, as in your saying: دار فلان بَيْنَ الحِيرة فالكوفة — that is absurd; and جلست بين عبد الله فزيدٍ (I sat between ʿAbdallāh then Zayd) — absurd, unless your seat takes up the whole space between them. The fāʾ is excluded where "إلى" is not appropriate only because the action there does not come in a continuous succession, whereas "إلى" requires two nouns between which the action runs [Translator's note: continuously] — even if it is like the blink of an eye, and however short the existing distance between them. So the fāʾ is appropriate where "إلى" is, because you say: the rain took its first part, then such-and-such, up to its end. And since the action is, in meaning, extensive, one thing after another, there is in it an interpretation akin to the conditional (jazāʾ). Similar to this is that they said: إن تأتنى فأنت مُحسنٌ (if you come to me, then you are doing good), while it is absurd to say: إن تأتنى وأنت محسن; they accepted the fāʾ as an apodosis in the conditional, but the wāw was not appropriate.

Al-Kisāʾī said: I heard a Bedouin who had seen the new crescent say: الحمد لله ما إِهلالَك إلى سَرارِك (praise be to Allah, from your appearing to your vanishing), meaning: between your appearing and your vanishing. They placed the accusative that would have been on "بَيْنَ" onto what follows it when it was dropped, so that it would be known that the meaning of "بَيْنَ" is intended. Al-Kisāʾī reported from some Arabs: الشّنَقُ: ما خَمْسا إلى خمس وعشرين (al-shanaq is what is between five and twenty-five), meaning: between five and twenty-five. Al-shanaq is the number of camels on which the obligatory levy is not due; the [Translator's note: corresponding term] for cattle is al-awqāṣ.

His words: ﴿مَاذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَـٰذَا مَثَلاً يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيراً وَيَهْدِي بِهِ كَثِيراً﴾: as though they said — and Allah knows best — What did Allah intend by a parable that not everyone understands, by which this one is led astray and that one is guided? Allah said: ﴿وَمَا يُضِلُّ بِهِ إِلاَّ الْفَاسِقِينَ﴾.

farraa:28-28.t:
His words: ﴿كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً﴾ is by way of wonder and rebuke, not a pure question; [i.e.] woe to you, how can you disbelieve! It is like His words: ﴿فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ﴾. His words: ﴿كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is "while you had been (وقد كنتم)"; were it not for the implied "قد", the like of it would not be permissible in speech. Do you not see that He said in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿إِنْ كَانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ دُبُرٍ فَكَذَبَتْ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: then she has lied (فقد كذبت)? And your saying to a man: أصبحتَ كَثُرَ مالُك (you have come to be with your wealth increased) is permissible only when you mean قد كَثُرَ مالُك, because both have already happened, so the second is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the first, and a ḥāl [Translator's note: that is a past verb] can only be with «قد» implied or overt. Similar to it in the Book of Allah: "أَوْ جَاءُوكُمْ حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ", meaning — and Allah knows best — [they came to you with their breasts already constricted]. One of the readers — al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī — read: "حَصِرَةً صدورهم".

It is as though he did not know the way [Translator's note: the past verb works] in أصبح عبد الله قام (ʿAbdallāh came to be standing) or أقبل أخذ شاة (he came forward, having taken a sheep), as though he meant: فقد أخَذَ شاة. When the first [Translator's note: verb] has not [Translator's note: really] passed, the second is not permissible either with قد or without it, as in your saying: كاد قام (he almost stood) or أراد قام (he wanted, stood), because wanting is something that may happen while the action does not. For that reason your saying عسى قام (perhaps he stood) is absurd: although عسى has the form faʿala, it refers to the future; so one may not say عسى قد قام, nor عسى قام, nor كاد قد قام, nor كاد قام, because what follows them cannot be past. But if you bring يكون with عسى and كاد it becomes sound, and you say: عسى أن يكون قد ذهب (perhaps he has gone), as Allah said: ﴿قُلْ عَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُمْ بَعْضُ الَّذى تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾.

His words: ﴿وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً فَأَحْيَاكُمْ﴾ means: sperm-drops; and everything that separates from the body, such as hair or a sperm-drop, is dead — and Allah knows best. He says: then He gave you life from the sperm-drops, then He will cause you to die after life, then He will give you life for the Resurrection.

farraa:29-29.t: His words: ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَسَوَّاهُنَّ﴾. Al-istiwāʾ in the speech of the Arabs has two senses. One is that a man reaches full maturity [and] his youth comes to its peak, or that something straightens out from crookedness — these are two senses. A third sense is that you say: He was turned towards so-and-so, then he "istawā" towards me (عليّ) reviling me — and "إليّ" is the same — meaning he turned to me and against me. This is the meaning of His words ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾ — and Allah knows best. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Then He istawā to the heaven" means: He ascended. This is like your saying of a man: He was standing and then istawā sitting, or he was sitting and then istawā standing. All of this is permissible in the speech of the Arabs. As for His words: ﴿ثُمَّ ٱسْتَوَىٰ إِلَى ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَسَوَّاهُنَّ﴾, «السماء» (the heaven) has a plural meaning, so He said "فَسَوَّاهُنّ" according to the known meaning, namely that they are seven heavens. Likewise the plural is applied to the earth, though it is one; and the singular [Translator's note: i.e. dual] is applied to the two of them though they are plural: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ﴾, then He said: ﴿وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ and did not say «بينهن» (between them [Translator's note: plural]). This is proof of what (I have told you).

farraa:31-31.t: His words: ﴿وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ ٱلأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلْمَلاَئِكَةِ﴾. ﴿عرضهم﴾ (He presented them) [Translator's note: with the masculine plural pronoun] follows the approach of the persons of the beings and the rest of creation. Had the names alone been intended, without the persons, "عرضهنّ" and "عرضها" would have been permissible. In the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbdallāh it is "ثم عرضهنّ", and in the version of Ubayy "ثم عرضها". If you say "عرضها", it may refer to the names without the persons, or to the persons without the names.

farraa:33-33.t: His words: ﴿يَآءَادَمُ أَنبِئْهُمْ بِأَسْمَآئِهِمْْ﴾. If you pronounce the hamza, you say ﴿أَنْبِئْهُمْ﴾, and kasra of the hāʾ and the mīm is not permissible, because it is a hamza, not a yāʾ that would make it like "عليهِم". If you drop the hamza, whether you then keep the yāʾ or not, ḍamma or kasra of "هِمُ" is permissible, as I described to you for "عليهِم" and "عليهُم".

farraa:148-148.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ﴾ means a qibla; ﴿هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا﴾: facing it. The verb belongs to "كلّ" (each); He means: turning his face to it.
Turning (tawliya) in this place is facing towards; in ﴿يولُّوكُم الأدبار﴾ and ﴿ثُمَّ وَلَّيتم مُدْبِرين﴾ it is turning away. It is like your saying in speech "inṣarif ilayya", i.e. come to me, and "inṣarif ilā ahlika", i.e. go to your family. Ibn ʿAbbās and others read "هو مُوَلاَّها", and so did Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, making the verb fall upon him [i.e. passive]. The meaning is one. And Allah knows best.
His saying: ﴿أَيْنَ مَا تَكُونُواْ...(148)﴾ — when you see interrogative particles joined to (ما), such as "أينما", "متى ما", "أىٌّ ما", "حيث ما", "كيف ما" and ﴿أيّاًمَّا تدعوا﴾, they are conditional (jazāʾ) and not interrogative. When they are not joined to (ما), the interrogative predominates in them, and the conditional is permissible in them.
When they are conditional, you put both verbs in the jussive: the verb with "أينما" and its sisters, and its answer, as in His saying ﴿أَيْنَ مَا تَكُونُواْ يَأْتِ بِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾. If you put the fāʾ in the answer, you put the answer in the nominative; you say in the like of it in speech: "aynamā takun fa-ātīka" (wherever you are, I come to you). So too the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿ومن كفر فَأُمتِّعه﴾.
When they are interrogative, you put the verb following "أين" and "كيف" in the nominative, then you put the second verb in the jussive, so that it is an answer to the question in the sense of a conditional; as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿هل أَدُلُّكُمْ على تجارةٍ تُنْجِيِكم مِن عَذابٍ أليم﴾, then He answered the question with the jussive, saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿يغفرْ لَكُمْ ذنوبَكم﴾.
When you put a fāʾ in the answer to a question, you use the accusative, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿لولا أَخَّرْتنِى إلى أَجلٍ قرِيبٍ فأَصَّدّقَ﴾ — so He used the accusative.
When you come to the conjoined verbs (ʿuṭūf) in the conditional, having answered it with the fāʾ, you have three options in the conjoined verb. If you wish, you put the conjoined verb in the nominative, as in your saying "in taʾtinī fa-innī ahlu dhāka, wa-tuʾjaru wa-tuḥmadu" (if you come to me, I am worthy of that, and you will be rewarded and praised); this is the normal way of speech. If you wish, you put it in the jussive, making it as if referred back to the position of the fāʾ; the nominative is on [the pattern of] what follows the fāʾ. The Readers have read "من يضلِلِ الله فلا هادِى له ويَذَرْهُم" in the nominative and the jussive. Likewise ﴿إِنْ تُبْدُوا الصّدقاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِى وإنْ تُخْفُوها وتُؤْتُوها الفقراءَ فَهْوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ ويُكَفِّرْ﴾, jussive and nominative. Had you used the accusative, on the pattern by which the conjoined verbs of a conditional take the accusative when it is complete, you would be right, as the poet said:
فإن يَهْلِكِ النعمانُ تُعْرَ مِطَّيةٌ * وتُخْبَأَ فى جوفِ العِيابِ قُطُوعُها
(If al-Nuʿmān perishes, a mount will be left unsaddled, and its saddle-gear hidden away inside the bags.)
And if you use the jussive for a conjoined verb after having used the accusative, referring it back to the first, it is correct, as he said after this verse:
وتَنْحِطْ حَصَانٌ آخِرَ اللّيلِ نَحْطةً * تَقَصَّمُ مِنها - أَو تَكادُ - ضُلوعها
(And a chaste woman will heave a sigh at the end of the night, from which her ribs break — or nearly.)
This is frequent in poetry and speech. The accusative in conjoined verbs is most common when there is no fāʾ in the answer of the conditional; when there is the fāʾ, it is the nominative and the jussive.
When you answer a question with the fāʾ and use the accusative, put the conjoined verbs in the accusative; if you put them in the jussive, it is correct. Of this is His saying regarding the hypocrites: ﴿لَوْلاَ أَخَّرْتَنِى إلى أَجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ فَأَصَّدَّق وأَكُنْ﴾ — you refer "وأَكُنْ" back to the position of the fāʾ, because it is in the position of the jussive, since the verb, had it occurred in its place without the fāʾ, would be jussive. The accusative is by referring it to what follows it, so you say "وأكونَ"; and in the reading of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd it is "وأكون" with the wāw, and some of the Readers have read it so. He said: I consider that correct, because the wāw is sometimes omitted in writing while intended, because of how often it is dropped and added in speech. Do you not see that they write "الرحمن" and "سليمن" dropping the alif, while it is pronounced? For this reason it is permissible. The wāw has been dropped from His saying ﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِية﴾ and from His saying ﴿وَيَدْعُ الإِنْسانُ بالشّرِّ﴾ — the verse — while the recitation intends the wāw to be present. And they dropped two alifs from "الأيكة", writing it in one place "ليكة", while in another place it is "الأَيْكة"; and the Readers read it in full. This is a witness for the permissibility of "وأكون من الصَّالِحينَ".
One of the poets said:
فأَبلُونِى بَلِيَّتَكُم لَعَلِّى * أُصلُكُمْ وأَسْتَدْرِجْ نَوَيّا
(So grant me your favour; perhaps I will make peace with you and draw back my intention.) [Translator's note: "أُصلُكُمْ" as printed is unclear; it is commonly cited as "أُصالِحُكُمْ", which the gloss follows.]
He put (وأستدرجْ) in the jussive. If you wish, you refer it to the position of the implied fāʾ in "لعلّى"; and if you wish, you take it as being in the position of the nominative and the jīm was made quiescent because of the many successive vowels. Some of the Readers read "لا يَحْزُنْهُمُ الفَزَعُ الأَكْبَر" with the jussive while intending the nominative, and they read "أَنُلْزِمْكُموها وأَنْتُمْ لها كارِهون"; and the nominative is dearer to me than the jussive.
His saying: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ...(148)﴾ — the Arabs say: "This is a matter that has no wijha, no jiha, no wajh (direction)". I heard them say: "Turn the stone — jihatun mā lahu, wijhatu mā lahu, wajhun mā lahu" (it has some direction). And they say: "Put it other than this waḍʿa, ḍiʿa, ḍaʿa (placing)." Its meaning is: turn the stone, for it has a direction. It is a proverb whose origin is in building: they say, when you see a stone in a building not settling in its place, turn it around, for you will hit upon its right side. Had they used the accusative, on [the sense of] "turn it to its direction", it would have been correct.

farraa:150-151.t:
His saying: ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَيْكُمْ حُجَّةٌ إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾ — someone may say: how did He except "those who did wrong" in this place? Perhaps they imagined that what follows "إلاّ" differs from what precedes it: if what precedes "إلاّ" is an agent [of an affirmed verb], what follows it is excluded from the verb mentioned; and if the verb is negated of what precedes it, it is affirmed for what follows "إلا". As you say "The people went except Zayd" — Zayd is excluded from going; and "The people did not go except Zayd" — Zayd went, and the going is affirmed for Zayd.
So His saying ﴿إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾ [means: except those of them who did wrong] — they have no argument, ﴿فلا تَخْشَوْهُمْ﴾. It is as you say in speech: "All the people praise [you] except the one who wrongs you and transgresses against you", for his enmity is of no account, nor is his abandoning praise because of the enmity.
Likewise the wrongdoer has no argument; and he has been called a wrongdoer.
Some of the grammarians have said: "إلا" in this place has the status of the wāw (and), as if He said ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَيْكُمْ حُجَّةٌ﴾ nor for those who did wrong. This is correct in exegesis but wrong in Arabic. "إلا" has the status of the wāw only when you conjoin it to an exception before it; there it takes the status of the wāw, as in your saying "So-and-so owes me a thousand except ten except a hundred": by the second (إلاّ) you mean to go back to the thousand, as if you had overlooked the hundred and then made it up, saying "oh, except a hundred". So the meaning is: he owes me a thousand and a hundred. And [similarly] you say "The people went except your brother — oh, except your father", excepting the second, meaning: except your father and except your brother; as the poet said:
ما بالمدينةِ دار غيرُ واحدةٍ * دارُ الخليفة إلا دارُ مَروْانا
(There is no house in Medina but one — the house of the Caliph — except the house of Marwān.)
As if he meant: there is no house in Medina except the house of the Caliph and the house of Marwān.
His saying: ﴿وَٱخْشَوْنِي﴾ — the yāʾ is retained in it and not retained elsewhere, and all of that is correct. They only allowed dropping the yāʾ because the kasra of the nūn indicates it; the Arabs are not shy of dropping the yāʾ from the end of a word when what precedes it has kasra. Of that is "رَبِّى أَكْرَمَنِ" and "أَهانَنِ" in Sūrat al-Fajr, and His saying ﴿أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ﴾; and without the nūn, "المُناد" and "الداع"; and it is much. They make do for the yāʾ with the kasra of what precedes it, and for the wāw with the ḍamma of what precedes it, as in His saying ﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانيةَ﴾ and ﴿وَيدْعُ الإنْسانُ﴾ and the like.
