The Arabs may even drop the wāw when it is the plural wāw, making do with the ḍamma before it: they say for "ḍarabū" "qad ḍarabu", and for "qālū" "qad qālu dhālika"; this is among Hawāzin and Upper Qays. One of them recited to me:
إذا ما شاءُ ضرُّوا من أرادوا * ولا يألو لهم أحد ضرارا
(Whenever they wish, they harm whom they want, and no one spares effort in harming them.)
Al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
متى تقول خَلَتْ من أهلِها الدارُ * كأنهم بجناحى طائر طاروا
(Whenever you say "the abode is empty of its people", it is as if they had flown off on the two wings of a bird.)
And one of them recited to me:
فلو أَن الأطبّا كانُ عِندِى * وكان مع الأَطِباءِ الأسَاة
(Had the physicians been with me, and with the physicians the healers…)
They do that with the feminine yāʾ, as in the saying of ʿAntara:
إن العدوّ لهم إِليك وسِيلة * إِن يأْخذوكِ تكحَّلِى وتَخَضَّبِ
(The enemy has a means of reaching you: if they take you, put on kohl and dye yourself with henna.)
They drop (the feminine yāʾ), though it is the sign of the female, making do with the kasra.
His saying: ﴿كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا فِيكُمْ﴾ is an answer to His saying ﴿فاذْكُرونِى أَذْكُرْكُمْ﴾: "as We sent"; so this is an answer (placed before and after [i.e. with inversion]).
There is another view: you make it part of what precedes it, of His saying ﴿أذكركم﴾. Do you not see that He has given His saying ﴿اذكرونى﴾ a jussive answer? (That is evidence) that the kāf in (كما) belongs to what precedes it; for you say in speech "As I have done good, do good", and you do not need to set a condition for (أحسن), because the kāf is a condition; its meaning is: do as I have done. This is more sound (anfadh) in Arabic than the first view, which is what the exegesis brought. And it is correct, like a conditional that has two answers, as in your saying "If so-and-so comes to you, go to him; you will please him": "فأتِه" and "ترضه" have become two answers.

farraa:152-152.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱشْكُرُواْ لِي﴾ — the Arabs hardly ever say "shakartuka" (I thanked you); they say "shakartu laka" and "naṣaḥtu laka" (I gave you sincere counsel).
They do not say "naṣaḥtuka", though both are sometimes said. One of the poets said:
هُمُ جَمعوا بُؤْسَى ونُعْمَى عَليكُمُ * فهلاّ شكرتَ القومَ إذ لم تقاتِلِ
(They heaped upon you both hardship and favour; so why did you not thank the people, since you did not fight?)
And al-Nābigha said:
نصحتُ بنِى عوفٍ فلم يَتَقبّلوا * رسولى ولم تَنجحْ لديهِم وسائلِى
(I counselled Banū ʿAwf, but they did not receive my messenger, and my means of approach did not succeed with them.)

farraa:154-154.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَقُولُواْ لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ﴾ — nominative, by implying a pronoun standing for their names, as in your saying: Do not say "they are dead"; rather they are alive.
The accusative is not permissible in "أموات", because saying does not act upon nouns when their subjects are implied or made overt; just as "qultu ʿAbdallāha qāʾiman" is not permissible, so the accusative of "أموات" is not permissible, because you are implying their names. The accusative after "saying" is permissible only when the noun has the sense of a saying. Of that is "qultu khayran" and "qultu sharran" (I said good, I said evil): you see "good" and "evil" in the accusative because they are sayings, as if you said: I said fine or ugly words. You say "qultu laka khayran" and "qultu laka khayrun", and both are permissible: if you make "good" a saying you put it in the accusative, as if you said "I said words to you"; if you put it in the nominative, it is not the saying, but rather it is like your saying "qultu laka mālun" [Translator's note: i.e. "I said to you: [there is] wealth", a quoted sentence].
So build on this whatever comes to you. Of the nominative is His saying ﴿سيقولُون ثَلاثَةٌ رَابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ﴾, and "خمسةٌ" and "سبعةٌ": it cannot be accusative, because it is a report about them containing implied nouns, as in your saying "they are three", "they are five". As for His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ طَاعةٌ﴾, it is nominative on a different basis. That is, it used to be said to the Arabs: "You must go on raids in winter and summer", and they would say "hearing and obedience", meaning: from us is hearing and obedience; so the speech ran in the nominative. Had it been accusative, in the sense of "we hear a hearing and obey an obedience", it would have been correct.
Likewise His saying, blessed and exalted, in Sūrat Muḥammad ﷺ: ﴿فَأَوْلَى لَهُم طَاعةٌ وقَوْلٌ مَعْرُوف﴾. He reproached and threatened them with His saying "فأولى لهم" (woe to them), then mentioned what they say, so He said: they say, when they are commanded, "Obedience!" — "فإذا عزم الأمر" (but when the matter was resolved) they shrank back and lied and did not do it. So Allah, blessed and exalted, said ﴿فلَوْ صَدَقُوا الله لكانَ خَيْراً لهم﴾. Some of them may say: "طاعة" is nominative only by His saying "لهم", [i.e.] "they should have obedience"; and that is nothing.
And Allah knows best. It is also said [that it means]: "وذكِر فيها القِتال" (and fighting was mentioned in it) "and obedience", the wāw being implied; but that is not, in our view, among the ways of the Arabs; yet if it agrees with the exegesis, it is correct.

farraa:155-155.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُمْ بِشَيْءٍ مِّنَ ٱلْخَوْفِ وَٱلْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ ٱلأَمَوَالِ وَٱلأَنفُسِ وَٱلثَّمَرَاتِ﴾ — He did not say (بأشياء) (with things) although they differ. That is because "مِن" indicates that for each kind of them there is an implied "شىء": with something of fear and something of such-and-such. Had it been "بأشياء" it would have been correct.

farraa:156-156.t:
His saying: ﴿قَالُواْ إِنَّا للَّهِ﴾ — the Arabs do not give kasra to (إنا) except in this place, with the lām, specifically in expressing grief. When they do not say (لِلّه), they give it fatḥa and say "innā li-Zaydin muḥibbūn" (we love Zayd) and "innā li-rabbinā ḥāmidūn ʿābidūn" (we praise and worship our Lord).
It was given kasra in ﴿إِنَّا للَّهِ﴾ only because it was so used that it became like a single word, so the nūn was inclined towards kasra (imāla) because of the kasra of the lām in "لِلّه"; as they say "hālik" and "kāfir" — the kāf of "kāfir" is given kasra [i.e. imāla] because of the kasra [after] the alif, since it is a single word. So "إنا لِلّهِ" became like a single word because of their frequent use of it, as they said "al-ḥamdi lillāhi".

farraa:158-158.t:
His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ حَجَّ ٱلْبَيْتَ أَوِ ٱعْتَمَرَ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا﴾ — the Muslims had disliked going between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa because of two idols that were on them; they disliked that it should be a veneration of the two idols. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلصَّفَا وَٱلْمَرْوَةَ مِن شَعَآئِرِ ٱللَّهِ فَمَنْ حَجَّ ٱلْبَيْتَ أَوِ ٱعْتَمَرَ فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا﴾. Some read it "أَلاَّ يطَّوف" (that he not go round), and this can be in two ways. One is that you make "لا" with "أنْ" a ṣila (filler) in the sense of cancellation, as He said ﴿ما مَنَعَك أَلاَّ تَسْجُدَ إذْ أَمَرْتُك﴾, meaning: what prevented you from prostrating. The other is that you make going between them something whose omission is permitted. The first is what is acted upon.
His saying: ﴿وَمَن تَطَوَّعَ خَيْراً﴾ — you give it fatḥa (as a past verb). The companions of ʿAbdullāh, and Ḥamza, [read] "وَمَنْ يَطَّوَّعْ", because in the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is "يتطوع".

farraa:159-159.t:
His saying: ﴿أُولَـٰئِكَ يَلعَنُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَيَلْعَنُهُمُ ٱللاَّعِنُونَ﴾ — Ibn ʿAbbās said: "اللاعِنون" (those who curse) are everything on the face of the earth except the two weighty ones (al-thaqalān, mankind and jinn).
[And] ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said: When two men curse each other, and one of them curses his fellow while neither deserves the curse, the curse returns to whoever deserves it; and if neither of them deserves it, it returns to the Jews who concealed what Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed. So he made the curse [come] from people who curse one another, according to what he explained.

farraa:246-246.t:
His saying: ﴿ٱبْعَثْ لَنَا مَلِكاً نُّقَاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — (نُقَاتِلْ) is jussive (majzūm); its nominative is not permissible. If it were read with the yāʾ, "yuqātil," both its nominative and its jussive would be permissible. As for the jussive, it is as the apodosis to the command; as for the nominative, it is that you make (yuqātilu) a ṣila (relative clause) for al-malik, as if you had said: send for us the one who will fight.
So when you see after the command an indefinite noun, after which comes a verb that refers back to it by a pronoun, or in which verb it is suitable to imply the noun, both the nominative and the jussive are permissible in it. You say in speech: "Teach me knowledge that I may benefit from (antafiʿu bihi)," as if you said: "Teach me that from which I benefit"; and if you put (antafiʿ) in the jussive, making it a condition [i.e. apodosis] for the command, as if you had not mentioned the knowledge, that is permissible. If you drop "bihi," it can only be jussive, because the pronoun is not permissible in (antafiʿ); do you not see that you do not say: "Teach me knowledge that I benefit it (antafiʿuhu)"?
If you say: "Why then did you not use the nominative, intending the implied (bihi)?" I say: it is not permissible to imply two words [Translator's note: the preposition and its pronoun]; therefore only the jussive is permissible in His saying (نقاتل).
Similar to it: ﴿اقتُلُوا يُوسُفَ أو اطْرَحُوهُ أرْضاً يَخْلُ لَكُمْ وَجْه أبيكم﴾ — only the jussive is permissible, because "yakhlu" does not refer back with a mention of the land. Had it been "a land that will be free (takhlu) for you," the nominative and the jussive would be permissible, as He said: ﴿رَبَّنَا وابْعَثْ فِيهم رَسُولا مِنهم يَتْلُو عليهم آياتِك ويعلِّمُهُمُ الكتَابَ والحِكمة ويزكِّيهم﴾, and as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿خُذْ مِن أَمْوَالِهِم صدقة تُطَهِّرهم وتُزَكِّيهِم﴾; had it been jussive it would be correct, for in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "أنزِل علينا مائدة من السماءِ تَكُنْ لنا عِيدا", while in our reading it is with the wāw: "takūnu".
Of it is what in which the jussive is better: that is when the verb that may be put in the jussive or nominative is in one verse, and the noun for which the verb would be a ṣila is in the verse before it; then the jussive is better because the noun is cut off from its ṣila. Of that: ﴿فهَبْ لِى مِن لدنك ولِيّاً. يرِثنى﴾ — Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read it in the jussive — and Ḥamza read it in the nominative, "yarithunī" [Translator's note: so in the text; elsewhere Ḥamza is reported with the jussive here], for this reason, and some of the Readers also read it in the nominative — since (وليا) was the end of a verse, His saying (يرثنى) was cut off from it, so the jussive was good. Of that is His saying: ﴿وابْعَثْ فى المدائن حاشِرين. يَأتُوك﴾ in the jussive. Had it been nominative as a ṣila of "al-ḥāshirīn," you would say: yaʾtūnaka.
If the noun after which comes a verb referring back to it is definite — of the kind in whose indefinite two possibilities are allowed — you use the jussive, saying: "Send your brother to me, he will bring (yuṣib) news"; it can only be jussive, because al-akh is definite and a definite cannot take a ṣila [of this kind]. Of it is His saying: ﴿أَرْسِلْهُ مَعَنَا غَداً يَرْتَعْ وَيَلْعَبْ﴾ — the hāʾ is definite, and "ghadan" is definite, so there is only the jussive in it; and like His saying: ﴿قاتِلوهم يُعَذِّبْهُمُ الله﴾ — jussive and nothing else.
Of this there is a type where, when after its definite noun there is a verb belonging to it, the nominative and the jussive are both permissible; like His saying: ﴿فَذَرُوهَا تَأْكُلْ فى أَرْضِ الله﴾ and His saying: ﴿ذَرْهُمْ يأْكُلُوا﴾; had it been nominative it would be correct, as He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ثُمَّ ذَرْهُمْ فى خَوْضِهِم يَلْعَبُون﴾, and did not say: yalʿabū.
As for its nominative, it is that you make "yalʿabūna" in the position of the accusative, as if you said in speech: "Leave them playing (lāʿibīna)." Likewise daʿhum, khallihim and utrukhum. Every verb that can act on a definite noun and on its action has these two possibilities, and the jussive is the proper way of speech in it, because the condition sits well in it and because the command in it is easy; do you not see that you say: "Tell him, and let him stand with you"?
If you see that the second verb admits the test of the command [i.e. can be recast as a command], it has both possibilities in the same manner. In one of the two readings: "ذَرْهُمْ يَأْكُلُونَ ويَتَمَتَّعون ويلهِيهم الأَمل".
There is another way in it that sits well with the first verb. Of that: "Instruct him to come (yaʾti) to Zayd," or "Command him," or "Send to him." This goes the way of speech [qawl], and its jussive is akin to a command intended for him anew. It is put in the jussive only as a condition [apodosis] of its first [part]. Of that is your saying: "Command ʿAbdullāh, he will go (yadhhab) with us"; do you not see that "say" can be put in the place of (mur)? And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿قُلْ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَغْفِرُوا لِلذين لاَ يَرْجُونَ أيَّامَ الله﴾ — "yaghfirū" is in the position of the jussive, and the interpretation — and Allah knows best — is: Say to those who believe: forgive; as a condition [apodosis] of the command that carries the interpretation of reported speech (ḥikāya). Similar to it: ﴿قل لِعبادِى يَقُولُوا الَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَن﴾ — you put it in the jussive by the condition "qul." Some said: [it is jussive] by the intention of a command in these words: of saying, commanding and instructing. It was said to them: if it is jussive as reported speech, then you ought to say to a man to his face: "I told you you stand (taqum)," and you ought to say: "I commanded you you go (tadhhab) with us." This is evidence that it is a condition of the command. If you say: "But the poet said:
فلا تستطِلْ منّى بقائى ومُدّتِى * ولكن يكن للخير فيك نصيب
(Do not find my survival and my lifespan too long; rather, let goodness have a share in you.)"
I say: this is jussive by the intention of a command, because the beginning of the speech is a prohibition, and his saying (ولكن) is a conjunction and not an apodosis; he meant: but let goodness have a share in you. Similar to it is the other's saying:
من كان لا يزعم أنى شاعرُ * فَيَدْنُ منى تنهَه المزاجِر
(Whoever does not allow that I am a poet, let him draw near me — the rebukes will restrain him.)
He made the fāʾ the answer of the condition and implied in (fa-yadnu) a lām that puts [it] in the jussive. And the other said:
فقلت ادْعِى وأَدْعُ فإنَّ أَنْدَى * لصوتٍ أن ينادِىَ داعيان
(So I said: Call out, and let me call, for the farthest-carrying for a voice is that two callers call.)
He meant: wa-li-adʿu. And in his saying (وأَدْع) there is a trace of the condition, even though it is a command whose first part is conjoined on its last. It is like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿اتَّبِعوا سبِيلنا ولْنحمِل خطاياكم﴾, and Allah knows best. As for His saying: ﴿ذَرُونِى أَقْتُلْ مُوسَى وَلْيَدْعُ رَبَّه﴾, it does not have the interpretation of a condition; it is purely a command, because dropping the wāw and turning it back to the condition (does not sit well, so it is not a condition); do you not see that it does not sit well to say: "Leave me, I will kill him, he will call (yadʿu)," as "Follow our way, we will carry (taḥmil) your sins" sits well? [Translator's note: so in the text: تَحْمل.]
The Arabs do not give an apodosis to a prohibition as they give one to a command. That is because the prohibition comes with negation, and the Arabs do not give an apodosis to any negation; they answer it only with the fāʾ. And they joined the prohibition, when it is with lā, to laysa and mā and their sisters among negations. So if you see a prohibition after whose noun there is a verb, put that verb in the nominative. You say: "Do not let him hit him (yaḍribuhu)," and "Do not leave him hitting you (yaḍribuka)." They made it nominative since its end did not match its beginning, since in its beginning there is negation and in its end there is no negation. If you said: "Do not leave him — let him not harm you (lā yuʾdhika)," the jussive and the nominative would be permissible, since its beginning is like its end; as you say in the command: "Leave him, he sleeps (yanāmu)," and "Leave him, he will sleep (yanam)," since there is no negation in either. If you command and then put (lā) in the verb, you use the nominative, again because of their difference, saying: "Come to us — we will not harm you (lā nusīʾu ilayka)," as in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿وأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بالصَّلاَةِ واصْطَبِرْ عليها لا نسألك رِزقا﴾ — [since] the beginning of the speech was a command and its end a negation with (lā), and they differed, (lā) was made in the sense of laysa, so it was put in the nominative. Of that is His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿فَقَاتِلْ فِى سَبِيلِ الله لاَ تُكَلَّفُ إلاّ نَفْسَكَ﴾ and His saying: ﴿يَأَيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا عَلَيْكُم أَنْفُسَكم لا يَضُرُّكُم مَنْ ضَلَّ إذَا اهْتديتم﴾ — nominative. And of it is His saying: ﴿فاجعل بيننا وبينك مَوْعِداً لا نُخلِفُهُ﴾ — you use the nominative, and had you intended the condition it would be permissible by the analogy of grammar. Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and Ḥamza read: "فاضْرِبْ لهم طرِيقا فى البحر يَبَساً لا تخف دركا ولا تخشى" as a pure apodosis.
If you say: "Then how was the yāʾ kept in (تخشى)?" I say: there are three ways regarding that. If you wish, you make "wa-lā takhshā" a fresh start after the jussive. If you wish, you make (takhshā) in the position of the jussive even though the yāʾ is in it, because some of the Arabs do that; one of Banū ʿAbs said:
ألم يأتيك والأنباءُ تَنْمِى * بما لاقت لَبُونُ بنى زياد
(Has it not reached you — and the news spreads — what the milch-camels of Banū Ziyād met with?)
So the yāʾ was kept in (يأتيك) while it is in the position of the jussive, because he saw it as quiescent and left it in its quiescence, as is done with the other letters. And one of Banū Ḥanīfa recited to me:
قال لها مِن تحتها وما استوى * هُزِّى إليِك الجِذْع يَجنِيك الجَنَى
(He said to her from beneath her, before he had grown: Shake the trunk toward you, it will yield you the ripe fruit.)
and he ought to have said: yajniki. And one of them recited to me with the wāw:
هجوتَ زَبّان ثم جئت معتذِرا * من سبّ زَبَّان لم تهجو ولم تدع
(You lampooned Zabbān, then came apologizing for insulting Zabbān — you did not [truly] lampoon, nor did you leave off.)
The third way is that the yāʾ is an extension (ṣila) of the fatḥa of the shīn, as Imruʾ al-Qays said:
* ألا أيُّها الليلُ الطويل ألا انجلى *
(O long night, will you not clear away?)
This yāʾ is not the final radical of the verb; it is an extension of the kasra of the lām, just as rhymes are extended by the vowel of their rhyme-letter, like the saying of al-Aʿshā:
* بانت سُعَادُ وأمسى حبلُها انقطاعا *
(Suʿād has gone away, and her bond has come to be severed.)
and the other's saying:
* أمِن أُمِّ أوفى دِمْنةٌ لم تكلمى *
(Is it of Umm Awfā — a campsite trace that does not speak?)
The second [verb] may be jussive, when it has (lā), on the intention of a prohibition while carrying some meaning of the condition, just as in His saying ﴿وَلْنَحْمِلْ خَطَايَاكُمْ﴾ there is a trace of the condition while it is a command. Of that is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿يأيُّها النَّمل ادْخُلُوا مَساكِنَكُم لا يَحْطِمَنَّكُم سُلَيْمانُ وجُنُوده﴾ — the meaning, and Allah knows best: if you do not enter, you will be crushed; and it is a pure prohibition, because had it been an apodosis neither the heavy nor the light nūn would enter it; do you not see that you do not say: "If you hit me I will surely hit you (aḍribannaka)," except in poetic necessity, as in his saying:
فمهما تشأ منه فَزَارةُ تُعْطِكُم * ومهما تَشَأ منه فَزَارةُ تمنعَا
(Whatever of it Fazāra wishes, it will give you; and whatever of it Fazāra wishes, it will surely withhold.)
His saying: ﴿وَمَا لَنَآ أَلاَّ نُقَاتِلَ﴾ — (أَن) came in one place and was dropped in another. He said in another place: ﴿وَمَا لَكُمْ لا تُؤْمِنونَ بالله والرَّسُولُ يَدْعُوكم﴾, and He said in another place: ﴿وما لنا ألاَّ نتوكّل على الله﴾. Whoever drops (an), the word is in the manner of Arabic in which there is no problem, and the verb is in the position of the accusative [Translator's note: as a ḥāl], like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فما لِلَّذينَ كفروا قِبَلَكَ مُهْطعين﴾ and like His saying: ﴿فما لَكُمْ فى المنافِقِين فِئَتَيْنِ﴾. This is the proper way of speech in your saying: mā laka? mā bāluka? and mā shaʾnuka?: that you put what follows it in the accusative when it is a noun, and in the nominative when it is a verb beginning with yāʾ, tāʾ, nūn or alif, like the poet's saying:
* مالك تَرْغِين ولا تَرْغُو الخَلِفْ *
(What is wrong with you that you groan, while the pregnant she-camel does not groan?)
Al-khalifa: the one with her young in her belly.
As for when He said (أن), it is of what goes toward the meaning that admits the entry of (an); do you not see that your saying to a man: "What is wrong with you that you do not pray in congregation?" means "What prevents you from praying?" So (an) was put into (mā laka) since its meaning agreed with the meaning of preventing. The proof of that is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿مَا مَنَعَكَ أن لا تسجد إذ أمرتك﴾ and in another place: ﴿مالك ألاّ تكون مع الساجدين﴾; the story of Iblīs is one, and He said it in two wordings whose meaning is one even though they differ.
Similar to it — what is carried on a meaning different from its counterpart in wording — is the poet's saying:
يقول إذا اقْلَوْلى عليها وأقْرَدَتْ * ألا هل أخو عيشٍ لذيذ بدائم
(He says, when he mounts high upon her and she grows still: Is the man of a pleasant life ever lasting?)
He put the bāʾ in (hal), which is interrogative, whereas the bāʾ enters only the mā of negation, as when you say: "You are not one to say (mā anta bi-qāʾil)." Since the intention in (hal) was negation, the bāʾ was put in for it. Similar to it is His saying in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "كَيْفَ يكونُ لِلمشْرِكين عَهْدٌ": [meaning] the idolaters have no [covenant]. Likewise the poet's saying:
فاذهب فأىُّ فتىً فى الناس أحرزه * من يومه ظُلَمٌ دُعْج ولا جَبَل
(Go, then: what young man among people have pitch-dark shadows protected from his fated day — nor a mountain?)
(he answered it with lā) as though the meaning of "what young man among people have they protected" is: pitch-dark shadows do not protect the young man from his fated day, nor does a mountain. Al-Kisāʾī said: I heard the Arabs say: "Where were you to escape me (ayna kunta li-tanjuwa minnī)!" because the meaning is: you were not going to escape me; so he put the lām in (ayna) because its meaning is negation: you were not going to escape me. And the poet said:
فهذى سيوف يا صُدَىُّ بن مالك * كثير ولكن أين بالسيف ضارب
(Here are swords, O Ṣudayy ibn Mālik, many — but where is one who strikes with the sword?)
He meant: there is no one striking with the sword; had he not meant (laysa), the expression would not be permissible, because the bāʾ belongs to the ṣila of (ḍārib), and the complement of a noun is not put before it; do you not see that you do not say: "I struck with the slave girl a guarantor," until you say: "I struck a guarantor with the slave girl"? [Translator's note: the example is as written; the point is the word order of the prepositional complement.] And it is permissible to say: "There is no guarantor for the slave girl (laysa bi-l-jāriya kafīl)," because (laysa) is the counterpart of (mā), since it is not proper for it to put the noun in the nominative just as (mā) does not put it in the nominative.
Al-Kisāʾī said of their putting (an) in (mā laka): it is like His saying: "What is wrong with you in not fighting (mā lakum fī allā tuqātilū)." Had it been as he said, it would be permissible in speech to say: "What is wrong with you that you stood (an qumta)," and "What is wrong with you that you are standing (annaka qāʾim)," because you say "in your standing" both past and future; that is not permissible, because preventing comes only with the future: you say: "I prevented you from standing (an taqūma)," and you do not say: "I prevented you that you stood (an qumta)."
Therefore it comes in (mā laka) with the future and does not come with the continuous or the past. That is a witness to the agreement of the meaning of mā laka and mā manaʿaka. Some grammarians have said: it is among the cases where the wāw is implied, deleted from what is like your saying in speech: "What have you to do with going to so-and-so (mā laka wa-li-an tadhhaba)?" — so the wāw was dropped from it because (an) is a word not firmly established among nouns.
It was said [to him]: "Do you permit me to say: mā laka an taqūma, and not permit: mā laka al-qiyāma?" [He said]: "Because al-qiyām is a sound noun and (an) is a noun that is not sound." He argued from the saying of the Arabs: "Beware of speaking (iyyāka an tatakallama)," and claimed that the meaning is: iyyāka wa-an tatakallama. This was refuted against him by the fact that the Arabs say: "Beware of uttering falsehood (iyyāka bi-l-bāṭili an tanṭiqa)"; had the wāw been implied with (an), the verbs after the wāw could not act on what precedes it; do you not see that it is not permissible to say: "I hit you with the slave girl, and you are a guarantor," meaning: and you are a guarantor for the slave girl? And you say: "I saw you, and it is us you want (wa-iyyānā turīdu)," and it is not permissible: "I saw you us, and you want." The poet said:
فبُحْ بالسرائر فى أهلها * وإيّاك فى غيرهم أن تبوحا
(Disclose secrets among those fit for them, and beware of disclosing them among others.)
So the verb after (an) was allowed to act on his saying (فى غيرهم), and that shows that implying the wāw with (an) is not permissible.
As for the poet's saying:
* فإياك المَحَايِن أن تحينا *
(Beware of the places of perdition, lest you perish.)
he warned him, saying "iyyāka," then intended a pause, then began (al-maḥāyin) with another command, as if he said: beware of the places of perdition. Had he meant something like "iyyāka wa-l-bāṭila," dropping the wāw would not be permissible, because it is a noun made to follow a noun in its accusative, so it would be like his saying outside [the case of] the command: "You and your opinion," and "every garment and its price"; just as "You your opinion" or "every garment its price" is not permissible, so "iyyāka al-bāṭila" is not permissible when you mean: iyyāka wa-l-bāṭila.

farraa:249-249.t:
His saying: ﴿فَشَرِبُواْ مِنْهُ إِلاَّ قَلِيلاً مِّنْهُمْ﴾ — in one of the two readings: "إلا قليلٌ منهم" (in the nominative).
The proper way with (illā) is that what follows it is put in the accusative when what precedes it contains no negation. When what precedes illā contains negation, you make what follows it follow what precedes it [in case], whether it is definite or indefinite.
As for the definite, it is your saying: "The people did not go except Zayd (illā Zaydun)." As for the indefinite, it is your saying: "There is no one in it except your slave (illā ghulāmuka)"; this has not come from the Arabs except with what follows illā following what precedes it. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ما فعلوه إلاّ قليل مِنهم﴾, because in (faʿalūhu) there is a definite noun [Translator's note: the pronoun], so the nominative was the proper way in the negation that negates the act of them and affirms it for what follows illā. In the reading of Ubayy it is "ما فعلوه إلا قليلا", as if he negated the act and made what follows illā as though cut off from the beginning of the speech, as when you say: "The people did not stand — except, O Allah, a man (illā rajulan)." So if you intend the cut-off [exception] you use the accusative, and if you intend the connected [exception] you use the nominative. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿فلولا كانت قرية آمنت فنفعها إِيمانها إلا قوم يونس﴾ — this is on this meaning; and similar to it: ﴿فلولا كان مِن القُرُونِ مِن قَبْلِكم أُولُو بقِيّةٍ ينهون عن الفساد فى الأرض﴾, then He said: ﴿إلا قلِيلا ممن أَنجينا منهم﴾. The beginning of the speech — even though it is a question — is a negation, because lawlā is equivalent to hallā; do you not see that when you say to a man: (hallā qumta, "why did you not stand?") its meaning is: you did not stand. Had what follows (illā) in these two verses been nominative with the intention of connection, it would have been correct, like His saying: ﴿لو كان فيهما آلهة إلاَّ اللّهُ لفسدتا﴾ — this is the intention of connection, because it is not permissible to pause on what precedes (illā).
If you do not see a noun before (illā), make what precedes it act on what follows it. You say: (mā qāma illā Zaydun) — you put (Zayd) in the nominative because you make (qāma) act, since you found no noun for (qāma) [before illā]. Likewise: "I hit none but your brother (illā akhāka)," and "I passed by none but your brother (illā bi-akhīka)."
When what precedes (illā) is indefinite with a negation, you make what follows illā follow what precedes it, as when you say: "There is no one with me except your brother (illā akhūka)." If you put illā first, you put in the accusative what you used to put in the nominative, saying: "None came to me except your brother — no one (mā atānī illā akhāka aḥadun)." That is because (illā) was conjoined onto what preceded it, so it followed it; when it was put first, it was prevented from following something that is after it, so they chose the exception [accusative]. Similar to it is the poet's saying:
لَمِيَّة مُوحِشاً طَلَلٌ * يلوح كأنه خِلَل
(Mayya has a desolate ruin that gleams as if it were sheath-linings.)
The meaning is: Mayya has a desolate ruin (ṭalalun mūḥishun); its nominative was right because it followed al-ṭalal, but when it was put first, it could not follow al-ṭalal which comes after it. Its nominative may be permissible if you make it like a noun of which al-ṭalal is an explanation, as you say: "I have a Khurāsānī — a slave girl (khurāsāniyyatun jāriyatun)," though the proper way is the accusative in khurāsāniyya. Some of the Arabs put in the nominative what is placed first with illā according to this explanation. He said: and they recited to us:
بالثِنْىِ أسفلَ من جَمَّاءَ ليس له * إلاَّ بنيهِ وإلا عِرْسَه شِيعَ
(At the bend below Jammāʾ, he has no followers save his sons and save his wife.)
And it is recited: illā banūhu wa-illā ʿirsuhu. Abū Tharwān recited:
ما كان منذ تركنا أهل أَسْمنُةٍ * إلا الوجيفَ لها رِعْىٌ ولا عَلَفُ
(Since we left the people of Asmuna, she has had no pasture nor fodder save hard travel.)
and someone else recited it in the nominative. Dhū al-Rumma said:
مُقَزَّعٌ أطلسُ الأطمارِ ليس له * إلا الضِرَاءَ وإلا صيدَها نَشَبُ
(Thin-haired, in grey rags, he has no property save his hunting hounds and save what they hunt.)
Its nominative is on the basis that he built his speech on: "he has nothing but the hounds and their prey," and then mentioned (nashab) at the end of the speech; it becomes clear if you put its place at the beginning of the speech.
﴿كَم مِّن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةًً﴾ — in the reading of Ubayy: "كأيّن مِن فِئةٍ قليلة غلبت", and they are two dialects. Likewise ﴿وكأيّن من نبى﴾ — they are all dialects whose meaning is the meaning of kam. If you drop (min), the indefinite noun has the accusative and the genitive. Of that is the saying of the Arabs: "How many a noble man (kam rajulin karīmin) I have seen!" and "How many a vast army (kam jayshan jarrāran) I have defeated!" These are two ways: they are put in the accusative and in the genitive, and the verb in meaning acts on [them]. If the verb does not act on [it] but belongs to the noun [as its agent], the accusative and the genitive are also permissible; and it is permissible to make the verb act and put the indefinite in the nominative by it, saying: "How many a noble man (kam rajulun karīmun) has come to me," putting it in the nominative by its verb; and you make the verb act on it if it falls on it, saying: "How many a vast army (kam jayshan jarrāran) I have defeated," putting it in the accusative by hazamtu. They recited the poet's saying:
كم عمَّة لك يا جَرِيرُ وخالة * فَدْعاء قد حَلَبَتْ علىَّ عِشارِى
(How many a paternal aunt of yours, O Jarīr, and maternal aunt with crooked fingers have milked my ten-month pregnant camels for me!)
in the nominative, the accusative and the genitive. Whoever uses the accusative says: the origin of kam was the interrogative, and the indefinite after it is a specification like the specification of numbers; so we left it in the declarative in its own manner and as it was in the interrogative, and put in the accusative the indefinites after (kam), as you say: "I have such-and-such dirhams (dirhaman)." Whoever uses the genitive says: min has long accompanied the indefinite with kam, so when we deleted it, we made its intention operative, and put it in the genitive, just as the Arabs said, when one of them was asked: "How are you this morning?" — "Well (khayrin), may Allah keep you well," in the genitive, meaning: bi-khayrin. As for whoever uses the nominative, he made the later verb operative [and] intended the verb to come first, as if he said: how many times has a noble man come to me. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
تَبُوصُ وكَمْ مِن دونها من مفازةٍ * وكم أرضُ جَدْب دونها ولُصُوصُ
(She draws away — and how many a desert lies short of her, and how many a barren land and thieves lie short of her!)
He used the nominative on the intention of putting the verb first. The verb is made to come first in intention only because indefinites do not precede their verbs [i.e. their predicates]; do you not see that you say: "There is nothing with me (mā ʿindī shayʾun)," and you do not say: "mā shayʾun ʿindī"?

farraa:161-161.t:
His saying: ﴿إِن الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَمَاتُوا وَهُمْ كُفَّارٌ أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ — "الملائكة والناس" are in the position of the genitive (khafḍ); the curse is annexed to them, in the sense: upon them is the curse of Allah, the curse of the angels and the curse of the people. Al-Ḥasan read it "لعنة اللّهِ والملائِكةُ والناسُ أجمعون", which is permissible in Arabic, even though it differs from the written text. That is because your saying (عليهم لعنة اللّهِ) is like your saying "Allah curses them, and the angels and the people curse them". The Arabs say "ʿajibtu min ẓulmika nafsaka" (I marvelled at your wronging yourself), putting "nafs" in the accusative, because the kāf is nominative in interpretation [i.e. the agent]. And they say "ʿajibtu min ghalabatika nafsuka" (I marvelled at your self's overpowering you), putting "nafs" in the nominative, because the kāf is accusative in interpretation. So build on this whatever comes to you.
Of that is the Arabs' saying "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭi l-buyūti baʿḍuhā ʿalā baʿḍin" and "baʿḍihā ʿalā baʿḍin" (I marvelled at the houses falling one upon another). Whoever uses the nominative refers "baʿḍ" to the interpretation of "the houses", because they are nominative [in sense]; do you not see that the meaning is: I marvelled that they fell, one upon another? And whoever uses the genitive makes it follow the wording of "the houses", as if he said: at the falling of one of them upon another. The nominative is best when the first [noun], which is nominative or accusative in interpretation, has been replaced by a pronoun, as in your saying "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭihā". Here you say "ʿajibtu min tasāquṭihā baʿḍuhā ʿalā baʿḍin", because when the genitive is a pronoun it is ugly to qualify it with an overt noun, so it is referred to the meaning, which would be nominative if overt; and the genitive is permissible. You do the like of this with what is accusative in interpretation, saying "ʿajibtu min idkhālihim baʿḍahum fī ithri baʿḍin" (I marvelled at their bringing in some of them after others): you prefer the accusative in (baʿḍahum), and the genitive is permissible.

farraa:164-164.t: His saying: ﴿وَتَصْرِيفِ ٱلرِّيَاحِ﴾ — it comes once as a south wind, once as a north wind, and as an east wind and a west wind. That is its turning about.

farraa:165-165.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ أَندَاداً يُحِبُّونَهُمْ كَحُبِّ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — He means — and Allah knows best — they love the rivals as the believers love Allah. Then He said: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ أَشَدُّ حُبّاً للَّهِ﴾ than those [are] for the rivals.
His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ يَرَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوۤاْ إِذْ يَرَوْنَ ٱلْعَذَابَ﴾ — He makes "يرى" act upon "أن القوة لله وأن الله", and its answer (jawāb) is left out. And Allah knows best.
(And His saying): ﴿ولَوْ أنَّ قُرْآناً سُيِّرَتْ به الجِبالُ أَوْ قُطِّعَتْ﴾ — leaving out the answer is frequent in the Qur'an, because the meanings of Paradise and the Fire are repeated and known. If you wish, you give kasra to both "إنّ"s and make "يرى" act upon "إذ" in meaning. Giving fatḥa to both "أنّ"s with the yāʾ [reading يرى] is better than giving them kasra.
Whoever reads "وَلَوْ تَرَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا" with the tāʾ, the normal way of speech would be to say "إن القوة..." with kasra, "وإِن..."; because "ترى" has acted upon (الذين ظلموا), so "إِن — (وإنّ)" are begun afresh. Had you given them fatḥa, by repeating the seeing from "ترى" and from "يرى", it would have been correct, as if He said: "ولو ترى الذين ظلموا إذ يرون العذاب" — they see ﴿أَنَّ ٱلْقُوَّةَ للَّهِ جَمِيعاً﴾.

farraa:170-170.t:
His saying: ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ﴾ — you give this wāw fatḥa, because it is "wa-law" of conjunction onto which the interrogative alif has been brought; it is not (أو) whose wāw is quiescent, because the alif of "أَوْ" may not be dropped, while the interrogative alif can be dropped: you say "wa-law kāna", and "a-wa-law kāna" when you ask a question.
Allah reproached them with this only because they said ﴿بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ مَآ أَلْفَيْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَآءَنَآ﴾. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: O Muḥammad, say ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ﴾. He said "آباؤهم" because of their absence; had it been "آباؤكم" it would be permissible, because the command to speak occurs as an address, as in your saying "Say to Zayd: let him stand" and "Say to him: stand". Similar are ﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ الشَّيْطَانُ يَدْعُوهُمْ﴾ and ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا﴾.
Whoever makes the wāw quiescent in His saying ﴿أَوْ آبَاؤُنا الأَوَّلُونَ﴾ in al-Wāqiʿa and the like of it in the Qur'an makes it "أو" which affirms one of two. And this wāw, in having fatḥa, is like His saying ﴿أَثُمَّ إِذا مَا وَقَعَ﴾: the interrogative alif entered upon "ثُمّ"; and likewise "أفلم يسِيروا".

farraa:171-171.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي يَنْعِقُ﴾ — He annexed the likeness to those who disbelieve, then likened them to the shepherd, and did not say "like the sheep". The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: the likeness of those who disbelieve is (like the likeness of the beasts) which understand nothing of what the shepherd says beyond the sound; if he said to them "graze" or "drink", they would not know what he was saying to them. Such is the likeness of those who disbelieve regarding what comes to them of the Qur'an and the warning of the Messenger. So the comparison was annexed to the shepherd, while the meaning — and Allah knows best — is about the herd. This is common in the speech of the Arabs: they say "So-and-so fears you as the fear of the lion", the meaning being "as his fear of the lion", because the lion is the one known to be feared. The poet said:
لقد خِفْتُ حتى ما تزِيدُ مخافتِى * على وَعِلٍ فى ذى المَطَارة عاقِلِ
(I feared so much that my fear does not exceed that of a mountain goat taking refuge in Dhū l-Maṭāra.)
The meaning is: until the fear of a mountain goat does not exceed my fear. Another said:
كانت فرِيضةَ ما تقول كما * كان الزِناءُ فرِيضةَ الرَّجْمِ
(What you say was an obligation, just as adultery was the obligation of stoning.)
The meaning is: as stoning was the obligation for adultery. The poet takes liberties with placing the word in its proper order because the meaning is clear to the Arabs. One of them recited to me:
إِن سِراجا لكرِيم مَفْخَرُهْ * تَحْلَى بِهِ العينُ إِذا ما تَجْهَرُهْ
(Sirāj is noble in his glory; the eye is adorned by him when it beholds him.)
The eye is not adorned by him; rather he is adorned by it.
There is another meaning in it: you annex the likeness to (الذين كفروا) while its annexation in meaning is to the admonition, as if you said: the likeness of admonishing those who disbelieve, and of their admonisher, is like that of the one who calls out [to the flock]; just as you say "When you meet so-and-so, greet him with the greeting of the emir", meaning only: as you greet the emir.
The poet said:
فلستُ مُسَلَّما ما دمْتُ حيّاً * على زيدٍ بِتسلِيم الأمير
(As long as I live I will not greet Zayd with the greeting of the emir.)
All is correct.
His saying: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لاَ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ — nominative, and this is the normal way of speech, because it is a fresh statement, as shown by His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾, just as you say in speech: "He is deaf, so he does not hear; he is mute, so he does not speak." Had it been accusative by way of censure (shatm), like the words at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara in the reading of ʿAbdullāh, "وتركهم فى ظلماتٍ لا يبصِرون صُمّاً بُكْماً عُمْياً", it would be permissible. [Translator's note: the text has "الشمّ"; it is evidently "الشتم" (censure).]

farraa:173-173.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْمَيْتَةَ وَٱلدَّمَ وَلَحْمَ ٱلْخِنزِيرِ﴾ — accusative, because "حرّم" acts upon them. That is because your saying "إنّا" [Translator's note: so in the text; evidently "إنّما"] has two aspects. One is that you make "إنّما" a single particle, then let the verbs that come after it act upon the nouns: if they are nominative-governing you use the nominative, and if accusative-governing you use the accusative. So you say: "innamā dakhaltu dāraka" (I only entered your house), "innamā aʿjabatnī dāruka" (only your house pleased me), "innamā mālī māluka" (my wealth is only your wealth). Here it is a single particle.
The other aspect is that you make [Translator's note: the text has "بجعل", for "تجعل"] "ما" separate from (إنّ), so that "ما" has the sense of "الذى" (that which). When it is so, you join it to what "الذى" is joined to [i.e. a ṣila], then put the noun that comes after the ṣila in the nominative, as in your saying "inna mā akhadhta māluka" (what you took is your wealth) and "inna mā rakibta dābbatuka" (what you rode is your mount), meaning: inna lladhī rakibta dābbatuka, inna lladhī akhadhta māluka. So treat them according to this.
It occurs in the Revelation in more than one place. Of that is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿إِنَّمَا اللّهُ إِلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾ and ﴿إِنَّمَا أَنْت نَذِيرٌ﴾ — these are a single particle, it and "إنّ", because "الذى" is not fitting in the place of "ما".
As for the one in the manner of (الذى), it is His saying ﴿إنَّمَا صَنَعُوا كَيْدُ سَاحِرٍ﴾, meaning: that which they made is the plot of a sorcerer. Had a reader read "إِنما صنعوا كيدَ ساحِرٍ" in the accusative, it would be correct if he made "إنّ" and "ما" a single particle. And His saying ﴿إِنَّمَا اتَّخَذْتُمْ مِنْ دُونِ اللّهِ أَوْثَاناً مَوَدَّةَ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾: some put "المودّة" in the accusative and others in the nominative, according to the two aspects I have explained to you. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "إنما مودَّةُ بَيْنِكُمْ فِى الحياةِ الدنيا"; this is an argument for whoever puts "المودّة" in the nominative, because it is begun afresh and "taking" does not act upon it. So it is like your saying: "What you made is not beneficial — [it is] a friendship among you, then it will be cut off afterwards." If you wish, you make "المودّة" nominative by "بين"; and if you wish, you imply before it a noun that makes it nominative, as in His saying "سُورَةٌ أَنْزَلْنَاهَا", and as in His saying ﴿لم يَلْبَثُوا إِلاَّ سَاعَةً مِنْ نَهَارٍ بَلاَغٌ فَهَلْ يُهْلَكُ﴾.
When you see "إنَّما" with, at its end, a noun denoting people or the like — that to which "مَنْ" applies — do not take "ما" in it in the manner of (الذى), because the Arabs hardly ever use "ما" for people. Of that is "innamā ḍarabtu akhāka" (I only struck your brother); and do not say "akhūka", because "ما" is not used for people.
When the noun after "إنَّما" and its ṣila is not of people, both aspects are permissible for you: you say "innamā sakantu dāraka" (I only lived in your house) and, if you wish, "dāruka" (what I lived in is your house). The Arabs do in some speech use "ما" for people, but it is not frequent. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "وَالنَّهَارِ إِذا تَجَلَّى والذَّكَرِ والأُنْثَى", and in our reading: "ومَا خَلَقَ الذَّكَرَ والأُنْثَى". Whoever makes "ما خلق" refer to the male and the female may put "الذكرِ والأنثى" in the genitive, as if He said: and by the One who created — the male and the female. And whoever puts "الذكر" in the accusative makes "ما" and "خلق" like His saying "and by His creating the male and the female", making "خلق" act upon it. The genitive in it, according to the reading of ʿAbdullāh, is good, and the accusative is more common.
Had you read "إنّما حَرَّم عليكم الميتةُ" in the nominative, it would be a valid view. Some read "إنما حُرِّم عليكم المِّيتةُ", and here only the nominative of "الميتة" and "الدم" is permissible: because if you make "إنّما" a single particle, you put "الميتة" and "الدم" in the nominative since it is a verb whose agent is not named [i.e. passive]; and if you take "ما" in the manner of (الذى), you put "الميتة" and "الدم" in the nominative because it is the khabar (predicate) of "ما".
His saying: ﴿وَمَآ أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ — al-ihlāl: what was called out over the slaughtered animals for other than Allah. [His saying] ﴿فَمَنِ ٱضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلاَ عَادٍ﴾ — [(غير) in this place is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the one compelled, as if you said: whoever is compelled, not transgressing and not exceeding] — it is lawful for him. The accusative here is like His saying ﴿أُحِلَّتْ لَكُمْ بَهِيمَةُ الأَنْعَامِ إِلاَّ مَا يُتْلَى عَلَيْكُمْ غَيْرَ مُحِلِّى الصَّيْدِ﴾, and similar is ﴿إِلاَّ أَنْ يُؤْذَنَ لَكُمْ إِلَى طَعَامٍ غَيْرَ نَاظِرِينَ إِنَاهُ﴾. "غير" here means "لا"; "لا" is fitting in its place, because "لا" fits in the place of "غير". When you see "غير" in whose place "لا" is fitting, it differs from the "غير" in whose place "لا" is not fitting.
Carrion is not lawful for the one compelled if he attacks people with his sword or is on one of the paths of disobedience. It is said that the one who eats it should not eat his fill of it, nor take any of it as provision.
He is only granted a concession in what keeps him alive.

farraa:175-175.t: His saying: ﴿فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ﴾ — there are two views on it. One, its meaning is: what is it that made them endure the Fire? The other view: how bold they are towards the Fire! Al-Kisāʾī said: The judge of Yemen asked me while he was in Mecca, saying: "Two men of the Arabs brought a dispute before me, and one of them swore [falsely] regarding his fellow's right, so [the other] said to him: 'How enduring you are towards Allah (mā aṣbaraka ʿalā llāh)!'" In this it may be meant: how enduring you are of the punishment of Allah; then "the punishment" is dropped and it becomes [complete] speech, as you say "How like your generosity is to Ḥātim", [meaning to Ḥātim's generosity].

farraa:35-35.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَقْرَبَا هَـٰذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا﴾. If you wish, you make ﴿فتكونا﴾ an answer (jawāb), in the accusative; and if you wish, you conjoin it to the beginning of the speech, so that it is jussive (majzūm), as in the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:
فقلتُ له صَوِّبْ ولا تَجْهَدَنَّهُ * فَيُذْرِكَ مِنْ أُخْرَى الْقَطاةِ فَتَزْلِقُ
(I said to him: "Lower him [Translator's note: your horse] and do not overtax him, lest he throw you off the back of his rump and you slip.")
— where he used the jussive. The meaning of the jussive is as if it were a repetition of the prohibition, as when someone says: لا تذهب ولا تعرض لأحد (do not go, and do not accost anyone). The meaning of the answer with the accusative is: do not do this, lest it be done to you in requital. When a word was conjoined to something not of its kind, and at its beginning there was an element (ḥādith) [Translator's note: i.e. the prohibition] that is not appropriate in the second, it was put in the accusative. Similar to it are His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِى﴾, ﴿لاَ تَفْتَرُوا علَىَ اللّهِ كَذِباً فَيُسْحِتَكُمْ بِعَذَابٍ﴾ and ﴿لاَ تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ فَتَذَرُوهَا كَالْمُعَلَّقَةِ﴾. Whatever is a negation has the same [Translator's note: two possibilities] as this. The nominative is not permissible in either of the two ways, unless you intend a fresh start (istiʾnāf), differing from both meanings, as in your saying to a man: لا تركب إلى فلان فيركبُ إليك (do not ride to so-and-so; he will ride to you), meaning: do not ride to him, for he will ride to you. This differs from both meanings because it is a fresh start. The poet said:
أَلَمْ تَسْألِ الَّرْبعَ الْقَدِيمَ فَيَنْطِقُ * وَهَلْ تُخْبِرَنْكَ الْيَوْمَ بَيْدَاءُ سَمْلَقُ
(Did you not ask the old encampment — and it will speak? Yet can a bare, empty desert tell you anything today?)
He meant: did you not ask the encampment, for it will tell you about its people; then he turned back on himself and gave himself the lie, as Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā al-Muzanī said:
قِفْ بِالدِّيارِ التى لَمْ يَعْفُها القِدَمُ * بَلَى وغَيَّرها الأَرْواحُ والدِّيَمُ
(Halt at the abodes that age has not effaced — nay, the winds and the steady rains have changed them.)
— so he gave himself the lie. As for His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَطْرُدِ الّذينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَدَاةِ والْعَشِىّ﴾, its answer is His words: ﴿فَتَكُونَ مِنَ الظَّالِمينَ﴾, while the fāʾ in His words "فَتَطْرُدَهُمْ" is an answer to His words "مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِمْ مِنْ شَىْءٍ". So in His words "فَتَكُونَ مِنَ الظَّالِمينَ" both the jussive and the accusative are possible, as I have explained to you, while in His words "فَتَطْرُدَهُمْ" only the accusative is possible, because the fāʾ there refers back to a maḥall [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term for an adverb or prepositional phrase], namely His words "مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِمْ", and "عليك" is not of the same kind as the verb. Whenever what precedes the fāʾ is a noun containing no verb, or a maḥall such as "عندك", "عليك" and "خلفك", or a past verb such as "قام" and "قعد", only the accusative is possible in the answer with the fāʾ. It was permissible in his words * فَيُذْرِكَ مِنْ أُخْرَى الْقَطَاةِ فَتَزْلُقْ * because what precedes the fāʾ is a yafʿalu [Translator's note: i.e. imperfect] and what follows it is a yafʿalu, and these are of the same kind as one another; because it is a future verb, what applies to the first of it can apply to the last, and what applies to the last can apply to the first, since it is a future verb.

farraa:36-36.t: His words: ﴿وَقُلْنَا ٱهْبِطُواْ بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ وَلَكُمْ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ﴾. He addressed Adam and his wife — and it is also said: Adam and Iblīs — and He said "اهبطوا" (go down, [Translator's note: plural]) meaning him and his offspring, so it is as if He addressed them all. It is like His words: ﴿فَقَالَ لَهَا وللأَرْضِ ائْتِيا طَوْعاً أَوْ كَرْهاً قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا طَائِعِينَ﴾, the meaning — and Allah knows best — being: we have come, with all the creatures in us, willingly. Similar to it is the saying of Ibrāhīm: "رَبَّنَا وَاجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ", then he said: ﴿وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَاً﴾ — and in the reading of ʿAbdallāh "وَأَرِهِمْ مَنَاسِكَهُمْ" — so he used the plural before his offspring existed. An example of this in ordinary speech, by which the meaning becomes clear, is your saying to a man: قد تزوّجتَ ووُلِدََ لك فكثُرْتم وعَزَزتم (you married and children were born to you, so you [Translator's note: plural] became many and strong).

farraa:37-37.t: His words: ﴿فَتَلَقَّىٰ آدَمُ مِن رَّبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٍ﴾: ﴿آدَمُ﴾ is nominative and «الكلمات» is in the position of the accusative. One of the readers read: "فَتَلَقَّى آدَمَ مِنْ رَبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٌ", making the verb belong to the words; and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is the same, because whatever has met you, you have met it, and whatever has reached you, you have reached it. In our reading it is: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمين", and in the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbdallāh: "لاَيَنَالُ عَهْدِى الظَّالِمُونَ".

farraa:40-40.t:
His words: ﴿ٱذْكُرُواْ نِعْمَتِيَ [ٱلَّتِي أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ]﴾: the meaning is: do not forget My favour; let it be kept in your remembrance. Likewise every mention of remembering the favour means — and Allah knows best — this: keep it and do not forget. In the version (ḥarf) of ʿAbdallāh: "ادَّكِروا", and in another place: "وتَذَكَّروا ما فيه". An example in ordinary speech is your saying: "اذكُرْ مَكانى مِنْ أبيك" (remember my standing with your father).

As for the fatḥa on the yāʾ of "نِعْمَتِى": every yāʾ of the speaker has two dialects: leaving it unvowelled (al-irsāl), i.e. quiescent, and giving it fatḥa. When it meets alif and lām, the Arabs chose the dialect in which the yāʾ is vowelled and disliked the other, because the lām is quiescent and the yāʾ would drop before it because of its own quiescence; and they found it ugly to say "نعمتِى التى", so that it would seem genitive without annexation. So they took the more secure and clearer of the two ways. Yet making it quiescent before alif and lām is permissible: Allah said: ﴿يا عِبَادِى الّذِيِنَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾, and it has been read with the yāʾ unvowelled and with fatḥa. Likewise, everything in the Qur'an in which the yāʾ is present [Translator's note: in writing] has both ways; and where the yāʾ is not present, it is not given fatḥa.

As for His words: ﴿فَبَشِّرْ عِبَادِ. الّذِيِنَ يَسْتمِعُونَ الْقَوْلَ﴾, this is without a yāʾ, so its yāʾ is not given fatḥa, since it is dropped; and by this everything of its kind in the Qur'an is to be measured. His words: ﴿فما آتَانِىََ اللّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا اتَاكُمْ﴾: al-Kisāʾī claimed that the Arabs prefer fatḥa on the yāʾ before every alif with hamza other than the alif and lām [Translator's note: of the article], as in His words: ﴿إِنْ أَجْرِىَ إِلاَّ عَلَى اللّهِ﴾ and ﴿إِنِّىَ أَخَافُ اللّهَ﴾. I have not found that among the Arabs; I have found them leaving the yāʾ unvowelled, saying: عندِى أبوك (your father is with me); they do not say عندىَ أبوك with the yāʾ vowelled — unless they drop the hamza and put its fatḥa on the yāʾ, in this and the like. As for their sayings: لِىَ ألفان (I have two thousand) and بِىَ أخواك كفيلان (your two brothers are guarantors for me), they give fatḥa in these two [Translator's note: words] because of their shortness [Translator's note: lit. "their smallness"] [so they say: لىَ أخواك and لِىَ ألفان, because of their shortness], yet the analogy in these and in what precedes them is one.

farraa:41-41.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَشْتَرُواْ بِآيَاتِي ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً﴾. Everything of this kind in the Qur'an in which the price is put in the accusative and the bāʾ is attached to the thing sold or bought: that occurs mostly with two things neither of which is a recognised price, like dinars and dirhams. An example is: اشتريتُ ثوبا بكساء (I bought a garment for a cloak): you may make whichever of them you wish the price of the other, because neither is a currency (athmān). Everything that is not a currency — such as slaves, houses and all goods (ʿurūḍ) — follows this rule. But when you come to dirhams and dinars, you put the bāʾ on the price, as He said in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَرَاهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ﴾, because dirhams are always a price, and the bāʾ is attached only to prices. Such are His words: ﴿اشْتَرَوْا بآيَاتِ اللّهِ ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً﴾, ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا بِالآخِرَةِ﴾, ﴿اشتروا الضلالة بالهدى﴾ and ﴿والعذاب بالمغفرة﴾. So attach the bāʾ to whichever of the two you wish, until you come to dinars and dirhams: you attach the bāʾ to them when they are with goods. And if you buy one of them [meaning dinars and dirhams] with the other, you attach the bāʾ to whichever you wish, because each of them in this situation is both thing sold and price. If you want to know the difference between goods and dirhams: you know that whoever buys a slave for a specified thousand dirhams, then finds a defect in him and returns him, has no claim on the seller to take back his own thousand in particular, but only a thousand. But if he bought a slave for a slave-girl and then found a defect in him, he would not get back another slave-girl like her [Translator's note: but that very one]. That is proof that goods are not prices.

His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَكُونُوۤاْ أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ﴾: He made «كافر» singular though a plural precedes it. That is eloquent, good Arabic in a noun derived from a verb, such as the active and passive participle. The meaning intended is: do not be the first who disbelieves (أوّل مَن يكفر); "مَن" is dropped and the verb [Translator's note: i.e. the participle] takes its place, conveying the same feminine and plural that "مَن" conveys, while it is singular in form. In similar speech you may not say: أنتم أفضلُ رجلٍ (you [Translator's note: plural] are the best man), nor أنتما خير رجل (you two are the best man), because «رجل» takes dual, plural and singular, [so] its singular is distinguished from its plural, whereas «القائم» (the one standing) may stand for a thing [Translator's note: i.e. «ما»] and for «مَن», conveying both while singular. Do you not see that you may say: الجيْشُ مقبلٌ والجُنْد منهزمٌ (the army is advancing and the troops are routed), putting the predicate (fiʿl) in the singular because [Translator's note: the subject] is singular; but when you come to [Translator's note: non-derived] nouns you say: الجيش رجالٌ والجند رجالٌ (the army are men, the troops are men)? In this there is a clear explanation. The poet said:
وإذا هُمُ طَعِمُوا فَأَلأَمُ طاعِم * وإذا هُمُ جاعُوا فشَرُّ جِياعِ
(When they eat, they are the meanest of eaters; and when they are hungry, the worst of the hungry.)
So both its plural and its singular are permissible and good.

farraa:42-42.t:
His words: ﴿وَلاَ تَلْبِسُواْ ٱلْحَقَّ بِٱلْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُواْ ٱلْحَقَّ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. If you wish, you take "وتكتموا" to be in the position of the jussive, meaning: do not mix truth with falsehood and do not conceal the truth; you drop "لا" because it has come at the beginning of the speech. In the reading of Ubayy: "وَلاَ تَكُونُوا أَوّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ وَتَشْتَرُوا بِآيَاتِى ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً"; this is proof that the jussive in His words ﴿وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ﴾ is sound and correct. Similar to it: ﴿وَلاَ تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتُدْلُوا بِهَا إِلى الْحُكّامِ﴾, and likewise His words: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِيِنَ آمَنُوا لاَ تَخُونُوا اللّهَ وَالرَّسُولَ وَتَخُونُوا أَمَانَاتِكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. And if you wish, you make these words conjoined by the wāw accusative according to what the grammarians call al-ṣarf (diversion). If you say: What is al-ṣarf? I say: it is that you bring a wāw conjoining [Translator's note: a verb] to speech at whose beginning there is an element (ḥādith) that cannot properly be repeated on what is conjoined to it. When that is so, it is al-ṣarf, as in the words of the poet:
لاتَنْهَ عنْ خُلُقٍ وتأتِىَ مِثْلُهُ * عارٌعليْكَ إذا فَعلتَ عظِيمُ
(Do not forbid a trait while doing the like of it yourself; a great shame on you if you do.)
Do you not see that "لا" cannot be repeated in "تأتى مثله"? That is why it is called ṣarf: it is conjoined, yet the element preceding it cannot properly be repeated in it. Similar to it among nouns, which the Arabs put in the accusative though they are conjoined to a nominative, are their sayings: لَوْ تُركتَ والأسدَ لأكلَك (had you been left with the lion, it would have eaten you) and لَوْ خُلِّيت ورأيَك لَضَلَلْتَ (had you been left to your own opinion, you would have gone astray). Since it is not good in the second to say: "had you been left and had your opinion been left, you would have gone astray", they shrank from conjoining a word in which what occurred in the preceding one does not fit. He said: But the Arabs allow the nominative: لو تُرك عبدُالله والأسدُ لأكله (had ʿAbdallāh and the lion been left, it would have eaten him). So is it permissible for verbs put in the accusative by the wāw by way of ṣarf to be referred back to what precedes them, while they carry the meaning of ṣarf? I say: Yes. The Arabs say: لستُ لأبِى إِنْ لم أقتُلْك أو تذهبْ نفسى (I am not my father's son if I do not kill you or lose my life), and they say: والله لأضربنّك أو تسبقَنِّى فى الأرض (by Allah, I shall strike you, unless you outrun me across the land). This is referred back to the beginning of the speech, yet its meaning is ṣarf, because in the second the jussive with «لم» cannot be repeated, nor can the oath be repeated as "by Allah, you will outrun me". You will find this when you test the speech. Al-ṣarf with particles other than "لا" is frequent, but we have deferred mentioning it until its places come.

farraa:48-48.t:
His words: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً لاَّ تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْئاً﴾. Reference back to "day" and "night" may be made sometimes with the hāʾ alone and sometimes with the ṣifa [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's term for a preposition, here «في» with its pronoun], and that is permissible: as when you say "لا تجزى نفس عن نفس شيئا" and imply the ṣifa, then make it overt and say: "لا تجزى فيه نفس عن نفس شيئا" (on which no soul will avail another soul at all). Al-Kisāʾī did not allow implying the ṣifa in relative clauses (ṣilāt), and said: If I allowed implying the ṣifa here, I would allow: "أنت الذى تكلمتُ" (you are the one I spoke), when I mean "الذى تكلمتُ فيه" (the one about whom I spoke). Others, of the people of Basra, said: We do not allow the hāʾ, and it does not occur; in such a place it is only the ṣifa that is implied. Some Arabs recited to me:
يارُبَّ يَوْم لو تَنَزّاهُ حول * أَلْفَيْتَنى ذا عنزٍ وذا طول
(Many a day — had a crafty one leapt at it [Translator's note: i.e. at me on it], you would have found me resistant and strong.)
And another recited to me:
قد صَبَّحتْ صبَّحها السّلامُ * بِكَبِدٍ خالَطها سَنامُ * فى ساعة يُحَبُّها الطّعامُ *
(She brought in the morning — may peace greet her morning — a liver mixed with hump-fat, at an hour in which food is loved.)
— and he did not say «يُحَبّ فيها». What al-Kisāʾī imposed on himself does not apply to him, because in this place the ṣifa and the hāʾ agree in meaning: do you not see that you say آتيك يومَ الخميس and فى يوم الخميس (I will come to you [Translator's note: on] Thursday), and you see the meaning is one? But when you say كلمتُك (I spoke to you), it is different from كلّمتُ فيك (I spoke about you); and since the meaning differs, it is not permissible to imply the hāʾ in place of "فى", nor "فى" in place of the hāʾ.

farraa:258-260.t:
His saying: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِي حَآجَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ — the Arabs' insertion of (ilā) in this place is by way of expressing wonder (taʿajjub), as you say to a man: "Do you not see [look at] this!" The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: Have you seen the like of this, or have you seen anything like this! The proof of that is that He said: ﴿أَوْ كَٱلَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرْيَةٍ﴾, as though He said: Have you seen [anyone] like the one who disputed with Abraham about his Lord ﴿أَوْ كَٱلَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرْيَةٍ وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا﴾. This, in its manner, is like what I told you about mā laka and mā manaʿaka. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿قل لِمن الأرض وَمن فيها إن كنتم تعلمون. سيقولون لِلّه﴾, then He said, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿قل من ربُّ السموات السّبْع وربّ العرش العظيم. سيقولون لله﴾ — He made the lām the answer although it is not in the beginning of the speech. That is because when you say: "Who is the owner of this house?" and someone says to you: "It belongs to Zayd (li-Zaydin)," he has answered you with what you want; so his saying "Zayd" and "li-Zayd" are equal in meaning. He said: one of Banū ʿĀmir recited to me:
فأَعلمُ أننى سأكونُ رَمْساً * إذا سار النواجعُ لا يَسير
فقال السائرون لمن حفرتم * فقال المخبرون لهم: وزير
(I know that I shall become a buried grave which, when the seekers of pasture move on, does not move; and the travellers will say: For whom have you dug? And those who inform them will say: Wazīr.)
Similar to it in speech: a man says to you: "How are you this morning (kayfa aṣbaḥta)?" and you say: "Well (ṣāliḥun)," in the nominative; had you answered him according to his very word, you would have said: ṣāliḥan. Your informing about your state spared you from keeping to his word. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿ما كان محمد أَبا أَحدٍ مِن رِجالِكم ولكِن رسول الله﴾ — if you use the accusative, you mean: but he was the Messenger of Allah; and if you use the nominative, you give a statement, and the statement spares you from what precedes it. His saying: ﴿ولا تحسبن الذيِن قتِلوا فِى سبيل الله أمواتا بل أَحياء﴾ — nominative, and it is more proper than the accusative, because had it been accusative it would be on: but reckon them alive; and removing doubt from this place is better. Had it been accusative it would be correct, as you say: "Do not think him a liar; rather think him truthful." Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿أيحسب الإنسان أن لن نجمع عِظامه بلى قادِرين على أن نسوّى بنانه﴾ — if you wish, you derive the accusative of qādirīna from this interpretation, as if in similar speech someone says: "Do you think I will not visit you? Rather, soon, if Allah wills," as if he said: "Yes indeed — so reckon me your visitor." Even though the verb has fallen on (an lan najmaʿa), in interpretation it falls on the nouns. One of Banū Faqʿas recited to me:
أجِدَّك لن ترى بثُعَيلِبات * ولا بَيْدان نَاجيةً ذَمولا
ولا متداركٍ والشمسُ طِفْلٌ * ببعض نواشغ الوادى حُمولا
(Truly, you will not see at Thuʿaylibāt nor at Baydān a swift, ambling she-camel, nor one overtaking — while the sun is just setting — at some of the valley's water-channels, the litters of the departing.)
He said "wa-lā mutadārikin," and that shows that he meant: you are not one who sees at Thuʿaylibāt such-and-such, nor one overtaking.
Some grammarians say: we put (qādirīna) in the accusative on the basis that it was turned away from naqdiru; that is nothing. But there may be another way in it besides what I explained to you: it may come out of (najmaʿa) [as a ḥāl], as if in speech someone says: "Do you think I will not hit you? Yes indeed — being able to kill you," as if he said: "Yes indeed, I will hit you, being able to do more than hitting you."
His saying: ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾ — the speech has run with the assimilation (idghām) of the thāʾ, since it met the tāʾ while it was quiescent.
In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: (اتَّخَتُّمُ العجل) and (وإنى عُتُّ بربى وربكم), so the dhāl was also assimilated before the tāʾ. That is because they are related in the closeness of their point of articulation; the thāʾ and the dhāl have a heavy point of articulation, so assimilation was applied to them because of their heaviness; do you not see that their point of articulation is from the tip of the tongue? Likewise the ẓāʾ shares their heaviness. So whatever of these three letters comes to you, assimilate it. Not assimilating is not an error; it is only [a matter of] finding it heavy. The ṭāʾ and the dāl are also assimilated before the tāʾ when they are made quiescent, as in His saying: ﴿أحطت بما لم تحِط به﴾ — the ṭāʾ comes out in pronunciation as tāʾ, and it is closer to the tāʾ than the first letters; you find that when you test their two points of articulation.
His saying: ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ — the explanation came: it has not changed [by the passing of years over it, taken from al-sana]. The hāʾ may be part of its root [from your saying: "I sold it to him musānahatan (by the year)"; it is kept both in continuous reading and in pause. Whoever reads it continuously without the hāʾ derives it from al-musānāt, because the hāʾ and the wāw alternate as the final radical of sana], or it may be redundant, an extension, like His saying ﴿فبِهداهم اقتدِهْ﴾. Whoever makes the hāʾ redundant makes the faʿʿaltu form of it tasannaytu; do you not see that you make the plural of sana sanawāt, so tafaʿʿaltu is sound [on that basis]? And whoever says in [the diminutive of] sana: sunayna — even if that is rare — then tasannaytu may be tafaʿʿaltu with the nūn replaced by yāʾ because the nūns became many, as they said taẓannaytu, whose origin is al-ẓann. They have also said it is taken from His saying ﴿من حمإٍ مسنون﴾, meaning: changed. If it is so, it is also among those whose nūn is replaced by a yāʾ. We hold that its meaning is taken from al-sana, i.e. the years have not changed it. And Allah knows best.
Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna narrated to me, tracing it back to Zayd ibn Thābit, who said: there was written on a stone: "نَنشِزها" and "لم يتسن" and "وانظر"; and Zayd ibn Thābit [Translator's note: the text reads «وانظر إلى زيد بن ثابت», apparently garbled; rendered by sense] put four dots on the shīn and the zāy, and wrote (يتسنه) with the hāʾ. If you wish, you read it in continuous recitation in two ways: you keep the hāʾ and make it quiescent, or if you wish, you delete it. One of them recited to me:
فليست بسَنْهاء ولا رُجَّبِيَّة * ولكنْ عَرَايَا فى السنينَ الجوائح
(She is neither an old palm (sanhāʾ) nor a propped-up one, but [her fruit is] gifts in the devastating years.)
Al-rujjabiyya is the one that is about to fall, so it is supported around with stones. Al-sanhāʾ is the old palm tree. This is support for whoever pronounces the hāʾ in continuous reading.
His saying: ﴿وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾ — the wāw was put in it only on the intention of an implied verb after it, as if He said: and so that We make you a sign, We did that. This is frequent in the Quran. His saying ﴿آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾: when he was raised up, his beard and head were black while his grandchildren were grey, so he was a sign by that.
His saying ﴿ننشزها﴾ — Zayd ibn Thābit read it so; al-inshāz is moving them to their place.
Ibn ʿAbbās read it "nunshiruhā"; its inshār is bringing it to life. He argued from His saying: ﴿ثم إذا شاء أنشره﴾. Al-Ḥasan read — according to what has reached us — (nanshuruhā), taking it toward spreading out (nashr) as opposed to folding. The proper way is that you say: Allah anshara the dead, and they nasharū, when they came to life, as al-Aʿshā said:
* يا عجبا للميت الناشِرِ *
(How amazing — the dead man coming back to life!)
And I heard one of Banū al-Ḥārith say: "He had mange, then nashara," i.e. he recovered and came back to life. His saying: "فلما تبين له قال أعلم أنّ الله على كل شىء قدير" — Ibn ʿAbbās read it in the jussive [i.e. the imperative iʿlam], and in the readings of both Ubayy and ʿAbdullāh it is: "قيل له اعْلَمْ" ("it was said to him: Know"). Ibn ʿAbbās argued, saying: Is he better than Abraham and more knowledgeable? It was said to him: ﴿وَٱعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾. The generality read: "aʿlamu anna Allāha" ("I know that Allah"), and it is a good way, because the meaning is like a man's saying, at a display of power that becomes clear to him from the command of Allah: (I bear witness that there is no god but Allah). The other way is also clear.
His saying ﴿فَصُرْهُنَّ إِلَيْكَ﴾ — the generality read the ṣād with ḍamma, and the companions of ʿAbdullāh used to read the ṣād with kasra. They are two dialects. As for the ḍamma, it is common; as for the kasra, it is among Hudhayl and Sulaym. Al-Kisāʾī recited to me from one of Banū Sulaym:
وفَرْعٍ يصير الجِيدَ وَحْفٍ كأنه * على اللِيتِ قِنْوانُ الكروم الدوالح
(And thick hair that inclines the neck, as if, on the side of the neck, it were the heavy-laden clusters of vines.)
Its meaning is explained as: cut them up; and it is said: turn them [toward you]. We have not found "cut them up" known from these two forms; but I hold — and Allah knows best — that if it is from that, it is from ṣaraytu taṣrī, with its yāʾ moved forward, as they said ʿithtu and ʿathaytu. And the poet said:
صَرَتْ نظرة لو صادفت جَوْزَ دارِع * غَدَا والعَوَاصِى من دمِ الجوف تنعَرُ
(She cut short a glance which, had it met the middle of a mailed warrior, he would have gone off with his veins gushing blood from his inside.)
The Arabs say: "He spent the night yaṣrī in his basin," when he draws water, then stops, then draws water; perhaps it is from that.
And the poet said:
يقولون إن الشأم يقتلُ أهلَه * فمَنْ لِىَ إن لم آتِه بخُلُود
تَعَرَّب آبائى فهَلاَّ صَرَاهم * من الموت أن لم يذهبوا وجُدُودِى
(They say Syria kills its people — but who will grant me immortality if I do not go to it? My fathers and my grandfathers lived as Bedouin — did their not going [there] hold them back from death?)

farraa:177-177.t:
His saying: ﴿لَّيْسَ ٱلْبِرَّ أَن تُوَلُّواْ وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ — if you wish, you put "البِرّ" in the nominative and make "أن تولوا" in the position of the accusative; and if you wish, you put it in the accusative and make "أن تولّوا" in the position of the nominative, as He said: ﴿فَكَانَ عاقِبَتَهُمَا أَنَّهُمَا فِى النّارِ﴾, in much of the Qur'an. In one of the two readings it is "ليس البِرُّ بِأن"; for that reason we chose the nominative in "البِرّ". The meaning of His saying ﴿ليس البِرُّ بِأن تولوا وجوهكم قِبل المشرِقِ والمغرِبِ﴾ is: righteousness does not lie wholly in your turning towards prayer and the difference between the two qiblas — ﴿وَلَكِنّ البِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللّهِ﴾; then He described what He described to the end of the verse. These are among the attributes of the prophets, not of others.
As for His saying ﴿وَلكِنَّ البِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللّهِ﴾, it is of the speech of the Arabs to say: "Righteousness is only the truthful one who maintains his ties of kinship and conceals his charity", making the noun [i.e. person] the predicate of the action and the action the predicate of the noun, because it is a matter whose meaning is known.
As for the action made the predicate of a noun, it is His saying ﴿ولا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ بِمَا آتَاهُمُ اللّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ هُوَ خَيْراً لَهُمْ﴾: (هو) is a pronoun standing for the stinginess. This is for whoever makes "الذِين" in the position of the accusative and reads it "تحسبنَّ" with tāʾ. Whoever reads it with yāʾ makes "الذِين" in the position of the nominative and makes (هو) a support (ʿimād, i.e. separating pronoun) for the implied stinginess, making do with the mention of stinginess that is overt in "يبخلون". Similar to it in speech:
هم الملوك وأبناء الملوكِ لهم * والآخِذون بِهِ والساسة الأُوَلُ
(They are the kings and sons of kings; theirs it is; they are those who hold it and the foremost governors.)
His saying "به" means: the kingship. Another said:
إِذا نُهِى السفِيهُ جَرَى إليهِ * وخالف والسفِيه إِلى خِلافِ
(When the fool is forbidden, he runs towards it and disobeys — the fool inclines to disobedience.)
He means: towards foolishness.
As for the actions made predicates of persons, it is the poet's saying:
لعمرك ما الفِتيان أن تَنْبُت اللحى * ولكِنما الفِتانُ كُلُّ فتىً نَدِى
(By your life, young men are not [a matter of] beards sprouting; rather, young men are every generous youth.)
So he made "أنْ" [with its verb] the predicate of "الفتيان".
His saying: ﴿مَنْ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ﴾ — (من) is in the position of the nominative, and what follows it is its ṣila, until it reaches His saying ﴿وَٱلْمُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِهِمْ﴾; you refer "الموفون" back to "مَنْ", and "والموفون" is of the description of "مَن", as if: whoever believed, and whoever did and fulfilled. "الصابرِين" is put in the accusative because it is of the description of "مَنْ"; it was put in the accusative only because it is of the description of a single noun, so it is as if he took it towards praise. The Arabs break off from the attributes of a single [noun], when they run long, with praise or blame: they use the nominative when the noun is nominative, and they put some of the praise in the accusative, as if they intend to set apart what is in the accusative with renewed praise not following on from the beginning of the speech. Of that is the poet's saying:
لا يَبْعَدَنْ قومى الذين هُمُ * سُمُّ العُدَاةِ وآفة الجُزُرِ
النازِلِين بِكلّ معترَكٍ * والطَيِّبِينَ مَعاقِدَ الأُزُرِ
(May my people not perish, who are poison to enemies and the bane of slaughter-camels; who alight at every battlefield, and are pure where their waist-wrappers are tied.)
Sometimes they put (النازلون) and (الطيبون) in the nominative, and sometimes in the accusative by way of praise; the nominative is by making the end of the speech follow its beginning. One of the poets said:
إلى الملِكِ القَرْمِ وابنِ الهُمَام * وليثَ الكتِيبةِ فى المُزْدَحَمْ
وذا الرأى حين تُغَمُّ الأُمور * بِذاتِ الصليلِ وذاتِ الُّلجُمْ
(To the king, the chief, son of the valiant — the lion of the squadron in the press, the man of judgement when matters are clouded by [battles] of clanging [arms] and bridled [horses].)
He put (ليث الكتيبة) and (ذا الرأى) in the accusative by way of praise, while the noun before them is genitive, because they are of the description of one [person]; had the lion been other than the king, it could only be a follower [in case], as you say "I passed by the man and the woman" and the like. He said: one of them recited to me:
فليت التِى فيها النجوم تواضعت * على كل غثّ مِنهمُ وسَمينِ
غيوثَ الحَيَا فى كل مَحْلٍ ولَزْبَةٍ * أسود الشَّرَى يحمِين كلَّ عَرِينِ
(Would that [the sky] in which are the stars had come down upon every lean and fat one of them — rains of life-giving in every drought and hardship, lions of al-Sharā guarding every den.)
So he used the accusative. And we consider that in His saying ﴿لَكِنِ الرَّاسِخُونَ فى الْعِلْمِ مِنْهُمْ وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاَةَ وَالْمُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ the accusative of "المقِيمِين" is because it is a naʿt (adjective) of "الراسِخِين": its description grew long, and it was put in the accusative as I explained to you.
In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "والمقِيمون — والمؤتون", and in the reading of Ubayy: "والمقِيمين"; and our reading and the reading of Ubayy did not agree except upon what is correct. And Allah knows best.
Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Abū Muʿāwiya al-Ḍarīr narrated to me from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha, that she was asked about His saying ﴿إنّ هَذَانِ لَسَاحِرَانِ﴾, about His saying ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا والَّذِينَ هَادُوا وَالصَّابِئُونَ﴾ and about His saying ﴿وَالْمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاَةَ وَالْمُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾, and she said: "O son of my brother, this was a mistake of the scribe."
Al-Kisāʾī said about it: "والمقيمين" is in the position of the genitive, referred back to His saying ﴿بِما أنزِل إليك وما أنزِل مِن قبلِك﴾: and they believe in those who establish the prayer — they and those who give the zakāt.
He said: it is like His saying ﴿يُؤْمِنُ بِاللهِ ويُؤْمِنُ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. The grammarians used to say that "المقيمين" is referred back to ﴿بما أنزِل إِليك وما أنزِل مِن قبلك... إلى المقِيمِين﴾ [i.e. and to those who establish]; some of them [said]: "لكِنِ الراسِخون فِى العِلِم مِنهم" and of "المقيمين"; and some of them: "مِن قبلك" and before "المقيمين".
He — meaning al-Kisāʾī — refused the approach of praise which I explained to you only because he said: the one praised is not put in the accusative except when the sentence is complete, and the sentence is not complete in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.
