Do you not see that when you say "لكن الراسخون فى العلم منهم" up to His saying "والمقيمين — والمؤتون", you are as if waiting for its predicate? Its predicate is in His saying ﴿أُولئِك سَنُؤْتِيهِمْ أَجْراً عَظِيماً﴾. Most speech is as al-Kisāʾī described; but the Arabs, when the description runs long, treat the speech in the incomplete and the complete alike. Do you not see that they said in poetry:
حتى إِذا قَمِلت بطونُكُمُ * ورأيتُم أبناءكم شبُّوا
وقلبتم ظهر المِجَنِّ لنا * إنّ اللئِيم العاجزُ الخِبُّ
(Until, when your bellies grew fat and you saw your sons had grown up, and you turned the back of the shield against us — truly, the base one is the feeble, the deceitful.)
He made the answer of (حتى إذا) with the wāw, while there ought to have been no wāw in it, and it was made do with by following on, with no predicate after that. This is the most extreme of what I have described to you.
Similar is His saying ﴿حَتّى إِذَا جَاءُوهَا وَفُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُهَا وَقَالَ لَهُمْ خَزَنَتُها﴾, and similar is His saying ﴿فَلَمَّا أَسْلَمَا وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ وَنَادَيْنَاهُ أَنْ يَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ﴾ — He put it with the wāw. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "فَلَمَّا جَهَّزَهُمْ بِجَهَازِهِمْ وَجَعَلَ السِّقَايَةَ", and in our reading it is without the wāw. All is good Arabic.
Some of them said: "وآتى المال على حبهِ ذوِى القربى — والصابِرِين", putting "الصابرين" in the accusative by making the verb act upon them. The right view is that it is accusative with the intention of praise, because it is of the description of one thing. The Arabs say with indefinites what they say with definites: they say "marartu bi-rajulin jamīlin wa-shābban baʿdu" (I passed by a handsome man, and young besides), and "marartu bi-rajulin ʿāqilin wa-sharmaḥan ṭuwālan" (I passed by an intelligent man, and tall, very tall); and they recite his saying:
ويَأوِى إلى نِسوةٍ بائساتٍ * وشُعْثاً مراضِيعَ مِثل السَّعَالِى
(And he takes refuge with wretched women — dishevelled, nursing, like ghouls.)
(and "وَشُعْثٍ"): they make it genitive by having it follow the beginning of the speech, and accusative with the intention of blame in this place.

farraa:178-178.t:
His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِصَاصُ فِي ٱلْقَتْلَى ٱلْحُرُّ بِالْحُرِّ وَٱلْعَبْدُ بِٱلْعَبْدِ وَٱلأُنثَىٰ بِٱلأُنْثَىٰ﴾ — it was revealed about two tribes of the Arabs, one of which had superiority over the other in numbers and nobility; they used to marry their women without dowries. The lower of the two tribes killed some of the noble one, and the noble one swore that they would kill a male for a female and a free man for a slave, and double the [retaliation for] wounds. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed this to His Prophet; then it was abrogated by His saying ﴿وَكَتَبْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِيهَا أَنَّ النَّفْسَ بِالنَّفْسِ﴾ to the end of the verse. So the first is abrogated and is not judged by.
As for His saying ﴿فَٱتِّبَاعٌ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَأَدَآءٌ إِلَيْهِ بِإِحْسَانٍ﴾, it is nominative; and it has the status of a command in outward form, as you say "man laqiya l-ʿaduwwa fa-ṣabran wa-ḥtisāban" (whoever meets the enemy — then patience and seeking reward!). This is accusative, and its nominative is permissible. And His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿فَٱتِّبَاعٌ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ is nominative, and its accusative is permissible. The nominative was the normal way of speech in it only because it is general for whoever does [it], and is meant also for whoever has not done [it]; so it is as if He said: the rule in it is thus — hence the nominative. The verbal noun is put in the accusative when it is a command at a thing that happens and is not permanent, as in your saying to a man: "When you take up your work, then diligence, diligence! and pace, pace!"
You used the accusative because you did not intend generality by it, such that it would become like something binding upon whoever came to it and did it. Similar is His saying ﴿وَمَنْ قَتَلَهُ مِنْكُمْ مُتَعَمِّداً فَجَزَاءٌ مِثْلُ مَا قَتَلَ مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾, and similar is ﴿فَإمْسَاكٌ بِمَعْرُوفٍ أَوْ تَسْرِيحٌ بِإحْسَانٍ﴾; and the like of it in the Qur'an is much, all nominative, because they are general.
So it is as if He said: whoever does this, upon him is this.
As for His saying ﴿فَضَرْبَ الرِّقَابِ﴾, He was urging them to kill when they meet the enemy, and the urging was not like something made binding by an act before it; for that reason it is accusative. It is like your saying: "When you meet the enemy, then [say] lā ilāha illā llāh, Allāhu akbar, and [show] truthfulness at that encounter (tilka l-waqʿa)" — (al-Farrāʾ said: "dhālika" and "tilka" are the dialect of Quraysh, and Tamīm say "dhāka" and "tīka l-waqʿa") — as if it is urging them, and it is not obligatory upon them to say "Allāhu akbar". There is nothing of this whose accusative is not permissible, by making the command act upon it: "let him fast three days", "let him keep [her] in a keeping with kindness, or release [her] in a release with excellence".

farraa:179-179.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَكُمْ فِي ٱلْقِصَاصِ حَيَاةٌ﴾ — He says: when the offender knows that retaliation will be taken from him — that if he kills he will be killed — he refrains from killing, and so [the other] lives.
That is His saying: "حياة" (life).

farraa:180-180.t:
His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ — its meaning throughout the Qur'an is: it has been made obligatory upon you.
His saying: ﴿ٱلْوَصِيَّةُ لِلْوَالِدَيْنِ وَٱلأَقْرَبِينَ﴾ — a man used to bequeath whatever he liked of his wealth to whomever he wished, heir or other; then it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance. So there is no bequest for an heir, and the bequest is within the third and does not exceed it. Before this, one would bequeath all his wealth or whatever he liked of it.
"الوصِيَّة" is nominative by "كُتِب"; and if you wish, you take "كُتِب" in the sense of "قِيل" (it was said) and put "الوصية" in the nominative by the lām in "الوالدين" [i.e. as mubtadaʾ with its khabar], like His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿يوصِيكم الله فِى أولادِكم لِلذكر مِثل حظّ الأنثيين﴾.

farraa:182-182.t: His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ خَافَ مِن مُّوصٍ جَنَفاً﴾ — the Arabs say "waṣṣaytuka" and "awṣaytuka"; and in one of the two readings it is "وأوصى بِها إبراهِيم" with the alif. Al-janaf is injustice. ﴿فَأَصْلَحَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ — He mentioned only the testator; He said "بينهم" (between them) meaning the heirs and the beneficiaries of bequests. For that reason He said "بينهم" without mentioning them, because the meaning indicates that reconciliation can only be among the heirs and those to whom bequests were made.

farraa:265-266.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَوَدُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ لَهُ جَنَّةٌ مِّن نَّخِيلٍ وَأَعْنَابٍ﴾, then after that He said ﴿وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ﴾, then He said ﴿فَأَصَابَهَآ إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَٱحْتَرَقَتْ ﴾. Someone may say: Is it permissible in speech to say: "Would you like to obtain wealth and it was lost (fa-ḍāʿa)," meaning: and it is lost (fa-yaḍīʿu)? I said: Yes, that is permissible with wadidtu, because the Arabs meet it once with (an) and once with (law); they say: "I would like it if (law) you went away from us," [and] "I would like that (an) you go away from us." Since it is suitable with law and with an, and the meaning of both is the future, they allowed themselves to return faʿala in the interpretation of law onto yafʿalu with an. Therefore He said: fa-aṣābahā, and it is, in its manner, equivalent to law, since [law] resembles in in the sense of condition, so it was put in its places, and in was answered with the apodosis of law, and law with the apodosis of in. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿ولا تنكِحوا المشرِكاتِ حتى يُؤْمِنَّ ولأَمَةٌ مؤمنة خير مِن مشرِكة ولو أعجبتكم﴾, and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: even if (in) they please you. Then He said ﴿ولئن أَرْسَلْنَا رِيحا فرأوه مصفرا لظلوا [من بعده يكفرون]﴾, so la-in was answered with the answer of law, and the meaning of both is future. For that reason He said in the reading of Ubayy: "ودّ الذين كفروا لو تغفلون عن أسلِحتكم وأمتِعتِكم فيمِيلوا" — he referred it back to the interpretation: they would like you to (an) do. If you put (fa-yamīlūna) in the nominative, you refer it to the interpretation of law, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿ودّوا لو تدهِن فيدهنون﴾, and He also said ﴿وتودّون أن غير ذات الشوكةِ تكون لكْم﴾. Sometimes the Arabs combine both together; Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿وما عمِلت من سوء تودّ لو أن بينها وبينه أمدا بعيدا﴾. It is like the Arabs' combining mā and in, both being negations. The poet said:
قد يكسِبُ المالَ الهِدَانُ الجافى * بغير لا عَصْفٍ ولا اصطراف
(The coarse dullard may gain wealth without any toil or striving.)
And another said:
ما إن رأينا مثلهن لمعشر* سُود الرءوس فوالج وفُيُول
(We have never seen the like of them belonging to any folk — black-headed: Bactrian camels and elephants.)
That is because the difference of the two wordings makes one of them redundant (laghw). Similar to it is the poet's saying:
من النفر اللاء الذين إذا هُمُ * تهاب اللئام حَلْقة الباب قعقعوا
(Of the band who, when the base are in awe of the door-ring, rattle it.)
Do you not see that he said al-lāʾ alladhīna, and the meaning of both is alladhīna? Combining them was permitted because their wordings differ; had they agreed it would not be permissible: "mā mā qāma Zayd" is not permissible, nor "I passed by alladhīna alladhīna who go round." As for the poet's saying:
كماما أمرؤٌ فى معشرٍ غيرِ رَهطِه * ضعيفُ الكلام شخصُه متضائل
(Just as a man among a folk other than his own clan is weak of speech, his person diminished.)
they permitted combining mā with [mā] only because the first was joined to the kāf — as if it and the kāf were one noun — while the second was not joined, so combining them was found good. And it is in the saying of Allah ﴿كلاَّ لا وَزَر﴾: lā was joined [in kallā], and the other came separately, so their coupling was good. So if someone says: (mā mā qultu bi-ḥasanin, "what I said is not good"), that is permissible without fault, because he makes the first mā a negation and the second in the manner of alladhī. [Likewise if he said: "man man ʿindaka? (Who is the one with you?)" it is permissible, because he made the first man interrogative and the second in the manner of alladhī.] So when the meaning of the two words differs, combining them is permissible.
As for the poet's saying:
* كم نِعْمةٍ كانت لهاكم كم وكم *
(How many a favour was hers to you — how many, how many!)
this is only repetition of a word; had you stopped at the first, it would suffice you instead of the second. It is like your saying to a man: "Yes, yes," repeating it, or your saying: "Hurry, hurry," to intensify the meaning. This has nothing to do with the two preceding chapters. And the poet said:
هلاَّ سألتَ جُمُوعَ كنـ * دَةَ يوم ولَّواْ أين أينا
(Why did you not ask the hosts of Kinda, on the day they turned their backs: where, where?)
As for his saying: (lam arahu mundhu yawma yawma, "I have not seen him since such-and-such a day"), by the second is intended other than the first day; in meaning it is only: I have not seen him since a day you know. As for his saying:
نحمِى حقيقتَنا وبعـ * ضُ القوم يسقط بينَ بينا
(We defend what we must protect, while some of the folk fall in between.)
he meant: he falls neither among these nor among those. Their combination in this place is like their saying: "He is my neighbour bayta bayta (house by house)," and "I met him kaffata kaffata (face to face)," because the two kaffas are one from you and one from him. Likewise "He is my neighbour bayta bayta," from it: my house and his house are adjoining.
He said: How did He say His saying: ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ﴾, when this matter has passed? It was said: (kāna) is implied, so the speech is sound. Similar to it is that you say: "I have freed two slaves; and if I did not free two, then one at their value," the meaning being: unless I be [one who freed]; because it is past, kāna must be implied, since the speech is conditional. Similar to it is the poet's saying:
إذا ما انتسبنا لم تلِدْنى لئيمةٌ * ولم تجِدِى مِن أن تُقِرّى بها بُدّا
(When we trace our lineage, [you will find that] no base woman bore me, and you will find no escape from acknowledging it.)

farraa:267-267.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَسْتُمْ بِآخِذِيهِ إِلاَّ أَن تُغْمِضُواْ فِيهِ﴾ — (an) after illā was given fatḥa although it is in the manner of a condition. It was given fatḥa only because illā fell on it with a sense of the genitive that fits. So when you see (an) in a condition affected by a sense of genitive, accusative or nominative, it takes fatḥa. This is of that kind. The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: you would not take it except on closing your eyes, or with closing your eyes, or from closing your eyes — an unspecified preposition (ṣifa). What shows you that it is a condition is that you find the meaning: if you closed your eyes somewhat, you would take it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿إلا أن يخافا ألاَّ يقِيما حدودَ الله﴾, and similar to it ﴿إلاَّ أن يعفون﴾ — all this is condition; and His saying ﴿ولا تقولنَّ لِشىءٍ إنى فاعل ذلك غدا إلا أن يشاء الله﴾ — do you not see that the meaning is: do not say "I will do it" except with "if Allah wills" along with it? So when (illā) cut it off from the meaning of beginning, together with the intention of the genitive governor in it, it took fatḥa. Had (illā) not been in it, it would have been left with its kasra. Of that is your saying: "Do good, if (in) it is accepted from you." If you put in (illā), you say: "Do good, unless (illā allā) it is not accepted from you." Similar to it is His saying ﴿وأن تعفوا أقربُ للتقوى﴾, ﴿وأن تصوموا خير لكم﴾ — it is a condition, the meaning being: if you fast, it is better for you. When (an) became nominative by (khayr), it had something with which it stands in mutual nominative relation, so it took fatḥa and left the bounds of the condition. The accusative governor is likewise.
Similar to it — of the condition which, when a genitive, nominative or accusative governor falls on it, loses its jussive — is your saying: "Hit him, whoever he is (man kāna)," and "I will not come to you as long as I live (mā ʿishtu)." Man and mā are in the position of a condition, and the verb in both is nominative in meaning, because kāna and the verb before it have fallen on (man) and (mā), so it changed from the jussive without leaving the interpretation of the condition. The poet said:
فلستُ مقاتِلا أبداً قُرَيشا * مُصيبا رَغْمُ ذلك مَنْ أصابا
(I will never fight Quraysh, striking — despite that — whomever it strikes.)
in the interpretation of the nominative, because muṣīb falls on man.
Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic ﴿وللّهِ على الناسِ حِجّ البيتِ منِ استطاع﴾: if you make (man) referred back to the genitive of (al-nās), it is of this kind, and (istaṭāʿa) is in the position of the nominative; and if you intend a fresh start with man, it is a condition, and the verb after it is jussive, and you are content with what came before it as its apodosis. Likewise you say in speech: "Whichever of them stands (ayyuhum yaqum), hit [him]"; if you put the hitting first and make it act on ayy, you say: "Hit whichever of them stands (iḍrib ayyahum yaqūmu)." One of the Arabs said: "fa-ayyuhum mā akhadhahā rakiba ʿalā ayyihim yurīdu" ("whichever of them takes it, rides on whichever of them he wants"). And of it is the poet's saying:
فإنى لآتيكم تشَكُّرَ ما مضى * من الأمر واستيجابَ ما كان فى غد
(I come to you in gratitude for what has passed, and to earn whatever may be tomorrow.)
because, had it not been a condition, it would not be permissible to say: "kāna tomorrow," since (kāna) was created only for the past, except in the condition, where it is suitable for the future. It is as though he said: to earn whatever thing may be tomorrow.
Similar to in in the condition, in turning from kasra to fatḥa when a nominative governor affects it, is the saying of the Arabs: (qultu innaka qāʾim, "I said: you are standing"): inna takes kasra after "saying" in all its inflections. If you put in place of "saying" something with its meaning that can produce a genitive, nominative or accusative, you give anna fatḥa, saying: "I called out that you are standing (annaka)," and "I summoned," "I shouted," and "I cried out." That is because you say: "I called Zayd," "I summoned Zayd," "I called out to Zayd (bi-Zaydin)," ("I cried out to Zayd"), so you find these words stand alone with Zayd alone; whereas with "saying" it is not proper to say "I said Zayd (Zaydan)," nor "I said to Zayd (bi-Zaydin)." So quotation (ḥikāya) went through with "saying" and did not go through with calling, because it is satisfied with nouns. Unless a poet is compelled to give inna kasra after calling and the like; then it is permissible for him, as in his saying:
إنى سأبدى لك فيما أُبدِى * لى شَجَنان شَجَنٌ بنجد * وشَجَن لى ببلاد الهند *
(I shall disclose to you, among what I disclose: I have two longings — a longing in Najd, and a longing of mine in the land of India.)
Had inna appeared in this place, the proper way would have been to give it fatḥa. By analogy it takes kasra, because the nominative of the two shajans is evidence of the intention of "saying"; and giving anna fatḥa, had it appeared, would require you to say: "lī shajanayni shajanan bi-Najd."
So when you see "saying" fall on something in meaning, anna has fatḥa. Of that is that you say: "I said to you what I said: that you are unjust (annaka ẓālim)," because mā is in the position of the accusative. Likewise: "I said 'Zayd is righteous' — that he is righteous (annahu)," because your saying (I said Zayd is standing) is in the position of the accusative. Had you wanted inna to be referred back to the word before it, you would give it kasra and say: "I said what I said: your father is standing (inna abāka qāʾim)" — (and it is the [same] word as what precedes it); and if you give it fatḥa, it is something other than it. The saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted ﴿فلينظر الإنسان إلى طعامه أنَّا﴾ and innā — it has been read both ways. Whoever gives fatḥa intends to make anna in the position of the genitive and make it an explanation of the food and its cause, as if He said: to Our pouring the water and Our causing to grow what We caused to grow. Whoever gives kasra intends cutting off the looking from innā, as if He said: Let man look at his food; then He informed by way of a fresh start.

farraa:50-50.t: His words: ﴿فَأَنجَيْنَاكُمْ وَأَغْرَقْنَا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ وَأَنْتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ﴾. It is said: They were too occupied to look, screened by the sea that surrounded them from seeing Pharaoh and his drowning. But in speech it is like your saying: قد ضُرِبتَ وأهلُك يَنْظُرون فما أتَوْك ولا أغاثوك (you were beaten while your family were looking on, yet they did not come to you or help you); he means: they were near, within sight and hearing. Similar to it in the Qur'an: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى رَبِّكَ كَيْفَ مَدَّ الظِّلَّ﴾: there is no seeing here; it is only knowledge. «رأيت» has two senses: seeing of knowledge and seeing of the eye, as when you say: رأيتُ فِرعَوْنَ أعْتَى الخلق وأخْبَثَه (I saw Pharaoh to be the most insolent and wicked of creatures), though you did not see him; it only reached you. In this there is a clear explanation.

farraa:51-51.t: His words: ﴿وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسَىٰ أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾; then He said in another place: ﴿وَوَاعَدْنَا مُوسَى ثَلاَثِينَ ليلةً وأتْمَمْناها بِعَشْرٍ فَتَمَّ مِيقاتُ رَبِّهِ أرْبَعينَ ليلةً﴾. Someone may say: Why did He mention thirty and complete it with ten, when forty can be made up of twenty and twenty, or twenty-five and fifteen? It is answered: That was — and Allah knows best — because thirty was the number of a month, so the thirty were mentioned separately because of the month, namely Dhū al-Qaʿda, and "We completed it with ten" of Dhū al-Ḥijja. So the commentators said. It is for this story that the ten and the thirty were singled out for separate mention.

farraa:53-53.t:
His words: ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ وَٱلْفُرْقَانَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُون﴾. There are two ways in it. One: He meant ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ﴾, i.e. the Torah, and [Translator's note: gave] Muḥammad ﷺ ﴿ٱلْفُرْقَانَ﴾, ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُون﴾. His words ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَابَ﴾ are as though He addressed them, saying: We have given you the knowledge of Moses and Muḥammad, peace be upon them both, "that you may be guided"; because the Torah was revealed all at once and was not revealed in separate parts as the Qur'an was separated. That is one way. The other way: you make the Torah guidance and al-Furqān the like of it, so that it means: We gave Moses guidance as We gave Muḥammad ﷺ guidance. Everything the prophets brought is guidance and light. The Arabs do combine two words that are one in meaning when their wordings differ, as ʿAdī ibn Zayd said:
وقَدَّمَتِ الأَدِيمَ لِراهِشَيْهِ * وأَلْفَى قَوْلَها كذِباً ومَيْنَا
(She set the leather mat beneath his two wrist-veins [Translator's note: for him to be bled], and he found her word to be a lie and a falsehood.)
And their saying: بُعْداً وسُحْقاً (away! and far off!), where البُعد and السُّحق are one. That is another way. Some commentators said: the Book is the Torah, and al-Furqān is the parting of the sea for the Children of Israel. And some of them said: al-Furqān is the lawful and the unlawful that are in the Torah.

farraa:57-57.t: His words: ﴿ٱلْمَنَّ وَٱلسَّلْوَىٰ﴾. It has reached us that al-mann is this substance that falls on the thumām and ʿushar shrubs; it is sweet like honey. One of the commentators used to call it the taranjabīn that we know. And it has reached us that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Truffles are of the mann, and their water is a cure for the eye." As for al-salwā, it was a bird that came down upon them when they grew weary of the mann, resembling these quails (al-sumānā); al-salwā has no singular.

farraa:58-58.t:
His words: ﴿وَقُولُواْ حِطَّةٌ﴾. He says — and Allah knows best —: say what you have been commanded, i.e. "it is ḥiṭṭa (relief [Translator's note: from sins])"; but they turned instead to a phrase in Nabataean, and that is His words: ﴿فَبَدّلَ الَّذيِنَ ظَلَمُوا قَوْلاً غَيْرَ الَّذِى قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾.

It has reached me that Ibn ʿAbbās said: They were commanded to say: "We seek Allah's forgiveness." If that is so, then "حِطّة" ought to be accusative in the reading, because you say: قلتُ لا إله إلا الله (I said "there is no god but Allah"), and someone says: قلتَ كلمةً صالحة (you said a good word). Quotation (ḥikāya) applies only when something that governs the nominative, genitive or accusative could be implied before it; but when you gather all of that and make it a single "word", it is accusative by «القول», as when you say: مررت بزيد (I passed by Zayd), and then make this a "word" and say: قلت كلاما حسنا (I said a fine utterance); then you say: قلتُ زيدٌ قائمٌ (I said "Zayd is standing"), and he says: قلتَ كلاما (you said an utterance). And you say: قد ضربتُ عمرا (I have struck ʿAmr), and he likewise says: قلتَ كلمةً صالحة.

As for the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلاَثَةٌ رَابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ﴾ up to the end of the numbers He mentioned, it is nominative because a pronoun standing for their names precedes it: they will say: they are three — to the end of the verse. His words ﴿وَلاَ تَقُولُولُوا ثَلاَثَةٌ انْتَهُوا خَيْراً لَكُمْ﴾ [Translator's note: «تَقُولُولُوا» so in the text, for «تَقُولُوا»] are nominative, i.e. say: Allah is One, and do not say: the gods are three. His words: ﴿قَالُوا مَعْذِرَةً إِلى رَبِّكُم﴾ have two ways: if you mean "what we said is an excuse to your Lord", you use the nominative, and that is the preferred way; and if you mean "we said what we said as an excuse to Allah", that is a way of the accusative. As for His words: ﴿ويَقُولُونَ طاعَةٌ فإذا بَرَزُوا﴾, the Arabs say it only in the nominative. That is because people are commanded with something they dislike, and one of them says: سمعٌ وطاعةٌ (hearing and obedience), i.e. we entered upon this religion at its outset on the basis that we would hear and obey; so they say: we owe you what we began with; then they go out and act contrary, as He, Mighty and Majestic is He, said: ﴿فإذا بَرَزُوا مِن عِندِك[بيَّتَ طائفةٌ منهم غير الذى تقول]﴾ — [i.e.] when they go out from your presence, they change. Had you meant in similar speech "we will obey", so that obedience is an answer to the command itself, the accusative would be permissible, because every maṣdar (verbal noun) that stands in the place of faʿala and yafʿalu may be accusative, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿مَعَاذَ اللهِ أَنْ نَأخُذَ﴾ [its meaning, and Allah knows best, being: we seek refuge in Allah from taking]. Similar to it in al-Nūr: ﴿قُلْ لاَ تُقْسِمُوا طاعّةٌ مَعْرُوفَةٌ﴾: the nominative is on the sense "let there be from you what the people of hearing and obedience say". As for His words in al-Naḥl: ﴿وَإذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ ْمَاذَا أَنْزَلَ رَبُّكُم قالوا أَساطِيرُ الأَوّلِينَ﴾, this is the saying of the deniers, because they said: He has not sent down anything; this is only the legends of the ancients. As for those who believed, they affirmed it and said: أنزل ربُّنا خيراً (our Lord has sent down good). Had «خير» been nominative, on the sense "what He has sent down is good", it would have been correct; it would then be like His words: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ ماذَا يُنْفِقُونَ قُلِ الْعَفْوَ﴾ and ﴿قُلِ الْعَفْوُ﴾: the accusative is by the verb — "they spend the surplus" — and the nominative is on "what they spend is the surplus of wealth". His words: ﴿قَالُوا سلاماً قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾: as for «السلام» (the first), it is (an utterance that is said), so it is accusative because the verb falls on it, as though you said: قلتُ كلاماً (I said an utterance).

As for His words: ﴿قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾, it came to mean: we are "سَلاَمٌ" (peace), and you are "قَوْمٌ مُنْكَرُونَ" (a people unknown).

Some commentators say: ﴿قَالُوا سَلاَماً قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾ means they greeted him with peace and he returned it to them. Someone may then say: Why was «السلام» not nominative in both or accusative in both? I say: «السلام» has two meanings: when you mean by it an utterance, you put it in the accusative; and when you imply "عليكم" with it, you put it in the nominative. If you wish, you omit the implication from one of the two words and imply it in the other; if you wish, you put both in the nominative; and if you wish, you put both in the accusative. When the Arabs meet and say سلامٌ, [Translator's note: the others say]: سلامٌ, meaning they said "peace be upon you" and the others returned it. The accusative is permissible in one of the two readings: "قَالوا سَلاَماً قَالَ سَلاَماً". Someone of the Banū ʿUqayl recited to me:
فَقُلْنا السَّلامُ فاتَّقَتْ مِنْ أَمِيرِهَا * فَما كَانَ إِلاَّ وَمْؤُهَا بِالْحَواجِبِ
(We said: "Peace!" — and she was wary of her guardian, so there was nothing but a sign she made with her eyebrows.)
He put «السلام» in the nominative because he meant: we greeted her, and she was wary of returning the greeting to us. It is also permissible to put «السلام» in the accusative, as in your saying: قلنا الكلام (we said the utterance) — قلنا السلامَ. Similar to it: قرأت "الحمدَ" and قرأتُ "الحمدُ" (I read al-Ḥamd): when you say قرأت "الحمدَ" you make the verb fall on it; and when you use the nominative you make it a quotation, as in قرأتُ "الحمدُ لله".

farraa:60-60.t:
His words: ﴿ٱضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلْحَجَرَ فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْناً﴾: its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: so he struck, and there gushed forth. By His saying "فَانفَجَرَتْ" it is known that he struck, so the answer sufficed, since it conveys the meaning. Likewise His words: ﴿أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ فَانْفَلَقَ﴾. Similar to it (in ordinary speech) is your saying: أنا الذى أمرتك بالتجارة فاكتسبت الأموال (I am the one who commanded you to trade, and you acquired wealth); the meaning is: so you traded and acquired.

As for His words: ﴿قَدْ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُنَاسٍ مَّشْرَبَهُمْ﴾, someone may say: What need did the people have to know their drinking places, when we see rivers made to flow for people as a favour from Allah and His bounty to His servants, and He did not say of others: "every people knew their drinking place"? That was only — and Allah knows best — because it was a stone from which twelve springs gushed forth, according to the number of the tribes (asbāṭ), a spring for each tribe. When the people set out, or had drunk what sufficed them, the stone returned to what it had been and the springs went away; and when they needed them, the springs gushed forth from those same places, and each tribe came to their own spring from which they used to drink.

farraa:61-61.t:
As for His words: ﴿وَفُومِهَا وَعَدَسِهَا وَبَصَلِهَا﴾, al-fūm, according to what has been mentioned, is an old dialect word, (and it is) wheat; and bread too — both have been mentioned. One of them said: We heard (Arabs of) the people of this dialect say: فَوِّموا لنا (make bread for us), with doubling only, meaning: bake bread. In the reading of ʿAbdallāh it is "وَثُومِهَا" (its garlic), with thāʾ, and that seems the nearer of the two meanings to being correct, because it goes with what resembles it: lentils, onions and the like. The Arabs substitute fāʾ for thāʾ, saying جَدَثٌ and جَدَفٌ (grave), "they fell into an ʿāthūr of evil" and "an ʿāfūr of evil", and الأَثاثىّ and الأَثافىّ (hearth-stones). And I have heard many of the Banū Asad call (المَغافير "المغاثير").

His words: ﴿أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِي هُوَ أَدْنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِي هُوَ خَيْرٌ﴾: i.e. what is nearer, from al-dunuww (nearness); and it is also said: from al-danāʾa (baseness). The Arabs say: إنه لَدنىٌّ [and they do not use the hamza] يُدَنِّى فى الأمور, i.e. he pursues the base and petty side of affairs. Zuhayr al-Furqubī used to pronounce the hamza: "أَتَسْتَبْدِلونَ الّذِى هُوَ أدْنَأ بِالّذِى هو خيرٌ"; but we have not found the Arabs using the hamza in أدنى when it is from baseness, though in that connection they say: إنه لَدَانِئٌ خَبِيثٌ (he is base and vile) [when he is shameless], with the hamza. Someone of the Banū Kilāb recited to me:
باسِلَةُ الوَقْعِ سَرَابِيلُها * بِيضٌ إِلى دانِئِها الظَّاهِرِ
(Fierce in onset, its coats of mail are white, down to its lowly ones in plain view.)
He means the coats of mail, from its elite — meaning the squadron — down to its lowliest; he said "دانئها" meaning the lowliest. We used to hear the elders say: ما كنتَ دانِئاً ولقد دَناتَ (you were not base, yet you have become base), while the Arabs [Translator's note: generally] drop the hamza; and I do not think they transmitted it without having heard it.

His words: ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ مِصْراً﴾ is written with an alif. Names of countries are diptotes, whether light or heavy, whereas names of women, if one of them is light, are declined when they have three letters with the middle one quiescent, such as دَعْد, هِنْد and جُمْل. They are declined when women are named with them only because they recur and are much used as names, so they become light through their frequency, whereas names of countries hardly ever recur. If you wish, you take the alif in "مِصْرَا" as an alif on which one pauses, so that in connected speech you do not give it tanwīn, just as they wrote "سَلاَسِلاً" and "قَوَارِيراً" with alif, and most readers decline to inflect them (tark al-ijrāʾ). And if you wish, you take "مِصْرَ" to be other than the well-known Miṣr (Egypt), meaning: go down to some town (miṣr) among the towns, for what you have asked for is found only in villages and towns. The first way is dearer to me, because in the reading of ʿAbdallāh it is "اهْبِطوا مِصْرَ" without alif, and in the reading of Ubayy: "اهْبِطُوا فَإنّ لَكُمْ ما سَأَلْتُم واسْكُنُوا مِصْرَ"; and confirming that, it is without alif in Sūrat Yūsuf: ﴿ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللّهُ آمِنِينَ﴾.

Al-Aʿmash, when asked about it, said: It is the Miṣr over which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī is [Translator's note: governor].

farraa:63-63.t: His words: ﴿خُذُواْ مَآ آتَيْنَاكُم بِقُوَّةٍ﴾: He says: with earnestness, and by carrying out what has been made obligatory on you in it.

farraa:66-66.t: His words: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا نَكَالاً لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا وَمَوْعِظَةً لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: He means the transformation (al-maskha) into which they were transformed; it was made an exemplary punishment for the sins that had passed and for what would be done after it, so that [Translator's note: others] would fear doing what those who were transformed did, and be transformed [Translator's note: likewise].

farraa:183-183.t: His saying: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ — it may be asked: what was prescribed for those before us, when we see the Christians fasting more than our fasting and in a month other than ours? Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Muḥammad ibn Abān al-Qurashī narrated to me from Abū Umayya al-Ṭanāfisī, from al-Shaʿbī, that he said: "Even if I fasted the whole year, I would break my fast on the day of doubt, of which it is said 'it is of Shaʿbān' and it is said 'it is of Ramaḍān'." That is because the month of Ramaḍān was made obligatory on the Christians as it was made obligatory on us, and they moved it to a [fixed] season. That is because they would sometimes fast it in the intense heat, so they counted it thirty days. Then a generation of them came after them and took the safe course for themselves, fasting a day before the thirty days and a day after; then each later one kept following the practice of the earlier, until it reached fifty. That is His saying ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾.

farraa:184-184.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَّاماً مَّعْدُودَاتٍ﴾ — it is accusative because with every verb whose agent is not named [i.e. passive], when there are two nouns in it, one other than the other, you put one in the nominative and the other in the accusative, as you say "uʿṭiya ʿAbdullāhi l-māla" (ʿAbdullāh was given the wealth); and it does not matter whether the accusative one is definite or indefinite. If the second is a naʿt (adjective) of the first and both are overt, you put both in the nominative, saying "ḍuriba ʿAbdullāhi l-ẓarīfu" (ʿAbdullāh the elegant was struck) — you put it in the nominative because it is ʿAbdullāh. If it is indefinite you put it in the accusative, saying "ḍuriba ʿAbdullāhi rākiban" (riding), "maẓlūman" (wronged), "māshiyan" (walking) and "rākiban".
His saying: ﴿فَعِدَّةٌ مِّنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ — nominative, as I explained to you regarding His saying "فاتباع بالمعروفِ"; had it been accusative, it would have been correct.
His saying: ﴿وَعَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ فِدْيَةٌ﴾ — it is said: upon those who are able to fast but do not fast is to feed a poor person in place of every day on which they break the fast. And it is said: upon those who are able to is the fidya, meaning the ransom (fidāʾ). Then this was abrogated, and He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَأَن تَصُومُواْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾ than feeding.

farraa:185-185.t:
His saying: ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ﴾ — nominative, begun afresh, i.e. and for you is "شهر رمضان" ﴿ٱلَّذِيۤ أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْآنُ﴾. Al-Ḥasan read it in the accusative by way of repetition: "وان تصوموا" the month of Ramaḍān "خير لكم"; and the nominative is better.
It may also be accusative from His saying "كتِب عليكم الصيام" شهرَ رمضان, making the fasting act upon it: that you fast the month of Ramaḍān.
His saying ﴿فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ الشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ﴾ is evidence for the abrogation of feeding. He says: whoever is sound, not sick, or resident, not travelling, let him fast; ﴿وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضاً أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ﴾ makes it up. ﴿يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ﴾ in breaking the fast when travelling, ﴿وَلاَ يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ﴾ — fasting in it.
His saying: ﴿وَلِتُكْمِلُواْ ٱلْعِدَّةَ﴾ — in making up what you broke. This lām in His saying "وَلِتُكْمِلُوا الْعِدَّةَ" is the lām of kay (purpose); had [the wāw] been dropped, it would have been correct. The Arabs put it in their speech with a verb implied after it, and [with the wāw] it is not a condition for the verb before it. Do you not see that you say "I came to you so that you might be good to me", and you do not say "I came to you and so that you might be good to me"? If you say it, you mean: and so that you might be good to me, I came to you. It is frequent in the Qur'an. Of it is His saying ﴿ولِتصغى إليهِ أفئدة الذِين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة﴾, and of it is His saying ﴿وكَذَلِكَ نُرِى إِبْرَاهِيمَ مَلَكُوتَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ ولِيَكُونَ مِنَ الْموُقِنِينَ﴾: had there been no wāw in it, it would be a condition, in the sense of your saying "We showed him the dominion of the heavens so that he might be". When there is the wāw in it, it has a verb implied after it: ﴿ولِيكون مِن الموقنين﴾ We showed him. And of it (other than with) the lām is His saying ﴿إِنّا زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِزِينَةٍ الْكَوَاكِبِ﴾, then He said "وحِفْظاً": had there been no wāw, "الحفظ" would be accusative by "زيّنا". When there is the wāw in it and there is nothing before it to which it can be conjoined, it is evidence that it is accusative by a verb implied after "الحفظ", as in your saying in speech "qad atāka akhūka wa-mukriman laka" (your brother has come to you, and honouring you): you put "mukrim" in the accusative only by implying "atāka" after it.

farraa:186-186.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ — the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "How can our Lord be near, hearing our supplication, when you tell us that between us and Him are seven heavens, the thickness of each heaven a journey of five hundred years, and between each two the like of that?" So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ — I hear what they call. ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِى﴾ — it is said: it is the talbiya (the pilgrim's response "Labbayk").

farraa:187-187.t:
His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ ٱلصِّيَامِ ٱلرَّفَثُ إِلَىٰ نِسَآئِكُمْ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "فلا رُفُوث ولا فسوق"; it is sexual intercourse, according to what they mentioned. You put it in the nominative by "أحل لكم", because you did not name its agent.
His saying: ﴿فَٱلآنَ بَاشِرُوهُنَّ﴾ — He says: upon the concession which was revealed, and which they did not have before that. His saying ﴿وَٱبْتَغُواْ مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ وَكُلُواْ وَٱشْرَبُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ﴾ — it is said: the child; and it is said [read]: "اتبِعوا" with the ʿayn. Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about the two and said: they are the same.
His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ ٱلْخَيْطُ ٱلأَبْيَضُ مِنَ ٱلْخَيْطِ ٱلأَسْوَدِ﴾ — a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Is it the white thread and the black thread?" The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "You are broad of nape [i.e. dull]; it is the night from the day."
His saying: ﴿وَتُدْلُوا بِهَا إِلىَ الْحُكَّامِ﴾ — in the reading of Ubayy: "ولا تأكلوا أموالكم بينكم بِالباطِلِ ولا تدلوا بِها إِلَى الحُكَّامِ". This is like His saying ﴿وَلاَ تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ﴾, meaning: and do not conceal. If you wish, when "لا" is dropped from it, you may make it accusative by ṣarf (diversion), as you say "lā tasriq wa-tataṣaddaqa" (do not steal and [at the same time] give charity), meaning: do not combine this and that. The poet said:
لا تنه عن خُلُقٍ وتأتِىَ مِثله * عارٌ عليك إذا فعلتَ عظِيم
(Do not forbid a trait while doing its like; it is a great shame upon you if you do.)
The jussive is permissible in this verse, i.e. do not do either one of these two.

farraa:189-189.t:
His saying: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلأَهِلَّةِ﴾ — the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the waning and waxing of the moon: what is it? So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: that is for the appointed times of your Ḥajj and your ʿUmra, the falling due of your debts and the ending of your women's waiting periods.
His saying: ﴿وَلَيْسَ ٱلْبِرُّ بِأَن تَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِن ظُهُورِهَا وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ وَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِنْ أَبْوَابِهَا﴾ — that is because among the people of the Jāhiliyya — except Quraysh and those Arabs to whom Quraysh gave birth — a man, when he entered iḥrām outside the months of Ḥajj, in a house of clay or of hair or a tent, would make an opening in his house at its back and go out and come in through it, not going out by the door; and if he was of the people of tents and pavilions, he would go out from its back and come in by it. Once, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in iḥrām, and a man in iḥrām was watching him, he went in through the gate of a walled garden, and that man followed him. He said to him: "Keep away from me." He said: "Why?" He said: "You entered by the gate while in iḥrām." He said: "I am content with your practice and your guidance." The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "I am an Aḥmas." He said: "If you are an Aḥmas, then I am an Aḥmas." So Allah granted the man success, and Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed ﴿وَأْتُواْ ٱلْبُيُوتَ مِنْ أَبْوَابِهَا وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾. [Translator's note: the text has "ألا قريشا", evidently for "إلا قريشا" (except Quraysh). Aḥmas: one of the Ḥums, Quraysh and their kin, who held strict religious observances.]

farraa:191-191.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُقَاتِلُوهُمْ عِنْدَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ حَتَّىٰ يُقَاتِلُوكُمْ فِيهِ فَإِن قَاتَلُوكُمْ فَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ﴾ — this is a way the general body [of Readers] read it. The companions of ʿAbdullāh read: "ولا تَقْتلوهم عِند المسجِد الحرام حتى يَقْتلوكم فيه، فإن قَتَلوكم فاقتلوهم" (do not kill them … until they kill you …), and the meaning here is: if they begin with killing you, then kill them. The Arabs say "Banū so-and-so have been killed" when one of them has been killed.
On this basis is the reading of the companions of ʿAbdullāh; and all is good.
His saying: ﴿فإنِ انْتَهَوْا﴾ — and do not begin against you — ﴿فلا عُدْوَانَ﴾ against those who desisted; aggression is only against whoever did wrong: against whoever began against you and did not desist.
If someone says: "What about His saying ﴿فَلاَ عُدْوَانَ إِلاَّ عَلَى الظَّالمِينَ﴾ — is it aggression, when Allah has made it lawful for them?" we say: it is not aggression in meaning; it is only a word on the pattern of what came before it. Do you not see that He said: ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾? The aggression of the polytheists in wording is injustice in meaning, while the aggression which Allah made lawful and commanded the Muslims with is only retaliation; and retaliation is not injustice, even though its wording is the same. Similar is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَجَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُهُا﴾; it is not from Allah with the same meaning it has from the evildoer, because it is a recompense.

farraa:273-273.t: His saying: ﴿لاَ يَسْأَلُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ إِلْحَافاً﴾ — nor without importunity. Similar to it in speech is your saying: "Seldom have I seen the like of this man," when perhaps you have seen neither few nor many of his likes.

farraa:275-275.t: His saying: ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ ٱلرِّبَا﴾, i.e. in this world, ﴿لاَ يَقُومُونَ﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿إِلاَّ كَمَا يَقُومُ ٱلَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ ٱلشَّيْطَانُ مِنَ ٱلْمَسِّ ﴾. Al-mass is madness; one says: a mamsūs man.

farraa:278-278.t:
His saying: ﴿وَذَرُواْ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَا﴾ — someone may say: What is this usury that has a remainder, when a remainder can only be of something that has passed? That is because Thaqīf used to lend at usury to some people of Quraysh; then they made a settlement that the usury owed to them by Quraysh would not be reduced, while the usury owed by Thaqīf would be remitted from them. When the term fell due for Quraysh and the due was demanded of them, there was sent down to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿يٰأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَذَرُواْ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ ٱلرِّبَا إِن كُنْتُمْ مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾. This is the explanation of the remainder. They were commanded to take the principal sums, but they did not find them readily available, and they refused to remit the usury and defer the principal sums; so Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent down: ﴿وَإنْ كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ فَنَظِرَةٌ إِلىَ مَيْسَرَةٍ وَأَنْ تَصَّدّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾.
﴿وإن كان ذو عُسْرة﴾ of Quraysh, ﴿فنظرة﴾ O Thaqīf, (إلى ميسرة) — and they were needy. Then He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وأن تصدّقوا﴾ with the principal sums ﴿خير لكم﴾.

farraa:281-281.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾ — Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm narrated to us from al-Farrāʾ, who said: Abū Bakr ʿAyyāsh [Translator's note: so in the text; i.e. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh] narrated to me from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The last verse that Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought down was this: ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾; then he said: Put it at the head of the two hundred and eightieth [verse] of al-Baqara.

farraa:282-282.t:
His saying: ﴿إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى﴾ — this command is not an obligation; it is only good conduct and a mercy from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. If one writes, it is good, and if one does not write, there is no harm. It is like His saying ﴿وإذا حللتم فاصطادوا﴾, i.e. hunting has been made permissible to you. Likewise His saying ﴿فإذا قُضِيت الصلاة فانتشروا فى الأرض﴾ — dispersing and seeking are not an obligation after the Friday prayer; it is only a permission.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ كَاتِبٌ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ كَمَا عَلَّمَهُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ — the scribe was commanded not to refuse because of the scarcity of scribes in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
His saying ﴿فَلْيَكْتُبْ وَلْيُمْلِلِ ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾ — He commanded the one who owes the debt to dictate because he is the one against whom witness is borne.
Then He said ﴿فَإن كَانَ ٱلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ سَفِيهاً﴾, meaning ignorant, ﴿أَوْ ضَعِيفاً﴾ — a minor or a woman — ﴿أَوْ لاَ يَسْتَطِيعُ أَن يُمِلَّ هُوَ﴾ — being incapable of dictating — ﴿فَلْيُمْلِلْ وَلِيُّهُ﴾, meaning the owner of the debt. If you wish, you make the hāʾ refer to the one who has charge of the debt, and if you wish, you make it refer to the one from whom it is claimed.
All of that is permissible.
Then He, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ﴾, i.e. then let there be a man and two women; so it is put in the nominative by referring it back to the being [kāna, as its agent]. And if you wish, you say: then it is a man and two women. And [it would be permissible] had both been in the accusative, i.e. if they are not two men, then call to witness a man and two women. Most of what has come in the Quran of this kind is in the nominative, so this ran along with it.
His saying ﴿مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ أَن تَضِلَّ إْحْدَاهُمَا﴾ — with fatḥa on an, and it is also read with kasra. Whoever gives it kasra intends a beginning with it and makes it cut off from what precedes it. Whoever gives it fatḥa, it too is by way of condition, except that he intends there to be a fronting and postponing (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr) in it, so the condition and its apodosis became like a single word. Its meaning — and Allah knows best — is: call two women to witness in place of the man, so that the one who remembers may remind the one who forgets, if she forgets. When the condition was put first, it connected to what preceded it, and its apodosis was referred back to it.
Similar to it in speech is your saying: (It pleases me that the beggar asks and is given): what pleases you is the giving if he asks; neither the asking nor the poverty pleases you. Similar to it: "I secured myself with five camels lest a Muslim fall, so that I carry him" — you secured yourself with them only to carry the one who falls, not so that a Muslim should fall. This is evidence of the fronting and postponing.
Similar to it in the Book of Allah: ﴿ولولا أن تصِيبهم مصيبة بما قدّمت أيديهم فيقولوا ربنا لولا أرسلت إلينا رسولا﴾ — do you not see that the meaning is: were it not that they would say, if a calamity befell them because of what their hands had sent forth: why did You not send us a messenger? This is a clear approach.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يَأْبَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءُ إِذَا مَا دُعُواْ﴾ — to the judge.
﴿إِلاَّ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَارَةً حَاضِرَةً﴾ — it is read in the nominative and the accusative. If you wish, you make ﴿تُدِيرُونَهَا﴾ in the position of the accusative, so that kāna has a nominative and an accusative. And if you wish, you make "tudīrūnahā" in the position of the nominative. That is because it is permissible with indefinites for their verbs [i.e. predicates/attributes] to follow their nouns; for you say: "If there is a righteous one (aḥadun ṣāliḥun), then it is so-and-so," then you drop (aḥad) and say: "If there is a righteous [one] (ṣāliḥun), then it is so-and-so"; it is not specified, so its attribute was fit to be in place of its noun, since both were unknown. That was not fit with the definite, because the definite is specified and known, and its predicate does not agree with its wording or its meaning. If you say: "Then is it permissible to say: kāna akhūka al-qātilu, putting both in the nominative, because the predicate is definite and the noun is definite, so that they are put in the nominative because of agreement when both are definite, just as they were put in the nominative because of agreement with the indefinite?" I say: that is not permissible, because the attribute of a definite is an indication of it when it is identified, while the attribute of an indefinite is connected to it like the ṣila of alladhī. Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī recited to me:
أفاطمَ إنى هالك فتبيَّنى * ولا تجزعى كُلُّ النساء يئيم
ولا أُنَبأنْ بأنَّ وجهك شانَه * خُمُوشٌ وإن كان الحميم الحميم
(O Fāṭima, I am perishing, so be clear about it, and do not grieve — every woman is widowed; and let me not be told that scratches have marred your face, even if the close kinsman is the close kinsman.)
He put both in the nominative. He put the second ḥamīm in the nominative only because it is an intensification of the first; had al-ḥamīm not been in the speech [a second time], he would have put the first in the nominative [all the same]. Similar to it in speech: "We were nothing when you came to be (ḥīna kunta)," meaning when you became and came; so (kāna) is satisfied with the noun.
Among the indefinites put in the nominative is His saying ﴿وَإِنْ كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ﴾; in the reading of ʿAbdullāh and Ubayy: "وإن كان ذا عسرة". Both are permissible; when you use the accusative, you imply a noun in kāna, like the poet's saying:
لله قومى أىُّ قوم لحُرَّة * إذا كان يوما ذا كواكب أشنعا!
(To Allah belong my people — what a people for a free woman, when it is a hideous day with stars [visible at noon]!)
And another said:
أعينَىَّ هلاَّ تبكِيان عِفَاقا * إذا كان طعنا بينهم وعِناقا
(O my eyes, will you not weep for ʿIfāq, when it was spearing among them and grappling?)
They needed to imply a noun in (kāna) with the accusative only because the structure of (kāna) is that it have a nominative and an accusative; they found that (kāna) admits a nominative companion, so they implied it as unspecified.
His saying ﴿فإن كُنَّ نساء فوق اثنتين﴾ — here the nouns have been made overt. Had He said: fa-in kāna nisāʾ, the nominative and the accusative would be permissible. Similar to it ﴿إلا أن تكون تجارة عن تراض منكم﴾, and similar to it ﴿إلا أن يكون ميتة أو دما مسفوحا﴾; whoever says (takūna maytatun) [Translator's note: so in the text], both the nominative and the accusative are permissible in it. I said (takūna) because of the femininity of al-mayta. And His saying ﴿إنها إن تك مثقال حبة من خردل﴾ — if you say: al-mithqāl is masculine, so how did He say (taku)? I say: because al-mithqāl is in construct with al-ḥabba, and the meaning is in it, as though He said: if it be a grain. And the poet said:
على قبضة مرجوّة ظهرُ كفّه * فلا المرء مُسْتَحْىٍ ولا هو طاعم
(The back of his palm [is closed] on a hoped-for handful; the man is neither ashamed nor fed.)
because he took it toward the palm [Translator's note: the verse as quoted has no feminine verb; the relevant feminine agreement is evidently in the original context]. Similar to it is the other's saying:
وتَشْرَق بالقول الذى قد أذعته * كما شرِقت صَدْرُ القناة من الدم
(You will choke on the speech you have spread abroad, as the upper part of the spear chokes with blood.)
and his saying:
أبا عُرْوَ لا تبعَدْ فكلُّ ابن حُرَّة * ستدعوه داعى مَوْتة فيجيب
(O Abū ʿUrwa, may you not perish! Every son of a free woman — the caller of a death will call him and he will answer.)
He made the verb of al-dāʿī feminine although it is masculine, because he took it toward al-mawta. And another said:
قد صرَّح السيرُ عن كُتْمانَ وابتُذِلت * وَقْعُ المحاجِن بالمَهْرِيَّة الذُّقُن
(The journey has laid bare [the way] past Kutmān, and the blows of the crooks on the drooping-lipped Mahrī camels have become commonplace.)
He made the verb of al-waqʿ feminine although it is masculine, because he took it toward al-maḥājin.
His saying ﴿وَلاَ يُضَآرَّ كَاتِبٌ وَلاَ شَهِيدٌ﴾ — i.e. let a scribe not be summoned while he is busy, nor a witness.

farraa:283-283.t:
His saying: ﴿فَرِهَانٌ مَّقْبُوضَةٌ﴾ — Mujāhid read "فرُهُن" as the plural of rihān, just as He said "كلوا من ثُمُره" as the plural of thimār.
His saying: ﴿وَمَن يَكْتُمْهَا فَإِنَّهُ آثِمٌ قَلْبُهُ﴾ — [some permitted (qalbahu) in the accusative]; if it is correct, it is on the pattern of your saying: "You made your judgement foolish (safihta raʾyaka)" and "you made your heart sinful (athimta qalbaka)."

farraa:285-286.t:
His saying: ﴿غُفْرَانَكَ رَبَّنَا﴾ — a maṣdar (verbal noun) that has occurred in the position of a command, so it is put in the accusative. Similar to it: "The prayer, the prayer (al-ṣalāta al-ṣalāta)!" All nouns, maṣdars and others, are put in the accusative when you intend a command. As for nouns, it is your saying: "Allah, Allah (Allāha Allāha), O people!" Had it been put in the nominative on your saying: "It is Allah," so that it is a statement carrying the interpretation of a command, it would be permissible. One of them recited to me:
إن قوما منهم عُمَير وأشبا * ه عمير ومنهم السفّاح
لجديرون بالوفاء إذا قا * ل أخو النجدة السلاح ُالسلاحُ
(A people among whom are ʿUmayr and the likes of ʿUmayr, and among whom is al-Saffāḥ, are worthy of keeping faith when the man of valour says: "Weapons, weapons!")
Similar to it is that you say: "O you people, the night (al-laylu) — so hasten," meaning: this is the night, so hasten. Whoever puts al-layl in the accusative makes an implied verb before it act on it. Had it been said: ghufrānuka rabbanā (nominative), it would be permissible.
His saying ﴿لاَ يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْساً إِلاَّ وُسْعَهَا﴾.
Al-wusʿ is a noun of the same kind of meaning as al-wujd and al-juhd. Whoever says, for the like of al-wujd, al-wajd, and for the like of al-juhd, al-jahd, would say in similar speech: "lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wasʿahā."
Had it been said: wasʿahā, it would be permissible, but we have not heard it.
His saying ﴿رَبَّنَا وَلاَ تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَآ إِصْراً﴾ — al-iṣr is the covenant; likewise He said in Āl ʿImrān ﴿وأخذتم على ذلكم إصرى﴾. Al-iṣr here is the sin — the sin of the compact when they neglect it — as was made severe upon the Children of Israel.
The Readers have read "فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ مِنَ الله" — He says: then know it yourselves.
And some read: fa-ādhinū, i.e. then make known.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: "فإن لم تجدوا كاتبا فرهان مقبوضة" [Translator's note: he read كِتابًا? the text has كاتبا], and he said: a scribe may be found while the sheet and the inkwell are not found.

farraa:196-196.t:
His saying: ﴿وَأَتِمُّواْ ٱلْحَجَّ وَٱلْعُمْرَةَ للَّهِ﴾ — in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "وأَتِمُّوا الْحَجَّ والْعُمْرَةَ إلى البيت لِلّهِ". Had a reader read "والعمرةُ لله", putting "العمرة" in the nominative [it would be possible], because the one performing ʿUmra, when he comes to the House and circles it and [goes] between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa, is released from his ʿUmra; while in the Ḥajj he comes to ʿArafāt and all the rites. That is His saying ﴿وَأَتِمُّواْ ٱلْحَجَّ وَٱلْعُمْرَةَ للَّهِ﴾; He says: complete the ʿUmra up to the House, and the Ḥajj to the furthest of its rites.
﴿فَإنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ﴾ — the Arabs say of one whom fear or illness prevents from reaching the completion of his Ḥajj or ʿUmra, and of everything in which he is not forcibly constrained as with detention and prison, (it is said of the sick man): "qad uḥṣira" (he has been prevented); and in detention and constraint: "qad ḥuṣira" (he has been confined). This is the difference between them. Had you intended, regarding the constraint of the ruler, that it is a preventing cause, without going towards the act of an agent, you could say: "the man uḥṣira".
And had you said of illness and the like, "the illness — or the fear — has confined him (ḥaṣarahu)", you could say "ḥuṣirtum". And His saying "وسَيِّدا وحصورا" — [it is said] he is the one held back from women, because it is a cause [within him] and he is not detained. So build upon this.
His saying: ﴿فَمَا ٱسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ ٱلْهَدْيِ﴾ — "ما" is in the position of the nominative, because most of what has come of its like in the Qur'an is nominative.
Had you used the accusative, [it would be] on [the sense of] your saying: offer "ما استيسر" (what is easy).
The explanation of al-hady (offering) in this place is a camel, a cow or a sheep.
﴿فَمَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ﴾ the offering, fasts three days, the last of them being the day of ʿArafa, and the [other] two days within the ten; as for the seven, he fasts them when he returns, on his way, or if he wishes, when he reaches his family. "السبعة" may take the genitive, following "الثلاثة". If you put it in the accusative, it is permissible by a renewed verb, as you say in speech: "lā budda min liqāʾi akhīka wa-Zaydin" and "wa-Zaydan" (one must meet your brother and Zayd).
His saying: ﴿ذٰلِكَ لِمَن لَّمْ يَكُنْ أَهْلُهُ حَاضِرِي ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾ — He says: that is for whoever is among the strangers, not of the people of Mecca; as for the people of Mecca, that is not upon them. "ذلِك" is in the position of the nominative. "على" is fitting in the place of the lām, i.e. that is upon the strangers.
His saying: ﴿الْحَجُّ أَشْهُرٌ مَعْلُومَاتٌ﴾ — its meaning: the time of the Ḥajj is these months. Even though "فى" (in) is fitting in it, it is said only in the nominative; such is the speech of the Arabs: they say "the cold is two months, the heat is two months", and they do not use the accusative, because it is the measure of the Ḥajj. Similar is His saying: ﴿ولِسُلَيْمَانَ الرِّيحَ غُدُوُّهَا شَهْرٌ وَرَوَاحُهَا شَهْرٌ﴾. Had the months, or the month, been known [i.e. definite] in this sense, the accusative would be fitting in it. The normal way of speech is the nominative, because a noun, when it has the sense of a qualifier or of a place, is strengthened [in the accusative] when annexed to something. Do you not see that the Arabs say "huwa rajulun dūnaka" and "huwa rajulun dūnun" (he is a man inferior [to you])? They use the nominative when they use it alone, and the accusative when they annex it. And of their speech: "the Muslims are a side (jānibun), and the unbelievers are a side"; when they say "the Muslims are jāniba ṣāḥibihim" (at the side of their fellow), they use the accusative. That is because "the fellow" indicates a place, as you say "naḥwa ṣāḥibihim" (towards their fellow) and "qurba ṣāḥibihim" (near their fellow); when "the fellow" is dropped, you do not find it a place that you can tie to nearness to something or distance from it.
The known months are Shawwāl, Dhū l-Qaʿda and ten [days] of Dhū l-Ḥijja. The sacred months are al-Muḥarram, Rajab, Dhū l-Qaʿda and Dhū l-Ḥijja. It was only permissible to call them "months" when they are two months and ten [days] of a third, because the Arabs, when the time is for a thing in which the Ḥajj and the like take place, make it in naming for three and two; as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَاذْكُرُوا اللّهَ فِى أَيَّامٍ مَعْدُودَاتٍ فَمَنْ تَعَجَّلَ فِى يَوْمَيْنِ﴾, while he only hastens in a day and a half; and likewise it is on the third day of the days of Tashrīq, and none of them is complete. Likewise the Arabs say: "It is two days today since I have not seen him", while it is only a day and part of another. This is not permissible outside of [such] times, because the Arabs may do an act in less than an hour and then apply it to the day, the year, the nights and the days; it is said "I visited him this year", "I came to you today", "So-and-so was killed in the nights when al-Ḥajjāj was governor", because neither the beginning nor the end of the time is meant, so it is not taken in the sense of the whole number; only (that time) is meant.
As for His saying ﴿فَلاَ رَفَثَ وَلاَ فُسُوقَ وَلاَ جِدَالَ﴾ — it is said that al-rafath is sexual intercourse, al-fusūq is reviling, and al-jidāl is disputing — ﴿فِى الْحَجِّ﴾: the Readers put all of that in the accusative by the [lā of] exculpation (tabriʾa, i.e. the lā of generic negation), except Mujāhid, who put "الرفث" and "الفسوق" in the nominative and "الجدال" in the accusative. All of that is permissible. Whoever uses the accusative makes the end of the speech follow its beginning; and whoever puts some in the nominative and some in the accusative [does so] because the tabriʾa has two aspects: the nominative with nunation, and the accusative without the nunation. Had "الفسوق" and "الجدال" been put in the accusative with nunation, that would be permissible outside the Qur'an; because the Arabs, when they begin with the tabriʾa and put it in the accusative, do not put it in the accusative with nunation; then when they conjoin to it with "لا", there are two aspects in it: if you wish, you make "لا" suspended (muʿallaqa), [such that] its omission is permissible, and so with this intention you use the accusative with nunation, because "لا" has the sense of a ṣila (filler); and if you intend a fresh start by it, it is like its fellow and not suspended, so you use the accusative without nunation. The poet said about that:
رأت إبلى برمل جَدُودَ أ[نْ] لا * مَقِيلَ لها ولا شِرْباً نَقُوعا
(My camels saw in the sands of Jadūd that there was no midday resting place for them, and no thirst-quenching drink.)
He put nunation on "شرب", intending "لا" to be [as if] omitted; as another said:
فلا أبَ وابنا مِثلَُ مروان وابنِهِ * إذا هو بالمجدِ ارتدى وتأزّرا
(There is no father and son like Marwān and his son, when he dons glory as cloak and wrap.)
In its approach it is like the one addressed in the vocative: you say "yā ʿAmru wa-l-Ṣalta aqbilā" (O ʿAmr and al-Ṣalt, come forward), making "al-Ṣalt" follow ʿAmr while it has the alif and lām, because you intended it to follow him without the intention of "يا" with the alif and lām. If you did intend it, you would say "yā Zaydu wa-yā ayyuhā l-Ṣaltu aqbilā". If you drop "يأيها" while intending it, you use the accusative, as in the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿يَا جِبَالُ أَوِّبِى مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ﴾; "الطير" is accusative in two ways: with the intention of a vocative renewed for it, since calling it with what the mountains were called with was not sound; or, if you wish, you make a verb act upon it: "and We subjected to him the birds", the intention then being upon "We subjected". So in that it is a follower, as in the poet's saying:
ورأيت زوجَكِ فى الوغى * متقلِّدا سيفا ورمحا
(I saw your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear.)
And if you wish, you may put some of the tabriʾa in the nominative and some in the accusative; this is not of the reading of the Readers, but it comes in poems. Umayya said:
فلا لَغْوٌ ولا تأْثِيمَ فِيها * وما فاهوا به لَهُمُ مقيم
(There is no idle talk and no sinful speech in it, and what they utter abides for them.)
And another said:
ذاكم - وجَدِّكم - الصَّغَار بِعينهِ * لا أمَّ لِى إِن كان ذاك ولا أب
(That — by your fortune — is abasement itself; may I have no mother and no father if that should be.)
And before it:
وإِذا تكونُ شدِيدةٌ أُدعَى لها * وإِذا يحاس الحَيْس يدْعى جُنْدب
(When there is a hardship, I am called to it; and when the ḥays [date-and-butter dish] is mixed, Jundab is called.)

farraa:200-200.t:
His saying: ﴿فَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَآءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْراً﴾ — the Arabs, when they performed the Ḥajj in their Jāhiliyya, would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, and each of them would mention his father by his finest deeds: "O Allah, he used to maintain kinship ties and host the guest." So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿فَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَذِكْرِكُمْ آبَآءَكُمْ أَوْ أَشَدَّ ذِكْراً﴾ — for I am the One who did that for you and for them.
His saying: ﴿فَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ رَبَّنَآ آتِنَا فِي ٱلدُّنْيَا﴾ — the people of the Jāhiliyya used to ask for wealth, camels and sheep, so Allah revealed: "of them is one who asks for this world, and he has no خَلاَق in the Hereafter", meaning a share.

farraa:203-203.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ فِيۤ أَيَّامٍ مَّعْدُودَاتٍ﴾ — they are the ten [days]; [and] the known [days] (al-maʿlūmāt) are all the days of Tashrīq: the day of sacrifice and the three days of Tashrīq.
Some of the exegetes make the counted days (al-maʿdūdāt) the days of Tashrīq as well; as for the known days, they make them the day of sacrifice and two of the days of Tashrīq, because the slaughter takes place only on these three days. And some of them make the slaughter [extend] to the last of the days of Tashrīq, so that both "counted" and "known" apply to them, and the ten do not enter into them.
His saying: ﴿لِمَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ﴾ — He says: [whoever guards against] killing game in the Sanctuary. [Translator's note: the text says only "قتل الصيد فى الحرم", "killing game in the Sanctuary"; the bracketed words supply the evident sense.]

farraa:204-204.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيُشْهِدُ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا فِي قَلْبِهِ﴾ — this was a man whose talk pleased the Prophet ﷺ; he would tell him that he was with him and swear to that, saying "(Allah knows)". That is His saying "ويشهِد الله", i.e. he calls Allah to witness. It is also read "ويَشْهَدُ اللّهُ", in the nominative, "على ما فِى قلبِهِ" (and Allah bears witness to what is in his heart). His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ أَلَدُّ ٱلْخِصَامِ﴾ — one says of a man "he is aladd (most contentious)", of a people "ludd", of a woman "laddāʾ", and of women "ludd". The poet said:
اللدُّ أقرانُ الرجالِ اللُدِّ * ثم أُرَدِّى بِهِمُ مَنْ يَرْدِى
(The contentious are the match of contentious men; then with them I bring down whoever would fall.)
And it is said: "You were not aladd, but you have become contentious (ladidta), and you are contentious (taladdu)." When you overcome the man in disputation, (you say: ladadtuhu), so I overcome him (aludduhu) laddan.
The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَيُهْلِكَ الْحَرْثَ وَالنَّسْلَ﴾ — it is accusative. Some of them put "ويهلكُ" in the nominative, not referring it back to "لِيفسِد" but making it referred back to His saying ﴿ومِن الناسِ من يعجِبك قوله...ويهلِك﴾. The first view is better.

farraa:205-205.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ لاَ يُحِبُّ ٱلفَسَادَ﴾ — some of the Arabs say "fasada l-shayʾu fusūdan", like their saying "dhahaba dhuhūban" and "dhahāban", and "kasada kusūdan" and "kasādan".

farraa:208-208.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَتَّبِعُواْ خُطُوَاتِ ٱلشَّيْطَانِ﴾ — i.e. do not follow his traces, for they are disobedience.

farraa:210-210.t: His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلاَّ أَن يَأْتِيَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ مِّنَ ٱلْغَمَامِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ﴾ — nominative, referred back to (الله), blessed and exalted. Some of the people of Medina put it in the genitive, meaning "in canopies of cloud and among the angels". The nominative is better, because in the reading of ʿAbdullāh it is "هل ينظرون إِلا أن يأتيهم الله والملائكة فى ظللٍ من الغمامِ".

farraa:211-211.t:
His saying: ﴿سَلْ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ — it is not pronounced with hamza anywhere in the Qur'an, because had it been with hamza it would be "اسْأَل" with an alif. (Its hamza was dropped) only in the imperative specifically, because it occurs very frequently in speech; for that reason its hamza was dropped, as they said "kul" and "khudh" (eat, take): they did not use the hamza in the imperative, but used it in the prohibition and elsewhere. The Arabs may use the hamza in it; but in the Qur'an it has come without the hamza. Ḥamza al-Zayyāt used to pronounce the hamza in the imperative when the fāʾ or the wāw was in it, as in His saying ﴿واسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الّتِى كُنَّا فِيهَا﴾ and His saying ﴿فاسْأَلِ الّذِينَ يَقْرَءُونَ الْكِتَابَ﴾. I do not like that, because had it been with hamza, the alif would have been written in it, as they wrote it with the alif in His saying ﴿فاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقاً﴾ and ﴿واضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلاً﴾.
His saying: ﴿كَمْ آتَيْنَاهُم﴾ — its meaning: We brought them it [of a sign]. The Arabs say "ataytuka bi-āyatin" (I brought you a sign); when they drop the bāʾ, they say "ātaytuka āyatan", as came in al-Kahf: "آتِنا غداءنا", meaning: bring us our lunch.

farraa:67-67.t:
His words: ﴿أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُواً قَالَ﴾. This [Translator's note: i.e. «قال» without the fāʾ] is frequent in the Qur'an, and that is because it is an answer whose first part can stand without its last by pausing on it. One says: What did he say to you? And the speaker says: He said such-and-such. So it is as though the fact that a pause is good there allows the fāʾ to be dropped. You see it good at the heads of verses, since they are breaks (fuṣūl); for example: ﴿قال فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّها الْمُرْسَلونَ. قَالُوا إنّا أرْسِلْنا﴾. Yet the fāʾ is also good, as in His words: ﴿فَقَالَ الْملأَ الّذِين كَفَروا﴾. If it were within a single utterance, the Arabs would not drop the fāʾ from it; for example: قُمْتُ ففَعَلْت (I stood up and did): they do not say قمت فعلت, nor قلت قال, but rather قُلْتُ فقال (I said, and he said) and قُمْتُ فقام (I stood up, and he stood up), because these are a sequence (nasaq), not a question on which one pauses. Do you not see: "قال" Pharaoh "لِمَنْ حَوْلَه أَلاَ تَسْتَمِعُونَ. قال رَب‍ُّكم ورَبُّ آبائكم الأوّلين", in more places than I can count? Similar to it, apart from the verb, is frequent in the Book of Allah, with the wāw and without the wāw. As for what is with the wāw, it is His words: ﴿قُلْ أؤُنَبِّئُكُم بِخَيْرٍ مِنْ ذَلِكُمْ لِلّذينَ اتَّقَوْا عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾, then after that He said: ﴿الصّابِرينَ والصّادقينَ والْقَانِتينَ والْمُنفِقينَ والْمُسْتَغْفِرِينَ بالأَسْحاِر﴾. And He said in another place: ﴿التّائِبُونَ الْعَابِدُونَ الْحَامِدُونَ﴾ [Translator's note: i.e. without the wāw]. And He said elsewhere: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِيِنَ فَتَنُوا الْمُؤْمِنينَ والْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾, then in the following verse He said: ﴿إِنّ الّذينَ آمَنُوا﴾, and did not say «وإنّ». So learn from what has gone the explanation of what remains, for it comes only according to what I have told you of breaks, or of self-sufficient speech to which an answer comes. Some Arabs recited to me:
لمّا رأيتُ نَبَطاً أنْصَارَا * شَمَّرتُ عن رُكْبَتِىَ الإزَارَا * كُنْتُ لها مِنَ النَّصارى جَارَا *
(When I saw Nabataeans as helpers, I tucked up my waist-wrapper from my knees — I was, for her, a neighbour from among the Christians.) [Translator's note: the last hemistich follows without a conjunction, which is the point of the citation.]

farraa:68-68.t: His words: ﴿لاَّ فَارِضٌ وَلاَ بِكْرٌ عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذٰلِكَ﴾. «العوان» (middle-aged) is not a naʿt (adjective) of «البكر» (young), because she is neither old nor young: the speech ends at His words ﴿وَلاَ بِكْرٌ﴾, then He begins afresh and says: ﴿عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذٰلِكَ﴾. Of العوان one says: قد عوَّنَت (she has become middle-aged). Of الفارض (old): قد فَرَضَت, and some say: قد فَرُضَت. (As for البكر, we have not) heard a verb for it. البِكر has kasra on its first letter when it is a virgin among women, and البَكْر has fatḥa on its first letter, from the young ones (bikāra) of camels. Then He said "بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ", and "بَيْن" (between) is appropriate only with two nouns or more; it was appropriate with "ذلك" alone only because it carries the sense of two. Two actions [Translator's note: or clauses] may be gathered up by "ذلك" and "ذاك": do you not see that you say: أظنُّ زيدا أخاك (I think Zayd is your brother) and كان زيدٌ أخاك (Zayd was your brother) — «كان» must have two things, and «أظن» must have two things — and then you may say: قد كان ذاك (that was so) and أظنُّ ذلك (I think that)? The meaning in the two nouns that «ذلك» gathers up is: between old age and youth. Had one said in ordinary speech: بَيْنَ هاتَيْن or بين تَيْنِك (between these two / those two), meaning the old one and the young one, it would have been correct. And if they were mentioned again (it would appear only in the dual), because they are two nouns, not two actions; with actions [Translator's note: i.e. verbal nouns] you make what follows them singular: you say: إِقْبالُك وإِدْبارُك يَشُقُّ علىّ (your coming and your going is hard on me), but you do not say: أخوك وأبوك يزورُنِى (your brother and your father visits me). Among the things to which "بَيْن" may apply while being singular in form, standing for two or more, are His words: ﴿لاَنُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ﴾; but one may not say: لا نفرق بين رجل منهم (we make no distinction between a man of them), because «أحد» is not put in the dual as «رجل» is put in the dual and plural. If you wish you take «أحد» as meaning two, and if you wish as meaning more; of that kind is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَمَا مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ عَنْهُ حاجِزِينَ﴾. And you say: بَيْنَ أيِّهِم الْمَالُ؟ (among which of them is the wealth?) and بَيْنَ مَنْ قُسِم المالُ؟ (among whom was the wealth divided?): you treat "مَن" and "أَىّ" like «أحد», because they may stand for one and for many.

farraa:69-69.t:
His words: ﴿ٱدْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوْنُهَا﴾. «اللون» is nominative because you did not intend to make "ما" a ṣila (redundant particle) and say: بيّن لنا ما لونَها (make clear to us its colour) — though had a reader read it so, it would have been correct. Rather He meant — and Allah knows best —: pray to your Lord for us to make clear to us what thing its colour is. It was not appropriate for the verb to fall on «أيّ», because the basis of "أىّ" is the gathering together of a dispersed question: the speaker says: بين لنا أسوداءُ هى أم صَفْراء؟ (make clear to us: is it black or yellow?). Since it is not appropriate for «التبيّن» (making clear) to fall on the question in its dispersed form, it does not fall on «أيّ», because «أيّ» is the gathering up of that dispersed question. The same applies to everything like it in the Qur'an: let "ما" and "أىّ" be governed by the verb after them, and do not let the verb before them govern them when it is derived from knowledge, as in your saying: ما أعلم أَيُّهم قال ذاك (I do not know which of them said that), لا أعلمنّ أَيُّهم قال ذاك, and ما أدرِى أَيَّهم ضربت (I do not know which of them you struck). In knowing, informing, telling and the like, it is as I have described to you. Of this kind is the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَاهِيَهْ﴾ and ﴿وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ ما يَوْمُ الدَّينِ﴾: the second "ما" is nominative, made nominative by «يوم», as in your saying: ما أدراك أىُّ شئ يومُ الدّين (what will make you know what thing the Day of Judgement is?). Likewise the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ أَىُّ الْحِزْبَيْنِ أَحْصَى﴾: you made it nominative by «أحصى». And when the verb [Translator's note: after it] falls on «أيّ», you say: ما أدرى أَيَّهم ضربت. You refrained from letting the preceding verb of knowledge and the like fall on «أيّ» only because you find that the verb does not fall on «أيّ» in meaning. Do you not see that when you say: اذْهَبْ فاعلم أيُّهما قام (go and find out which of the two stood), you ask someone other than the two about their state, so you find the verb falling on the one who informs you — just as you say: سل أيُّهُمْ قام (ask which of them stood), meaning: ask people which of them stood? If you let the verb fall on "أىّ" and said: اسأل أيَّهُمْ قام, you would be as if implying «أيّ» a second time; because you say: سل زيدا أيُّهُمْ قام (ask Zayd which of them stood): when you let the verb fall on Zayd, "أىّ" comes after it. So likewise, when you let the verb fall on "أىّ", it leaves the meaning of the question; and that, if you intend it, is permissible: you say: لأضْرِبَنَّ أيَّهُم يقول ذاك (I will surely strike whichever of them says that), because striking does not fall on [a noun after which a question then comes; and that is because striking does not fall on] two [Translator's note: objects]. In asking you say: سل عبدالله عن كذا (ask ʿAbdallāh about such-and-such), as though you said: سله عن كذا (ask him about such-and-such); but one may not say ضربت عبدالله كذا وكذا (I struck ʿAbdallāh such-and-such), unless you mean a description of the striking; as for nouns, no.

The word of Allah: ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعةٍ أيُّهُم أشَدُّ على الرّحْمَنِ عِتيّاً﴾: whoever puts «أيّ» in the accusative lets «النزع» (plucking out) fall on it, and it is not a question; as though He said: then We shall surely pull out the insolent one who is the most severe. There are two ways of the nominative in it. One is that you make the verb content with «من» as what it falls on, as you say: قد قتلنا من كل قوم (we have killed some of every people) and أصبنا من كل طعام (we have had some of every food); then you begin «أيّ» afresh and make it nominative by what follows it, as He, Majestic and Mighty is He, said: ﴿يَبْتَغُونَ إلى رَبِّهِمُ الْوَسِيلَةَ أيُّهُمْ أَقْرَبُ﴾, i.e. they look to see which of them is nearest. Similar to it: ﴿يُلْقُونَ أقْلاَمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ﴾. As for the other way: in His words ﴿ثم لَنَنْزِعَنّ مِنْ كلِّ شِيعَةٍ﴾ [Translator's note: the meaning is] We shall pull out from those who formed factions (tashāyaʿū) over this, looking, in their factionalism, to see which of them is fiercest and most wicked, and which of them is most severe in insolence against the Most Merciful; «الشيعة» and «يتشايعون» are the same in meaning. There is a third way of the nominative: that you take ﴿ثُمّ لَننْزِعَنَّ مِنْ كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ﴾ as [Translator's note: pulling out] by calling, i.e. We shall surely call out: ﴿أيُّهُمْ أشدُّ على الرّحْمَنِ عِتيّاً﴾ — but this is not the way they intend. Similar to it, by which you can recognise it, are His words: ﴿أفَلَمْ يَيْأَسِ الَّذِيِنَ آمنَوُا أَنْ لَوْ يَشَاءُ اللَّهُ لهَدَى النَّاس جَميعاً﴾: some commentators said ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَيْأَسِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ means: did they not know? And the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: have they not despaired, knowing that had Allah willed He would have guided all people? Likewise "لَنَنْزِعَنّ": he says it means We shall pull them out by calling.

farraa:71-71.t: His words: ﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ لاَّ شِيَةَ فِيهَا﴾, without hamza. He says: there is no colour in her other than yellow. Some of them said: she is yellow, even her hooves and her horns are yellow.

farraa:72-72.t: His words: ﴿وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْساً فَٱدَّارَأْتُمْ فِيهَا﴾, and His words: ﴿وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسَى أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ and ﴿وَإِذْ فَرَقْنَا بِكُمُ الْبَحْرَ﴾. Someone may say: Where is the answer of "إذ", and to what is it conjoined? There are many like it in the Qur'an with the wāw and with no overt answer. The meaning — and Allah knows best — rests on implying "واذكروا إذ أنتم" (and remember when you were) or "إذ كنتم"; His saying "اذكروا" at the beginning of the speech sufficed, and then "إذ" came with the wāw, referring back to that.
